name: Slow Zoom In
definition: A slow zoom in is slow zoom in cinematography that tightens the frame by increasing focal length while the camera body stays locked. Perspective relations stay fixed: the world does not slide, it only enlarges as the lens compresses space.
narrative: The shot is a thought that closes without walking. Geography stays put, so the audience feels watched or analyzed rather than approached.
Faces grow, walls stay in the same relation, and the pressure is optical. Use it when attention must narrow and the room must not rearrange itself.
It is the wrong tool when you need to enter a mind by occupying the same air: that job belongs to a physical approach, because a zoom never changes the camera's station point.
how_it_works:
Lock a heavy tripod. Keep height, tilt, and nodal point still.
Drive focal length smoothly over several seconds and rehearse focus compensation as depth of field shallows. Compression increases: distant planes look closer to the subject even though nobody moved.
Prompt a locked camera body, a gradual optical zoom in, rising compression, and an explicit ban on dolly parallax.
when_to_use:
Use it to raise pressure on a still figure while the architecture stays legally the same. Concrete beat: a surveillance long-lens slowly isolating one person in a crowd.
Do not use it if foreground objects must peel and prove the camera walked.
compared_names: Push InA thought lands. Do not rush it.
Dolly InEnter a mind, a room, or a threat. Geography changes because the camera walks.
Crash Zoom InPunctuate a hit, a realization, or a comic sting.
compared_text: A Dolly In translates the whole camera, so foreground and background change speed. A Push In is a physical or virtual walk whose job is a realization landing.
A Crash Zoom In uses the same optical mechanism at sting speed. Stay on slow zoom in when the station point must not move.

prompt_example: From a distant fixed window, slowly zoom into a solitary woman waiting at the center of a city square. Eight seconds, no camera translation, no foreground parallax, patient observational mood. She never acknowledges the camera.
prompt_note: Smooth optical zoom only.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a Dolly In or a digital crop sold as a zoom. The tell is parallax: if a foreground chair slides against the wall, you translated.
The fix is a locked head, a true focal-length change, and a hold on the final tight frame.
faq: What is Slow Zoom In in film?
It is a gradual increase of focal length with the camera support still. The image tightens and space compresses, but the camera does not occupy a new position.
Slow Zoom In vs Dolly In
Dolly in walks the camera so perspective and parallax change. Slow zoom in only walks the lens: size grows, relative geometry of planes stays the same.
When should I use Slow Zoom In?
When you want pressure, scrutiny, or a slow isolation and you need the room to remain the same place. Skip it if the beat is actually entering the space.

name: Slow Zoom Out
definition: A slow zoom out widens the frame by decreasing focal length while the support stays put. More architecture and negative space enter the picture, yet the camera never travels, so true parallax does not appear.
narrative: The joke, the trap, or the social system was already around the person. The lens simply admits it.

Because the station point is unchanged, the reveal feels observational: we were always this far away, we only chose to see more. It is the wrong tool when the camera must retreat through a doorway, lose a foreground, or leave someone behind in real space.
Optical widening cannot walk out of a room.
how_it_works:
Lock the tripod and reverse the zoom. Start on a composed tight frame and pre-compose the wide end so heads, signs, and negative space land.
Focus will deepen as focal length shortens. Prompt a tripod-locked optical zoom out, no camera body travel, and name what architecture must appear by the last frame.
when_to_use:
Use it to reveal context, isolation, or an off-screen joke that was already in the location. Concrete beat: a tight face opening onto a dinner table that has been watching.
Do not use it to exit a location: that is a physical pull.

Dolly OutLeave someone behind, or show how small they are in the system.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
compared_text: A Pull Out and a Dolly Out move the camera backward, so foreground objects leave the frame with parallax. A slow zoom out only changes the lens angle of view.
If you also need a Slow Zoom In cousin in the same scene, keep both bodies locked so the pair stays optical.

name: Crash Zoom In
definition: A crash zoom is a rapid focal-length snap from a wider frame into a detail, usually without moving the camera. The punch is optical and conspicuous: size changes faster than a body can walk.
narrative: The shot punctuates a hit, a name, a weapon, or a comic sting. Artificiality is the point.
The audience is not invited to approach; they are struck by a lens. It is the wrong tool for a thought that should land over several seconds, and the wrong tool for geography.
After the snap, hold. If you keep zooming or add shake, the sting becomes noise.
how_it_works:
Keep the subject on the zoom center. Use a controlled fast zoom or, in post, a high-resolution crop that still behaves like optics, not a warp.
Expect radial motion blur during the snap, then a hard hold on the tight frame. Avoid autofocus hunting.
Prompt an aggressive optical punch-in under one second, zoom blur, then a locked tight hold, and ban a physical dolly.
when_to_use:
Use it to punctuate a hit, a realization, or a comic sting. Concrete beat: a name is spoken and the face slams into close-up.
Do not use it as a substitute for walking closer through a room.

A Whip Pan blurs by rotating the head, not by changing focal length. Crash zoom in is a snap of the lens, then a hold.

name: Dolly In
definition: A dolly in shot moves the entire camera through space on a wheeled or tracked support, advancing toward the subject at a measured pace. The nodal point walks, so foreground and background shift in parallax as the surroundings are progressively excluded.
narrative: The camera enters a mind, a room, or a threat by occupying new air. Unlike a cut, the audience experiences the change of attention continuously.

A small travel can make a thought feel consequential because space itself has agreed to close. It is the wrong tool when you want optical compression without new geography, or when the beat is only a sting.
If the track is longer than the thought, the move tours.
how_it_works:
Lay track or roll a wheeled dolly on a known axis. Fix focal length, usually a moderate spherical such as 40mm.
Keep eye height constant unless the story changes rank. Tie the arrival at close-up to a change in the actor's thought.
Foreground objects will slide. Prompt a physical dolly in on track, camera body gliding forward, parallax shifting, no optical zoom.
when_to_use:
Use it to enter a mind, a room, or a threat, because geography changes when the camera walks. Concrete beat: a medium two-shot that arrives on a lie forming in one face.
Do not use a digital zoom and call it a dolly.

Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
Tracking ShotAccompany a walker. The shot is a journey, not a picture.

Tracking Shot matches a mover instead of closing on a still thought.

name: Dutch Roll
definition: A Dutch roll rotates the camera around the lens axis over time, so a level horizon becomes a canted one. Unease arrives as a move, not as a frozen Dutch still.
narrative: The world itself tilts while we watch. Rank, gravity, and architecture go off their contract in duration rather than in a single locked cant.

You can stop on a Dutch angle, but the technique is the roll that got you there. It is the wrong tool when the floor is already the story (a listing ship), and the wrong tool if you needed a full continuous spin until up is gone.
A slow roll into a cant is not a revolving corridor.
how_it_works:
Rotate around the optical axis (roll), usually from a locked nodal point. Keep pan and tilt still unless you combine on purpose.
End on a readable Dutch or return to level when the character finds the floor. Prompt a slow roll on the lens axis, horizon rotating from level into a Dutch angle.
when_to_use:
Use it for unease that arrives in time, not as a still cant. Concrete beat: a level street, then the horizon slowly dies as a fever starts.
Do not start already tilted if the arrival is the point.
compared_names: Dutch AngleThe world is off its axis. Do not use as decoration.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
compared_text: A Dutch Angle is a still cant. A Camera Roll continues until gravity is optional, or uses a rotating set.
Dutch roll is the timed transition on the roll axis into (or out of) a Dutch. Do not confuse it with terrain incline.
Dutch AngleThe world is off its axis. Do not use as decoration.
Camera RollGravity is optional.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
in_film: The Third Man is the still-cant grammar this move can arrive at: Vienna off its axis. Do the Right Thing lets living camera attitude, including roll and cant, sit in a hot street.
Use the moving horizon, not a postcard of a tilted doorway.
prompt_template: Slow roll of the camera on its lens axis around [Subject], horizon rotating from level into a Dutch angle, the world itself tilting. For motion: the camera slowly rolls, tilting the horizon around [Subject] into a Dutch angle.
prompt_example: The camera slowly rolls, tilting the horizon around [Subject] into a Dutch angle.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a locked Dutch Angle or a full Camera Roll. The tell is a still tilt from frame one, or a continuous spin past 45 degrees with no stop.
The fix: start level, roll on axis over time, end on a chosen cant.
faq: What is Dutch Roll in film?
It is a camera roll around the lens axis over time, turning a level horizon into a Dutch angle (or the reverse) as a move.
Dutch Roll vs Dutch Angle
A Dutch angle is a still canted frame. Dutch roll is the motion that creates or releases that cant.
When should I use Dutch Roll?
When unease should arrive in duration. Do not use it if you only needed a locked cant, or a full gravity-free spin.
How do I prompt Dutch Roll for AI image or video?

Write camera slowly rolls on its lens axis, horizon from level into a Dutch angle around [Subject]. No pan, no full 360 roll unless you change technique.

name: Camera Roll
definition: A camera roll rotates the frame around the lens axis as if the world has lost its up, either by rolling the camera or by rotating a room around a weighted body. Gravity becomes optional, which is stronger than a small Dutch cant.
narrative: A familiar corridor can become an unstable physical system. The effect is strongest when bodies retain weight and surfaces remain solid: people walk on walls because the set or the camera has rewritten up.
It is the wrong tool for a 15-degree unease, and the wrong tool if you only tilted the image in post with no sense of mass. A tilted still is not a room physically rotating.
how_it_works:
Either roll the camera continuously around the optical axis, or build a rotating set and keep the camera's relationship designed. Practical work needs engineered sets, restrained objects, and stunt coordination.
Prompt a full camera roll, the frame rotating as if the world has lost its up, or a rotating corridor with weighted bodies.
when_to_use:
Use it when gravity is optional. Concrete beat: a fight in a hotel corridor whose floor becomes a wall.
Do not roll a quiet dialogue that only needed a Dutch.
compared_names: Dutch RollUnease that arrives in time, not as a still cant.

An 360-Degree Orbit circles a subject in yaw, changing azimuth, not rolling the horizon around the lens. Camera roll is about up and down swapping, not about walking around someone.

name: Double Dolly
definition: A double dolly shot moves performer and camera together on one rolling platform so their relative arrangement stays fixed. The actor appears to glide rather than walk: feet skating, weight transfer absent.
narrative: An interior state made external. Fate, dread, or transcendence carries the person through a hallway while the world slides.

It differs from a stabilized walk because normal stepping is missing on purpose. It is the wrong tool if the performer walks normally, and the wrong tool if only the camera dollies toward a planted actor.
Both must share the ride.
how_it_works:
Conceal a platform (or a virtual equivalent) that carries actor and camera. Coordinate speed so background parallax is the only travel.
For generation, keep the feet still and the body upright while the environment passes. Prompt a double dolly: subject and camera share one rolling platform, figure gliding, feet skating.
when_to_use:
Use it when an interior state should be made external: the person is carried by an idea. Concrete beat: an armed figure glides down a hallway, feet not walking.
Do not use it as a fancy walk-and-talk.
compared_names: Dolly InEnter a mind, a room, or a threat. Geography changes because the camera walks.
SteadicamLong connecting moves through architecture. Neither handheld nor dolly.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
compared_text: A Dolly In moves only the camera. Steadicam lets both walk, with normal gait.
Double dolly freezes the relationship and removes the walk. If the feet cycle, the float is gone.

name: SnorriCam
definition: A SnorriCam fixes the camera to the performer's body so the body remains stable relative to frame while the world moves. A rig points back at the wearer: the face stays pinned, the environment pitches around it.
narrative: Trap the audience in a body that cannot get out. Panic, intoxication, or dissociation becomes spatial because the person is locked to the image and the street will not sit still.
It is the wrong tool for a first-person view of what they see. A SnorriCam faces the wearer.
It is not a body-cam showing the world, and it is not a follow from behind.
how_it_works:
Use a safely fitted lightweight body rig, or reproduce the relative motion in a virtual scene. Preserve tiny bodily movements without letting the face float independently of the torso.
Prompt a SnorriCam body-mounted on the subject, camera locked to the torso, face pinned, world sloshing behind.
when_to_use:
Use it to trap the audience in a body that cannot get out. Concrete beat: a panicked walk down a sidewalk, pupils steady in frame, storefronts shearing.
Do not use it as POV of the sidewalk.
compared_names: Point of ViewForce identification. The audience is the character.
HandheldUrgency, documentary truth, or a mind that cannot sit still.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
compared_text: Point of View shows what they look at, from beside or as them. Handheld is an operator nearby, not bolted to the chest.
Locked-On glues the camera to a subject that may not be the wearer, often from outside a vehicle or a fall. SnorriCam is body-mounted and facing the actor.

name: Locked-On
definition: A locked-on shot keeps one object or face glued in frame while the world streams past, as if the camera were bolted to a vehicle, a fall, or a spinning set. The subject is the only stable point.
narrative: One thing is the only law in a moving world. A steering wheel, a spinning astronaut, a driver's eyes: everything else is weather.

The constraint is rigidity to the subject, not a vest walking nearby. It is the wrong tool when you wanted a body-mounted face rig, and the wrong tool when a normal track should keep a walking distance.
Bolted is not following.
how_it_works:
Mount to the subject, the vehicle, or match-move as if bolted. Distance and angle to the chosen object stay nearly constant; background parallax and rotation can be extreme.
Prompt a locked-on move, camera glued to one object or face, environment streaming past, as if bolted to a vehicle or a falling body.
when_to_use:
Use it when one thing is the only stable point in a moving world. Concrete beat: a close steering wheel and dash while the city smears the windows.
Do not use it for a sidewalk follow.

The job is coverage of conversation in motion, not a silent hunt. It is the wrong tool for a chase with no words, and the wrong tool for a seated interrogation.
If nobody is walking while talking, it is just a track.
how_it_works:
Steadicam or gimbal, often leading, sometimes flanking. Hold a moving medium, shoulder height, leave headroom for doorways.
Recorders and extras must be blocked as part of the path. Prompt walk-and-talk tracking, camera leading or flanking at medium, architecture flowing, corridor energy.

name: Hyperlapse
definition: A hyperlapse combines time-lapse with significant camera movement through space. Time is compressed while the camera advances in steps that assemble into a glide, so crowds and weather race along a real path.
narrative: Duration becomes velocity. A walk that would take an afternoon becomes a few seconds, but unlike a locked time-lapse the station point travels: streets are traversed, not merely watched from one roof.
It is the wrong tool for real-time tracking, and the wrong tool for a tripod time-lapse of clouds over a still city. If the camera did not move between frames, it is not a hyperlapse.
how_it_works:
Shoot discrete frames along a surveyed path (or simulate that in 3D), then play them at time-lapse rates. Align each frame so the move reads as a glide.
Crowds, traffic, and shadows should race. Prompt a hyperlapse toward or around the subject, time compressed, crowds and weather racing, camera advancing in steps that become a glide.
when_to_use:
Use it to show duration as velocity along a path. Concrete beat: approaching a monument while hours of foot traffic smear.
Do not hyperlapse a 6-second real-time conversation.
compared_names: Time-LapseShow weather, construction, or a night becoming morning.
Tracking ShotAccompany a walker. The shot is a journey, not a picture.
Slow Zoom InUse to raise pressure without changing geography. The world stays put; attention closes.
compared_text: Time-Lapse is often a locked or slowly panned interval. Tracking Shot is real-time travel.
Hyperlapse is both: interval shooting plus significant displacement. A Slider Shot interval on 100 centimeters is a tiny cousin, not a city traverse.

name: Slider Shot
definition: A slider shot is a short, precise linear move on a compact rail, often 60 to 120 centimeters. It adds parallax to an interview, product, or lock-off without a full dolly track.
narrative: A full dolly is too much. A few centimeters of travel can prove the room has depth: a microphone in the foreground slides against a face, a bottle turns against a window.
The move is small on purpose. It is the wrong tool for a city block, and the wrong tool if you needed a curve around a product.
If the rail is meters long, you are dollying. If the path is a circle, you are orbiting.
how_it_works:
Clamp a short rail, level it, choose a constant speed. Keep the move lateral or a tiny push; do not hide a zoom inside it.
Prompt a short slider move, 60 to 120 centimeters of lateral travel, product or interview parallax, precise and small.
when_to_use:
Use it when a full dolly is too much and a lock-off needs a little parallax. Concrete beat: an interview single with a lamp sliding in the foreground over 6 seconds.

name: Lazy Susan
definition: A lazy susan shot rotates the subject on a motorized turntable while the camera stays put, or the camera circles at a fixed product-hero radius. Distance holds, so scale does not change, and the far wall barely shears if the disc is what turns.
narrative: Use it to inspect. A coat, a bottle, a weapon, a figure treated as merchandise: every azimuth is offered without a cut.
Light should stay consistent so the object, not the room, is what changes. It is the wrong tool when geography matters.
If walls, extras, and lamps must slide to prove a living space, you want an orbit. A conversation, a chase, a blocked room: those need the camera to travel.
how_it_works:
The classic rig is a motorized disc under the subject; the camera is locked on sticks at eye or product height, often 50 to 85mm so the silhouette stays clean. Alternate: a circular slider at constant radius with the subject locked.
Either way, nodal distance is constant. Prompt a slow turntable rotation or a camera circling at product-hero distance, one revolution or a 90-degree reveal, no zoom.
when_to_use: Show an object or costume from every side: a dress on a dummy, a car on a cyc, a relic on glass. Do not use it for a talk; faces in dialogue do not need a spin.

name: Establishing Shot
definition: An establishing shot introduces or re-establishes location, geography, time of day, or social context. It is a job in the sequence, not a synonym for wide or extreme long shot.

name: Master Shot
definition: A master shot covers the complete dramatic action and the spatial geography of a scene in one setup. It is the skeleton you can play in full, then cut into.
narrative: A master protects the scene. If every close-up dies, you still have who sat where, who could reach the door, and how the argument moved through the room.

It is also the wrong tool as a lifeless wide you never intend to use, parked for safety while all the acting happens in mismatched singles. A moving master can carry the whole beat if blocking and camera path are designed together.

Set a camera that sees all essential blocking: seats, door, table, the path out. Size is often a Wide Shot or a loose Two-Shot, but the job is coverage of the action, not a particular crop.

A three-shot frames three principal people in one composition so their alliances, blocking, and who is left out are readable. It is not three close-ups in a row.
Three-Shot vs Two-Shot
A two-shot is a pair and the space between them. A three-shot adds a third principal and a triangle of politics. If the third person is only an out-of-focus extra, you still have a two-shot.
When should I use Three-Shot?
Use it when the scene's power is three-way: alliances, a hinge, an odd one out. Do not use it for a pair, and do not use it as a stand-in for a larger ensemble.

name: Group Shot
definition: A group shot frames a small ensemble as a relational unit, such as a family, a crew, or a jury. Position, height, and light say who belongs and who dominates.
narrative: A group shot is not a crowd still. It is a unit: people who share a table, a job, a crime, a bloodline.

The audience should be able to rank them at a glance: who sits, who stands, who is brightest, who is at the edge. It is the wrong tool when the politics are only two or three principals, or when you needed a master of action rather than a portrait of the unit.
Lighting everyone the same makes a yearbook. Let one face own the key, or let depth split generations.
how_it_works:
Stage in layers: seated foreground, standing mid, a doorway back. Who is highest, central, nearest, brightest.
A slightly wider lens (35mm to 50mm) holds the unit without turning them into ants; go longer if you want compression to stack them. Prompt: Group shot containing [Subject] among several figures, ensemble blocking, who owns the frame by position and light.
when_to_use: Use it for a family, a crew, a jury: the unit as the subject. Do not light every face equally if someone owns the room, and do not use a group shot when the beat has become a two-person fight.
compared_names: Master ShotProtect the scene. You can always go tighter.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: A Three-Shot is specifically three principals. A Master Shot covers the complete action; a group shot may be that master, or it may be a posed unit inside a larger scene.

Grammar: the unit, ranked.

A group shot frames a small ensemble as one relational unit so belonging and dominance read through blocking and light. It is more than a trio, still small enough that people remain individuals.
Group Shot vs Three-Shot

name: Insert Shot
definition: An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail: an object, a hand action, a screen, or text. It points at the thing that will matter, at real scale.
narrative: An insert is not a pretty prop break. It is a fact the wider coverage cannot prove: the handwriting, the latch, the cup of water beginning to tremble, the key in a palm.
Hands should be human-sized. The object should cut with the same key as the scene.
It is the wrong tool when you are leaving the action for a clock on the wall or a listener in another room: that is a cutaway. It is also the wrong tool as a glowing product hero.
If the object's specific mechanism never pays off, you may only have a MacGuffin in the plot, but the insert still has to be a readable picture of a thing.
how_it_works:
Size to the object. Match the scene's key side and color so the cut belongs.
Macro only if the detail is small; a letter can be a close crop on a 50mm. Keep hands at real scale, no giant fingers.
Prompt: Tight close-up of an object that carries the plot near [Subject]: a glass, a letter, a latch. Hands at real scale.
No glowing skin.
when_to_use: Use it to point at the thing that will matter later: a key, a letter, a latch, a trembling glass. Do not insert a decorative object that never returns, and do not light it like a catalog hero if it lives in a messy room.
compared_names: CutawayHide a cut, show a clock, or let the room comment.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

compared_text: A Cutaway leaves the primary action for context, a clock, or an observer. An Extreme Close-Up is a size; an insert is a job and may be that tight.
A cut-in tightens on something already proven in the wider shot, often on the same axis. A Gesture covers a body movement rather than an object.
Product lighting treats the object as a commercial portrait, which is a different job.

faq: What is Insert Shot in film?
An insert shot is a close view of a story-relevant detail, object, hand action, screen, or text. It is coverage of a plot fact, usually cut into a wider scene, with hands and objects at real scale.
Insert Shot vs Cutaway

An insert stays on a detail that belongs to the primary action: the letter in the hands, the latch, the glass. A cutaway leaves that action for a related piece of the world, such as a clock, a street, or a listener. If you have left the actor's beat, you are probably in a cutaway.
When should I use Insert Shot?
Use it when a detail will matter and the wide cannot prove it. Do not use it as decoration, and do not use it when you meant to leave the scene for context.

name: Cutaway
definition: A cutaway shot leaves the primary action for a related detail, observer, or part of the same world. It is used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair.
narrative: A cutaway is a brief exit: a clock, a kettle, a street, a person listening in a doorway. Its value is the relation it adds, not merely that it hides a bad join.
It can build anticipation, let the room comment, or imply that time has passed. It is the wrong tool when the object is the plot in the actor's hands: that is an insert.
It is also the wrong tool if the return to the main action restarts a gesture that should have continued. Check temporal logic.
A cutaway can be a pressure release; it can also cheat geography if the new view could not exist at that moment.
how_it_works:
Choose a detail that can plausibly be present now. Match ambient light and, in editorial thinking, room sound.
Return to the main action at a later phase of the motion, not at the same frame of a handshake. Prompt: Cutaway from [Subject] to a related detail in the same world, a pressure-release or information beat that is not an insert on the actor.
when_to_use: Use it to hide a cut, show a clock, or let the room comment: a kettle trembling during an argument, a courtyard while someone looks. Do not cut away to a new geography that implies false time, and do not call an object-in-hand a cutaway.

compared_text: An Insert Shot stays on a plot object inside the action. A Reaction Shot is a person's response, often a face; a cutaway might be that listener, or it might be a non-human detail.
A cut-in goes tighter on something already in the master, same space and often same axis, without leaving the beat. Cutaway means you left.

faq: What is Cutaway in film?
A cutaway is a shot away from the primary action, used for context, reaction, compression, or continuity repair. It might be a clock, a street, an observer, or a piece of the room.
Cutaway vs Insert Shot

An insert is a close view of a story object or hand fact inside the action. A cutaway leaves that action for a related view. Hands on the plot letter are an insert; the kettle on the stove during the fight is a cutaway.
When should I use Cutaway?
Use it to add a relation, hide a join, compress time, or let the world comment. Do not use it to show the object in the actor's hands, and do not return in a way that rewinds the action.

name: Reaction Shot
definition: A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. The important action is watching; the face (or body) is the cut.
narrative: A reaction shot is coverage of receiving. The gunshot, the insult, the courtyard window: we often learn what it meant by looking at the person who saw it.
Meaning can be constructed between shots. A relatively still face reads differently depending on what came before, which is the Kuleshov lesson, not a demand that you fake a historical clip.

It is the wrong tool when the speaker's line still needs to be seen, or when you over-act the response so the audience is told the emotion. It is a function, not a size: often a close-up, sometimes an MCU, occasionally a full-body flinch.
how_it_works:
Point the eyeline at the stimulus, even if that stimulus is offscreen. Hold.
Minimize explanatory mugging if you want the cut to do the work. Match Look Space and eyeline to the previous shot.
Size is usually Close-Up or Medium Close-Up. Prompt: Reaction close-up of [Subject] receiving news they cannot speak yet, the face as the cut.
when_to_use: Use it when the important action is watching: the face after an offscreen shot, the listener who cannot speak yet. Do not use it as a blink after every clause, and do not perform the entire emotion so the juxtaposition has nothing to do.
compared_names: Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.

compared_text: A Close-Up is a size; a reaction is why that size is here. Over-the-shoulder coverage still includes the partner as a shoulder; a reaction single can drop them.
A Cutaway may be a non-human comment; a reaction is a person's response. Keep the face fixed if you want to test Kuleshov; changing the expression changes the experiment.

Reuse the identical clip in three short edits: after a broken heirloom, after a sleeping puppy and after an unsigned contract. Generate the inserts separately and keep the reaction genuinely unchanged. Compare the meanings created by the juxtaposition.
prompt_example: Specify eyeline offscreen or toward a known object. For video, hold a small physical change (a swallow, a blink) rather than a tour of expressions.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a generic Close-Up of the speaker, or an overplayed grimace. The tell is mouth moving through the line, or eyebrows explaining the plot.

faq: What is Reaction Shot in film?
A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. It is a coverage function: the important action is watching, and the face or body is what the cut is about.
Reaction Shot vs Close-Up

A close-up is a crop: head and upper shoulders. A reaction shot is a job: this image exists because of what was just seen or heard. Reactions are often close-ups, but a close-up of someone speaking is not a reaction.
When should I use Reaction Shot?
Use it when watching is the event and the audience should read the receiver. Do not stack one after every sentence, and do not over-act the face if the cut is supposed to supply meaning.

name: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (OTS)
definition: Over-the-shoulder coverage, or an over the shoulder shot, puts a near shoulder or head in the foreground while the far face stays sharp. Paired reverses preserve relational space.
narrative: OTS is default dialogue coverage with spatial glue. The partner remains physically present even in a close view.

Shoulder size and how much it obstructs can make the observer feel dominant, intimate, or trapped. It is the wrong tool when you need to isolate someone as if the other person had left the room: that is a clean single.
It is also the wrong tool if both faces are equally sharp and complete: that is a two-shot. An over-the-shoulder shot is a framing choice.
Shot/reverse shot is an editing pattern. They are not synonyms.
how_it_works:
Place the camera beside one body, looking past a soft near shoulder at the far face. The far person looks at the near person, toward that shoulder, never into the lens.
Match foreground body position, head size, and eyeline on the reverse. The 180-degree line is the axis between the two bodies.
OTS coverage lives on one side of that line. If the near shoulder sits camera-right, the far face looks camera-right.
The reverse OTS swaps who is near, but it stays on the same side of the axis so screen direction does not flip. Crossing the line is not a style choice in this coverage: it makes two people look like they share a bench instead of a conversation.
Use focus and lighting to keep the speaking face sharp and the near cloth soft. Prompt: Over-the-shoulder framing of [Subject], near shoulder soft in foreground, the far face sharp, looking toward the near shoulder, 180-line held.
Never cross the 180-degree line. Draw the axis between the two people and keep the camera on one side of it. Far face looks at the near shoulder. The reverse stays on the same side of the axis. If they look into the lens or away from each other, it is no longer OTS coverage.
when_to_use: Use it as default dialogue coverage when you want the relationship to stay in the picture: a diner, a deposition, an interview through glass. Do not mismatch shoulder size on the reverse, and do not call a clean single an OTS.
compared_names: SingleIsolate. The other person is gone even if they are in the room.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: A Two-Shot gives both faces authorship. A Single removes the foreground partner; a dirty single may chew the edge without a true shoulder anchor.
A Reaction Shot may be taken as OTS or as a single. OTS means: near body fragment, far face subject.

mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a Two-Shot (both faces complete) or a Single (no shoulder). The tell is two people equally sharp, or a clean portrait.
The worse tell is a broken 180: the far person looks into the lens or away from the near shoulder, so the reverse would make them appear to sit on the same side. Fix: one soft shoulder, one sharp face looking at that shoulder, matched reverse, line held.
faq: What is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage in film?

Over-the-shoulder coverage frames the far person as the subject while a near shoulder or head anchors the foreground. Paired OTS shots keep two people in a shared geometry even when we are close on one face.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage vs Single

A single is one principal with no partner owning the foreground. OTS keeps a near shoulder or head in frame as a spatial glue. If the other person is gone from the rectangle, you have a single, even if they are still in the room.
When should I use Over-the-Shoulder Coverage?
Use it for dialogue that should keep the relationship physically present. Do not use it when isolation is the point, and do not mismatch the reverse.
How do I prompt Over-the-Shoulder Coverage for AI image or video?

Write Over-the-shoulder framing of [Subject], near shoulder soft in foreground, the far face sharp, looking toward the near shoulder. Name who is near. Hold the 180. For video, generate a matched reverse as a second shot on the same side of the line, rather than spinning the camera around them.
Does an over-the-shoulder shot break the 180-degree rule?

No. A correct OTS is how you hold the 180. The camera stays on one side of the line between the two people. The far face looks toward the near shoulder, not into the lens. Crossing that line flips screen direction and is a coverage error, not a look.

name: Single
definition: A single, in single shot cinematography, is a coverage shot of one principal character, not a one-take scene. A clean single keeps other bodies out; a dirty single lets a shoulder or blur from the partner chew the edge without becoming a true over-the-shoulder.
narrative: A single isolates. The other person can still be in the room, but they no longer author the frame.
This is how you make someone alone during a conversation, or how you give a listener a private beat. It is not a oner and not a long take; those are duration.
A single is occupancy: one principal. It is the wrong tool when the relationship must stay visible as a shoulder or as a shared two-shot.
Going to singles too early turns every scene into ping-pong. Going to a clean single at the right time can feel like the partner has been erased.
how_it_works:
Frame one person. For a clean single, keep edges empty of the partner (Clean Frame).
For a dirty single, allow a sliver of the other body as edge chew (Dirty Frame) without a composed foreground shoulder. Size is often Close-Up or Medium Close-Up, but a single can be a medium of one.
Prompt: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.
when_to_use: Use it to isolate: the other person is gone even if they are in the room. Do not leave a stray composed shoulder if you meant clean, and do not call a continuous long take a single just because one actor walks.

A single is a shot containing one principal character. Clean singles keep other bodies out; dirty singles let a bit of the partner chew the edge. It is coverage occupancy, not a synonym for a one-take scene.

OTS keeps a near shoulder or head as a compositional foreground while we watch the far face. A single removes that anchor so the frame belongs to one person. A dirty single is still a single; it is not a full OTS unless the near body is the viewpoint fragment.

definition: A cut-in, or cut in shot, moves from a wider view to a closer detail of something already present in that space, usually along the same axis. It proves a fact the wide cannot prove: the hands, the phone, the wound.

A cut-in is tighter, same world, same beat, often the same lens axis.

name: Gesture
definition: Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.
narrative: Sometimes the scene is not the face and not the prop, but the almost-touch, the glove tightening, the look that does not land. Gesture coverage treats that small action as the beat.
Duration matters: the movement has a start, a peak, and a settle. It is the wrong tool when the object is the fact (a key, a letter) rather than what the body does.
It is also the wrong tool as a wide master where fingers die in the noise of a room. Get close enough that the motion reads, then let it finish.
how_it_works:
Frame for the moving part. Hands often want a close crop without becoming a product shot; a glance may live in a Close-Up of the eyes.
Keep the body connected enough that the motion has a source (wrist, shoulder). Light to separate fingers from background.
Prompt: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.
when_to_use: Use it when the plot is in the fingers: an almost-touch in a corridor, a glove, a glass that does not quite rise. Do not cover it so wide the motion dies, and do not freeze it into an object insert.
compared_names: Insert ShotPoint at the thing that will matter later.
Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: An Insert Shot is usually the object as fact. A Close-Up is a size that may hold a gesture, or may hold a still face.
An Extreme Close-Up can be a fingertip as texture rather than as action. Gesture means the expressive movement is the subject.
If nothing moves, you probably wanted an insert.

prompt_template: Name the movement. Example: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.
prompt_example: Say what the body does (fingers almost touching, a look away). For video, one motion with a settle; do not add a camera tour.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot of a still object, or a Close-Up of a face that never moves. The tell is a static prop hero, or a wide where the hand is a blur.
Fix: size to the moving part, let the action complete.
faq: What is Gesture in film?

Gesture coverage is a shot sized and timed for a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a shift of weight. The meaning is the action, not a still object and not a wide master of the room.
Gesture vs Insert Shot

An insert shows a story object or detail, often still enough to read as a fact. Gesture shows what a body does with or without that object. A key in the palm can be an insert; the hesitation before the hand closes is gesture.
When should I use Gesture?
Use it when the beat is a small body action the wide cannot prove. Do not use it for a still product-like object, and do not bury the motion in a master.

Write Gesture close on [Subject], and name the hand, glance, or weight shift. For video, describe one motion and a settle. Keep the camera still unless the technique is a move.

name: Interview
definition: Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup: stable size, eyeline just off the lens, a listener implied. Someone is answering a question we often do not hear.
narrative: An interview frame is not merely an MCU. It is a social geometry: the subject speaks to a person beside the camera, look space opens toward that listener, and the audience sits in on an answered question.
Direct address into the lens is a different contract (confession, host, warning). It is the wrong tool when two fictional characters are in a scene together and you needed OTS or a two-shot.
It is also the wrong tool if the eyeline hits the glass and you did not mean to break the fourth wall. Keep the size stable; hunting around the face turns testimony into a music video.
how_it_works:
Size usually Medium Close-Up or a loose Close-Up. Camera at Eye Level.
Eyeline a few degrees off lens, toward an implied interviewer. Give Look Space on the look side.
Motivated, simple key; catchlight in the eyes. Prompt: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.
when_to_use: Use it when someone is answering a question we did not hear: documentary testimony, a fake-doc confession, a talking-head insert in a drama. Do not put the eyeline into the lens unless you mean direct address, and do not use this grammar for a two-person scene that should be OTS.
compared_names: Medium Close-UpTalk without losing body language.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: A Medium Close-Up is only a crop; interview is the off-lens eyeline plus implied listener. Eye level is the height.
Over-the-Shoulder would show the questioner. A video portrait holds a face as a study, often without the Q&A contract.
Interview means testimony geometry.

Grammar: someone is being asked.
prompt_template: Lock eyeline and size. Example: Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied.
prompt_example: Specify look space toward camera-left or camera-right. For video, hold; small hand motion is fine.
prompt_note: Do not stare down the lens unless you want direct address.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a generic Medium Close-Up with eyes into the lens, or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage of a scene. The tell is a host stare, or a second character in a fictional blocking.
Fix: off-lens eyeline, implied listener, stable talking-head size.
faq: What is Interview in film?

Interview cinematography is a talking-head setup in which the subject answers an offscreen questioner. Size is stable, the eyeline sits just off the lens, and a listener is implied even if we never see them.
Interview vs Medium Close-Up

MCU is a chest-up crop that can be used for any dialogue. Interview is a setup: off-lens eyeline, look space toward a questioner, testimony as the job. You can shoot an MCU that is not an interview, and an interview that is slightly tighter or looser than MCU.
When should I use Interview?

Use it for testimony, documentary talking heads, or a drama that borrows that contract. Do not use it when two characters should share a scene in OTS, and do not aim the eyes at the lens unless you mean direct address.
How do I prompt Interview for AI image or video?

Write Interview frame of [Subject], talking-head distance, eyeline just off lens, a listener implied. Add look space and eye-level. For video, hold the size; do not tour the room.

name: Product
definition: Product cinematography lights and frames an object the way a portrait treats a face: hero angle, catalog clarity, controlled reflections. The thing is the subject, not a plot insert in a messy room.
narrative: A product frame sells readability: logo plane, material, edges, how metal and glass behave. Speculars are designed, not accidental.
The background is often a sweep, a void, or a set built to disappear. It is the wrong tool when the object is a story fact inside a scene (a bloody letter on a kitchen table).
That is an insert, and it should keep the room's key. It is also the wrong tool if the camera orbits so fast the form never settles.
Show the object; let a Lazy Susan turn it if every side must read.
how_it_works:
Choose a hero three-quarter or a true elevation. Large soft sources for wrapping highlights; flags and cards to kill ugly speculars on chrome.
Macro only for texture. A turntable or a slow orbit is a separate move.
Prompt: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.
when_to_use: Use it to sell the thing by lighting it like a face: a phone, a bottle, a watch on a sweep. Do not use drama-insert mess if you need catalog clarity, and do not use this glamour on a plot object that should look found.
compared_names: Lazy SusanShow an object or costume from every side.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: An Insert Shot lives in scene coverage as a plot fact, matching the room. Macro is an optic for small texture, which a product shot may use.
A Lazy Susan is a rotation method. Product is the commercial portrait job: controlled reflections, hero angle, the object as subject.

Grammar: catalog clarity, not found-object dirt, unless the brief is worn-in hero.
prompt_template: Specify material (brushed aluminum, glass, leather) and the background (black sweep, white cyclorama). For video, one slow turn or a locked hero; do not add a person unless they are a scale hand.
prompt_example: Name the object as hero. Example: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot in dirty scene light, or a Macro texture with no hero angle. The tell is leftover room clutter, or a smear of uncontrolled speculars.
Fix: isolate the object, design the highlights, pick a hero angle.
faq: What is Product in film?

Product cinematography frames and lights an object as the subject, with catalog clarity and controlled reflections, the way a portrait treats a face. It is a commercial or hero-object job, not a synonym for any close-up of a thing.
Product vs Insert Shot

An insert is a story detail inside a scene, usually matching that scene's light. A product shot isolates the object as a hero, often on a sweep or void, with designed speculars. A bloody envelope on a table is an insert; a phone on black acrylic is product.
When should I use Product?
Use it when the object must read as a designed hero. Do not use it for a plot fact that should stay in the room, and do not let reflections go unmanaged on chrome and glass.

name: Video Portraits
definition: A video portrait is a sustained, simply covered study of one person: stable size, patient time, the face as the whole event. Duration is the intimacy; a person is enough.
narrative: A video portrait is not a close-up you cut away from after a line. You hold.
Blink, breath, a swallow, the tiny life in the face becomes the content. It sits closer to a painting that is allowed to live than to dialogue coverage.

It is the wrong tool when you need ping-pong coverage, a story insert, or a camera tour of the room. It is also the wrong tool if you freeze everything except one looping element: that is a cinemagraph.
Here the person is alive in small ways, and time is the point.
how_it_works:
Lock the camera. Size a Close-Up or Medium Close-Up.
Light a simple, stable key. Hold long enough that duration registers (several seconds, sometimes much more).
No motivated move unless a tiny push is the brief. Prompt still: Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy.
Motion brief: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still.
when_to_use: Use it when a person is enough: a Screen Test, a study, an almost-still that breathes. Do not add a tour, and do not cut away the moment a thought appears; the hold is the piece.
compared_names: Close-UpRead micro-expression. Default for important dialogue.
CinemagraphA photograph that refuses to die.
Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.
compared_text: A Close-Up is a size used inside coverage; it usually leaves. A Cinemagraph freezes most of the image and loops one isolated motion.
A Single is occupancy of one body in scene coverage. A video portrait is duration plus stillness of a person as the entire event.
Interview testimony has a questioner; this may have none.

The usual wrong cousin is a dialogue Close-Up that wants a reverse, or a Cinemagraph with a frozen body and a looping steam jet. The tell is a camera move, a cut on a line, or a dead freeze.

faq: What is Video Portraits in film?
A video portrait is a sustained study of one person at a stable size, with time itself as the intimacy. The face (or figure) is the whole event, almost still, with only tiny life in the features.
Video Portraits vs Close-Up

A close-up is a crop that often exists to deliver a line or a reaction, then leave. A video portrait uses a similar crop but stays: duration is the point. If you are about to cut to the other person, you are in coverage, not in a portrait study.
When should I use Video Portraits?
Use it when a person is enough and holding is the piece. Do not use it for ordinary shot/reverse, and do not turn it into a looping cinemagraph unless that is the brief.
How do I prompt Video Portraits for AI image or video?

Write Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy. For motion: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still. Lock the camera. Allow only blink, breath, or a swallow.

name: Wide Shot (WS)
definition: A wide shot shows the subject in full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage: do not isolate yet.
narrative: Size is a sentence. A wide shot maps who can reach the door, where the street goes, what weather is doing.
People are in the picture so we know the scale of the place, but the place is still talking. If you isolate too early, the scene loses its map.

It is the wrong tool when the beat is a face, a holster, or a head-to-toe costume portrait. It is also the wrong tool if the human has become an unreadable speck (extreme long shot) or if you only needed to declare the building before the scene (establishing as a job).
Use wide to keep geography in play, then change size when a new fact requires a tighter sentence.
how_it_works:
Keep enough architecture, street, or weather that doors, paths, and weather remain readable. Bodies should not fill the height the way they do in a full-body portrait.
A 24mm in a room or a longer lens across a square can both be wide; the crop is whether place still speaks. Prompt: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.
when_to_use: Use it when you must not isolate yet: who can reach the door, how far the platform runs, whether two groups can see each other. Do not crop into a full-body fashion frame and call it wide, and do not use it as a blank postcard with no relation to the scene's paths.
compared_names: Long ShotPlace a human in a world that could ignore them.
Establishing ShotOpen a scene. Tell us where and when.

compared_text: A Full Body makes the complete figure the subject, head to toe, place as a border. A Long Shot is the person-in-world size: full figure plus geography, still a locatable human.
An Extreme Long Shot is speck-scale land. An Establishing Shot is a where-and-when job that often uses a wide.
A Master Shot is the action skeleton, which may be wide if blocking needs it. Wide is the environment-forward coverage attitude, not a synonym for those four.

A wide shot shows the subject in a full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage, not a synonym for full body, long shot, or establishing shot.
Wide Shot vs Full Body

Full body is a complete figure as the subject, head to toe, with environment as a readable border. A wide shot keeps place in charge: doors, streets, and weather remain the sentence, and people are small enough not to isolate yet. If the person fills the frame height, you are in full body, not wide.

Write Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks. Name architecture and weather. Keep people from filling the height of the frame.

name: Eye Level
definition: An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a horizontal sightline and a level horizon. It is the default equal relationship: height and tilt assign no rank until you leave this setup.
narrative: Rank in a frame comes from where the lens sits and how it is pitched. Eye-level refuses that assignment.
Two people at matching eye height read as peers; the room does not look down on them, and they do not loom. Sit when they sit.
Stand when they stand. The judgment, if any, has to come from performance, costume, or light, not from geometry.
It is the wrong tool when the beat is surveillance, monument, or a map. A few degrees of pitch and you have already cut to a High Angle or a Low Angle.
A few inches down and you are in Shoulder Level, which is a companion, not a peer.
how_it_works:
Match the nodal point to the subject's eyes. Keep roll at zero so verticals stay vertical.
A 35mm to 50mm keeps perspective close to human vision; a wide from the same height will still stretch the room without changing rank. Height and tilt are independent: a camera at eye height that looks down is no longer an eye-level shot, it is a high angle from eye height.
Prompt it as camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down.
when_to_use:
Use it for a conversation that should not take sides, or for a face you want believed without the camera lobbying. Concrete beat: two adults at a kitchen table, seated eyes matched, no ceiling grab.
Do not look down or up unless you mean it.
compared_names: High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.
Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.
compared_text: High Angle pitches down and shrinks the figure. Low Angle pitches up and grows it.
Shoulder Level sits a few inches below the eyes, like a walking companion. Point of View is what the character sees, not a camera beside them at the same height.
Over-the-Shoulder Coverage keeps a near body in the foreground; eye-level can be a clean Single.
High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.
Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.
Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.
in_film: Tokyo Story holds domestic talk at human height so posture, not a power tilt, does the judging. Rosetta stays with her at her own eye line as she moves, refusing a look down.
Use those as grammar: match height to the person in the scene, keep the horizon honest.
prompt_template: Lead with height and pitch. Quote: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizontal sightline, equal relationship, no power tilt.
prompt_example: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizontal sightline, equal relationship, no power tilt.
prompt_note: Do not write mood words in place of the height.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a mild Low Angle, because generators treat a portrait as a poster. Tell: ceiling in frame, chin from below, verticals converging.
Fix: camera at eye height, horizon level, no tilt. If the subject is seated, sit the camera; standing eye-level on a seated person is already looking down.
faq: What is eye level in film?
An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a level horizon. The sightline is horizontal, so the frame does not assign power by looking up or down.
Eye level vs high angle
Eye level matches the subject's eyes and stays level. A high-angle shot raises the camera and pitches it down, so more floor enters and the figure occupies less of the rectangle.
When should I use eye level?
Use it when the relationship should read as equal: talk, witness, default coverage. Skip it when the beat needs vulnerability from above or monument from below.
How do I prompt eye level for AI image or video?

Write: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down. Name sit versus stand so the model does not look down on a seated body.

name: High Angle
definition: A high-angle shot looks downward at the subject from above eye level, an oblique pitch rather than a straight drop. More floor enters the frame, the figure occupies less of the rectangle, and the viewpoint reads as observation from above.
narrative: Height plus downward tilt is what assigns the smaller rank. A high angle can be pity, surveillance, or a clinical map of who can reach the door.

The face should still be a face: you see the crown and the shoulders, not only a scalp. Paths and distances that Eye Level would hide become readable because the floor is a diagram with walls still receding.
It is the wrong tool when you need a true plan view. If the tabletop must be a rectangle and bodies become pieces, you wanted Overhead Top-Down or a steep Bird's-Eye View.
It is also the wrong tool for a power confrontation; looking down on the boss fights the line.
how_it_works:
Raise the camera above the subject's eyes and pitch it down. Typical working range is a step-stool to a short ladder, 20 to 45 degrees of tilt, subject still recognizable through costume and contrast.
Top-light and ceiling practicals become the key more often, because you are now closer to the lights that hang. Keep roll level; a canted high angle is two techniques at once.
Prompt: high-angle shot looking down, figure diminished, more floor than sky, not top-down.
when_to_use:
Use it for vulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room that eye-level cannot draw. Concrete beat: a lone figure on a station platform, camera above the lamps, suitcase readable on the boards.
Do not use a high oblique when the shot must be strictly top-down.

Overhead Top-Down is 90 degrees, a flat-lay or room plan. Low Angle is the opposing pitch.
Crane Over is the move that can arrive at a high or overhead view.

Citizen Kane and Prisoners both look down when a person should feel watched or reduced. Borrow the downward pitch and the readable floor, not a poster.

A high-angle shot looks down at the subject from above eye level. The pitch is oblique, so you still read a person, only smaller in their space.
High angle vs bird's-eye view
A high angle is a downward look that keeps the face and the room in perspective. A bird's-eye view is much higher and steeper, often nearly straight down, until life reads as a map.
When should I use a high angle?
Use it when someone is vulnerable, watched, or when the floor plan of a room matters more than a power face. Do not use it as a default dramatic portrait.

name: Low Angle
definition: A low-angle shot looks upward at the subject from below eye level, so verticals converge and ceilings or sky take weight. The camera is not merely low; it is pitched up, and that pitch is what assigns monument or intimidation.
narrative: Looking up makes a body into architecture. Door frames, ceiling beams, and the underside of a chin enter the picture.
A boss in a doorway, a statue, a threat: the subject occupies the top of the frame and we occupy the floor. Citizen Kane built ceilings (and sometimes dug a pit) so the look-up had a real lid.
Do not confuse this with a low camera that stays level. A tatami or seated-height camera with a horizontal sightline is a height choice, close to seated Eye Level, not a low angle.
Ozu's rooms sit low without turning the family into towers. If you pitch up on that setup, you have changed the sentence.
It is the wrong tool for a peer conversation and for a true worm's view of a skyscraper. Moderate look-up is a portrait with rank.
Extreme look-up is Worm's-Eye View.
how_it_works:
Drop the camera below the subject's eyes (chest, waist, or a hole in the floor) and tilt up until verticals converge toward the top of the frame. A wider lens exaggerates the convergence; a longer lens from the same height still looks up but with less stretch.
Practicals on the ceiling become motivated keys. Keep roll level unless you are also doing a Dutch Angle.
Prompt: low-angle looking up, converging verticals, ceiling or sky in frame, not camera on the dirt looking straight up.
when_to_use:
Use it for power, monument, or intimidation: someone who should fill the doorway. Concrete beat: a standing figure shot from a seated listener, ceiling beams closing over the head.
Do not pitch up on every protagonist as a default poster.

name: Bird's-Eye View

name: Dutch Angle
definition: A Dutch angle rolls the camera so verticals and the horizon appear tilted. The cant is usually static: gravity's down is no longer the bottom of the frame, which is why the world reads as off its axis.
narrative: Pitch looks up or down. Roll breaks the floor.

A Dutch (canted, oblique) shot is a choice about gravity, not about power height. Use it when the moral or mental line is already bent: a sick city, a fight that will not stay fair, a mind that cannot stand up.
Adjacent level shots make the cant mean something. If every setup is Dutch, nothing is.
It is not a Low Angle. Looking up with a level roll is a different axis.
It is not a Dutch Roll either: that is the move that rotates into a cant during the shot. A static Dutch is a frozen decision.
how_it_works:
Rotate the camera around the lens axis. A readable working cant is about 15 to 30 degrees; past 45 the frame often just looks like a mistake.
Compose diagonals on purpose: stair rails, streets, a leaning body that agrees or argues with the roll. Keep the set rigid.
The sensation should come from the viewpoint, not from warped walls. Decide whether the reverse stays level for contrast.

name: Point of View
definition: A POV shot makes the camera function as a character's optical viewpoint: what they see at their eye height. The looker's head and shoulder stay out of the frame; we inhabit the look, not a seat behind it.

The camera sits at their eyes, aims where they aim, and refuses the back of their head. Identification is forced because the audience is briefly the character.
It is not Over-the-Shoulder Coverage, which keeps the looker's shoulder as a claim of with, not as. It is not First-Person, which lets a body own the lens for a long ride: hands, breath, locomotion.
A POV can be a single still insert. First-person is a body that keeps seeing.
Subjective sound (a ringing ear, a mute beach) can ride with a POV or sit on an objective picture. Do not confuse a hearing filter with this optical setup.

Put the camera at the named character's eye height and point it along their eyeline. Match lens choice to their attention: a longer glass for binocular looking, a wider field for a panicked scan.

name: Three-Quarter Angle
definition: A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.
narrative: Most coverage of a talking face lives here. You see both eyes, the bridge of the nose, and a cheek going away, which is enough skull to light and enough access to read a listen.

It is useful because it models the head and still connects to an offscreen partner along a natural eyeline. It is the wrong tool when you want a coin (use Profile) or a confession into the taking lens (use Fourth Wall).
It is also not a height: you can shoot three-quarter from Eye Level, Low Angle, or High Angle. The name is yaw, not tilt.
how_it_works:

name: Reverse Angle
definition: A reverse-angle shot views the same spatial relationship from the opposing side, completing the axis of a look, a dialogue, or a standoff. Geography flips; the 180-degree line is respected so screen direction still matches.
narrative: Someone looks. The reverse is who or what occupies the other pole.
In a diner, it is the other booth. In a gunfight, it is the other holster.
Matching size and height keeps the cut from feeling like a new scene. The reverse can be a clean Single or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage; the name is the axis, not the foreground shoulder.
Withholding the reverse is a different editorial choice: a look, a reaction, and no answering view. The Blair Witch Project and Rosemary's Baby live on that denial.
The reverse-angle shot itself is the answering camera, not the refusal of it.
how_it_works:
Hold the 180-line. Move the camera to the opposite side of the axis, still on the same side of the line, and match lens height to the new subject (sit versus stand, adult versus child).
Match shot size to the outgoing picture unless the cut is meant to punch. Eyelines must cross the same empty air.

name: First-Person
definition: A first-person camera makes the lens function as a character's bodily viewpoint, with a body that owns it: hands entering the frame, breath, tools, locomotion. It is subjective seeing as continuous embodiment, not a single optical insert.

Hands, a steering wheel, a gun, a door handled at the edge: those are the tells that a person, not an invisible observer, is looking. A Point of View shot can be one cut of what they see, clean of the owner.

Parent the camera to the character's head or upper chest with a human field of view (roughly 24mm to 35mm spherical, not a tiny action-cam unless that is diegetic). Allow hands, shoulders at the extreme edge, or a tool to enter.

name: Object POV
definition: An object-POV shot is the viewpoint of a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone, or a vehicle: the prop has eyes. The camera is parented to that object, so the object stays stable in the frame while the world moves relative to it.
narrative: Agency leaves the invisible observer and goes to a machine or a thing. A fork of a bicycle stays in the corner while cobbles rush.
A car body is fixed and the desert tears past. A phone slides across a table toward a face.

It is not First-Person, which is a human body with hands and breath. It is not a free drone that happens to start near a prop.
If the anchor object wanders inside the frame, the parent is broken.
how_it_works:
Use a professionally secured mount or a rigid virtual parent transform on the named object. Include a visible part of the anchor (barrel, rubber, chrome, glass edge).
Preserve vibration that belongs to the object; do not add a second operator path. Lens choice is often wide because the mount is close.

name: Incline
definition: An incline is a slight camera roll, a gentle cant of the floor rather than a full Dutch angle. The horizon is a few degrees off true, enough to suggest slope or unease without declaring that the world has fallen over.
narrative: A full Dutch Angle at 20 to 30 degrees is a statement: the axis is broken. Incline is the whisper.

Hallways that should feel 6 to 12 degrees wrong, a street that might be hill or might be mind, a conversation that is not yet a crisis. If the viewer can measure a lean at a glance, you probably overshot into Dutch.
It is still roll, not pitch. A camera looking up a real hill with a level bubble is not an incline; the floor is actually sloped and the frame is true.
Incline cheats gravity in the head, not in the set.
how_it_works:
Roll the camera a small amount, typically about 5 to 12 degrees, and lock it. Keep architecture readable and bodies upright in the world; only the frame is off.
Do not combine with a wide fisheye or the small cant disappears into distortion. Contrast with a level reverse if you want the incline to be felt.

when_to_use:
Use it when a full Dutch is too much and the floor should only suggest slope or unease. Concrete beat: a hotel corridor, 8 degrees of roll, wallpaper still a grid, a person walking toward camera.

name: Three-Point Lighting
definition: Three-point lighting, the basic three point lighting setup, places a key, a fill, and a backlight so a face is modeled from one dominant side, opened in the shadows, and separated from the background. The key is brightest and sets direction; fill and back exist only as ratios against it.
narrative: In a scene it is the default portrait grammar: the audience can read both eyes, the cheekbones have a light side and a shadow side, and the hair does not melt into the wall. Classical coverage uses it so reverse shots match, and so a close-up still feels like the same room as the master.
It is the wrong tool when the room already has a single honest source, or when the story wants a face half-erased. Teaching the setup is useful.
Leaving it on every night interior as three hidden movie lights is how a crime scene starts to look like a cosmetics ad.
how_it_works:
Place the key about 45 degrees off camera axis and 30 to 45 degrees above the eyes, large enough to be slightly soft unless the scene is harsh. 5 to 3 stops down so the shadow cheek still has pores.
Put backlight high and behind, often slightly opposite the key, warm or white, flagged so it rims hair and shoulders without flaring the lens. Prompt: Classic three-point lighting on [Subject]: key at 45 degrees, soft fill opening shadows, warm backlight rim, modeled volume.
when_to_use: Use it for a teachable talking-head or a studio close-up that must stay readable across a whole scene. Do not use it as the only language of a night interior that is supposed to be one lamp.

BacklightSeparate a dark figure from a dark world.
compared_text: Key light is the dominant source inside this setup, not the setup itself. Fill light only opens the key's shadows; it has no third direction.
Backlight is the rear unit that separates the figure. Rembrandt lighting and loop lighting are facial patterns you can make with the key while the other two points still exist.

name: Key Light
definition: A key light in key light cinematography is the principal source that sets the subject's dominant direction, shape, and exposure. Shadows fall away from it; every other light is measured against it.
narrative: Deciding the key is deciding where the world is lit from. A window, a bare bulb, the sun, or a hidden unit standing in for those things will tell the audience what time it is and who is exposed.
The rest of the plot of the lighting is contrast, color, and whether anyone else gets a face. It is the wrong tool to think of as a product.
You do not add a key on top of a finished picture. If two equally bright sources fight from opposite sides, you no longer have a key.
You have cross lighting or a flattened stand-off.

Pick one source and one side. Typical portrait keys sit 30 to 45 degrees off camera and above eye line; a split key sits at 90 degrees; a butterfly key sits on axis and high.

name: Fill Light
definition: Fill light reduces contrast or adds detail in areas the key does not reach, usually from the opposite side and at a lower level. It is a ratio tool, not a second sun.
narrative: In a scene fill decides how much of the dark you can still read: the far eye, the wall, a hand in a lap. A high fill ratio (close to the key) feels open and public.
A low fill ratio keeps mystery without crushing the face to a cut-out. It is the wrong tool when you want graphic black, or when bounce from the room already does the job.
Adding a frontal fill because a monitor looks noisy just flattens the key you spent an hour placing.
how_it_works:
Put fill opposite the key, larger and softer than the key so it does not cast a competing nose shadow. Control it with distance, scrim, or dimmer; common portrait ratios run from about 2:1 (gentle) to 8:1 (lean).
Color is often a touch cooler or neutral versus a warm key so the shadow side does not go orange. Bounce off a wall can be the fill with no extra lamp.

name: Backlight
definition: Backlight in backlight cinematography is light coming from behind the subject toward the camera, tracing edges and lifting the figure off the background. It may stay a thin rim or, in haze, become a visible shaft.

Place a small, weak source near camera, often just above the lens, dim enough that it does not flatten the key's shadow pattern. A white card, a dim LED, or a distant practical can be enough.
Color is usually white or matching the key; keep it out of the skin as much as possible. You want a pinpoint in the iris, not a beauty wash.

Use large sources, plenty of fill, and often bounce from walls and ceiling so the ratio sits near 2:1 or lower. Key can still have a side; it is just not a cliff.
Protect highlight detail on skin, icing, walls. Color is often daylight-balanced or pastel-friendly, sometimes slightly cool for sterile spaces, sometimes candy-warm.

name: Chiaroscuro
definition: Chiaroscuro lighting uses strong light-dark contrast to model volume and to create moral, psychological, or dramatic tension. Darkness withholds; the lit plane is what the scene will admit.
narrative: A single warm source, a face turning into light, the rest of the room falling away: the audience reads character as a matter of what remains visible. Tenebrism is the hard end of this, where everything beyond arm's reach is black.
Crime, period night, and religious doubt all use the same physics. It is the wrong tool for a wide that must describe architecture, or for comedy that needs a second face in the shadows.
Underexposing an even room is not chiaroscuro. You have to place a key and let falloff do the cutting.
how_it_works:
Place one motivated key (window, lamp, candle), reduce fill, and flag spill. The key is often warm, slightly high, and small enough to fall off fast.
Hardness can be moderately hard so planes of the face turn quickly. Keep enough separation that eyes and hands in the pool stay legible.

name: Rembrandt Lighting
definition: Rembrandt lighting, in rembrandt lighting terms, is a portrait pattern in which the key sits high and about 45 degrees off axis so the nose shadow joins the shadow cheek, leaving a small triangle of light under the shadow-side eye. The rest of that cheek stays dark.
narrative: The face becomes a painting with one lit plane and a pocket of light that proves the far eye still exists. Drama likes it because the head has volume without the graphic half-and-half of a split.

Period interiors and serious close-ups use it when the key could be a high window or a lamp. It is the wrong tool for a beauty close-up that should open both cheeks evenly, or for a character you want fully public.
If the nose shadow does not connect to the cheek shadow, you have loop lighting, not Rembrandt.
how_it_works:
Put a moderately hard or softly hard key high and roughly 45 degrees to one side, high enough that the nose shadow falls down and across until it meets the cheek shadow. The triangle sits below the far eye and should not spill across the whole far cheek.
Fill is low or absent. Color follows the source: warm interior, cooler window.
Short lighting (key on the far cheek) is the usual pairing. Prompt: Key light high and 45 degrees on [Subject], the near cheek in light, a small triangle of light on the shadow-side cheek, the rest of that cheek dark.
when_to_use: Use it for a classic dramatic portrait, a period close-up, a bargainer across a table. Do not use it when you need an even glamour wrap or a literal half-lit mask.

Bounce light would wrap the triangle away. Motivated lighting can create Rembrandt if the window sits in that high 45, but motivated is a justification, not this pattern.

name: Butterfly Lighting
definition: Butterfly lighting, also called Paramount lighting, places the key high and on the camera axis so a small butterfly-shaped shadow falls under the nose on the philtrum. Both cheeks stay open; both eyes take light.
narrative: This is beauty lighting with a structure: cheekbones lift, the nose has a tidy shadow, and the face stays symmetrical for the lens. Classical glamour portraits used it because a star looking into camera still has modeling, not a flat flash.
It is the wrong tool for a liar in half-light, a bruised antihero, or anyone whose story is asymmetry. If you swing the key off axis, the butterfly becomes a loop.
If you raise it to the ceiling and kill the frontal component, you get top light sockets.
how_it_works:
Center a large or medium source above the lens, aimed down at the face, high enough for the under-nose shadow but not so high the eye sockets collapse. A reflector under the chin is optional fill.
Hardness is usually soft to medium so skin wraps. Color is often tungsten or daylight beauty-neutral, not a green overhead.
