name: Loop Lighting
definition: Loop lighting creates a small nose shadow that loops toward the corner of the mouth and does not connect to the cheek shadow. The key sits slightly off axis and a little high, a middle step between butterfly and Rembrandt.
narrative: The face is shaped but still friendly: interviews, earnest close-ups, people we are supposed to trust. You get a hint of cheek shadow and a definite nose, without the painterly triangle or the glamour butterfly.
It is the wrong tool when you need a mask of light and dark, or a fashion-symmetric face. If that loop grows until it joins the cheek, you have crossed into Rembrandt.
If you center the key, you are back at butterfly.
how_it_works:
Offset the key about 30 to 45 degrees from the nose, slightly above eye line, softness medium so the loop is a clean comma, not a smear. Fill can sit opposite at a gentle ratio (2:1 to 4:1).
Color is usually the room: window daylight or soft tungsten. The shadow-side cheek still receives some light; that is the difference from Rembrandt.
Prompt: Loop lighting on [Subject], key slightly off-axis, a small loop shadow from the nose toward the corner of the mouth.

name: Split Lighting
definition: Split lighting divides the face into a lit half and a shadow half by placing the key at about 90 degrees to the nose, a vertical cut down the center line. There is no Rembrandt triangle and no loop; the far plane is largely gone.
narrative: Duality made as geometry: hero and liar, cop and crook, the same person cut in two. The audience gets one eye in light and one in almost nothing.
Music, crime, and moral argument use it because the cut is literal. It is the wrong tool for charm, romance, or any beat that needs both cheeks.
If you sneak fill across the center line, the split collapses into side lighting with wrap. If you raise the key and pull it forward, you may accidentally make Rembrandt.
how_it_works:
Put a relatively hard key at 90 degrees to the face, at about eye height, so the shadow edge runs down forehead, nose, and chin. Fill is near zero.
Color can be a hard white or a theatrical gel; the point is the cut, not prettiness. A true split is more severe than generic side light because the wrap over the nose is killed with flags if needed.
Prompt: Split lighting on [Subject], one half of the face in light, the other in shadow, a vertical moral cut.

name: Silhouette
definition: A silhouette shot places the subject dark against a brighter background so the figure reads as shape, not as a modeled face. Gesture and contour do the work; surface detail is gone.

Expose for the bright ground (sky, doorway, fire, sun disk). Keep the key off the subject, or far below the background.

name: Motivated Lighting
definition: Motivated lighting is designed to appear consistent with a visible or plausible story-world source: a window, a lamp, a sign, the sky. Hidden units may exist, but they match that source in direction, hardness, and color.
narrative: The room feels like a world rather than a studio. A hotel sconce, a kitchen window, a sodium street, an overcast sky: the key could have come from there even if a silk outside the window is doing the real work.
Control stays; theatricality hides. It is the wrong tool when the point is frankly theatrical (a follow spot, a beauty butterfly that no lamp in the room could throw).
Motivated is not the same as using only what is already there. That is available light.
It is also not the same as showing the bulb. That is a practical.
how_it_works:
Choose the story source first. Match camera-side direction to that window or fixture.
Match hardness: a distant sun stays hard; a sheer curtain becomes a large soft key; a bare bulb stays small. Match color: tungsten practicals around 2800 to 3200K, daylight windows nearer 5600K, sodium and neon as they are.
Hide extra units along the same axis, flagged to the same throw. Prompt: Motivated lighting on [Subject], every source justified by a window, lamp, or sign that could exist in the room.
when_to_use: Use it for realism with control, a hotel corridor, a kitchen at 4 p.m., a car at night that should feel streetlit. Do not use it as an excuse to keep a frontal beauty key that no source in the space could explain.

name: Practical Lighting

name: Bounce Light
definition: Bounce lighting reflects light from a surface (wall, ceiling, poly, card) before it reaches the subject, so the apparent source becomes that large surface. Direction remains, but shadow edges soften and wrap.
narrative: You keep a window side or a lamp side without the brutality of the bare source. Faces wrap, rooms feel inhabited, and the key still has a direction because the bounce surface occupies a place in the world.
Period interiors and daylight rooms use it so skin does not speckle. It is the wrong tool when you need razor shadows, a gobo pattern, or a hard split.
Bounce is a method, not a facial pattern: it is not Rembrandt, not split, not butterfly. Those patterns die if you bounce too much.
how_it_works:
Aim a lamp or the sun at a white or neutral surface, then let that surface light the subject. Larger and closer bounce means softer light.
Color picks up the bounce surface: white stays honest, a cream wall warms, a green wall will tint. The key side is the side of the bounce, not the lamp behind it.
Prompt: Bounce light on [Subject], key ricocheted off a white wall or poly, wrapping, gentle, large-source softness.

name: Side Lighting
definition: Side lighting keys primarily from one side, around 90 degrees to the camera-subject line, so shape and texture are emphasized. Half the form goes toward light, half toward shadow.
narrative: A face or a landscape becomes sculpture. Sweat, wood grain, and cheekbones show because the light rakes.

how_it_works:
Place the key at about 90 degrees, at a height that fits the story (eye height for a face, raking low sun for ground texture). Hardness is often hard so texture reads; soft side light exists as a large window in a side wall.

name: Underlighting
definition: Underlighting, also called uplighting, lights from below the face so shadows climb the cheekbones and the tops of the eye sockets. The modeling is the reverse of daylight and often reads as uncanny.

A candle on a table can underlight if it sits below the chin, but candlelight is a source type that can also sit beside a face. Underlighting is the direction.
how_it_works:
Place a lamp, flame, or panel below the chin, pointing up. Keep it close so inverse-square falloff hits the face and dies on the ceiling.
Hardness is often hard or small-soft (a phone screen is a smallish source). Color is flame-warm, screen-cool, or theatrical green; the climb of the shadows is the tell.

name: Cross Lighting

name: Volumetric Light

name: Rule of Thirds
definition: The rule of thirds in rule of thirds cinematography divides the frame into nine equal cells and parks important masses on those lines or at their four intersections. The horizon usually sits on an upper or lower third so land and sky are not equal partners, and the subject usually sits off-center with look-space in the larger remaining field.
narrative: Treat the frame as a diagram of who owns space. Thirds is a default, not a law.
A face on a power intersection hands the bigger rectangle to the look, the weather, or the threat. The strip behind the head is leftover, not decoration.
It is the wrong tool when the beat needs a formal altar, a trap, or a joke about order. Dead-center ritual, short-sided panic, and poster symmetry all break the grid on purpose.
If you apply thirds to every close-up, the diagram stops meaning anything. A model that hears only balanced composition will center the face and split the sky in half.
Name which intersection holds the eyes and which third holds the horizon.
how_it_works:
Turn on the 3x3 overlay on the monitor. Place eyes, a head, or a landmark on an intersection, not in the dead middle of a cell.
Keep the camera level unless a roll is the point. A 35mm to 50mm keeps the grid honest.
Ultra-wide glass stretches the outer thirds into cartoon corners. Telephoto compresses them into stacked bands.
Prompt: Rule-of-thirds placement of [Subject] on a power intersection, horizon on a third, breathing room in the look direction.
when_to_use: Use it on a landscape walk, a single looking off, or an establishing wide that must feel occupied without becoming an altar. Do not treat it as a religion on every close-up, title card, or ritual tableau.

Days of Heaven does the same with prairie and sky. There Will Be Blood often offsets a figure so land outweighs the person.
These are grammar, not frames to copy.

mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is dead-center portrait posing as thirds. The tell is a face on the optical axis with equal sky and equal leftover on both ears.
The fix is to slide the eyes to an intersection and give the look the larger field, or admit you wanted Central Framing and shoot that instead.
faq: What is rule of thirds in film?

It is a 3x3 grid overlaid on the frame. Important masses sit on the lines or at the four intersections so the picture is offset by default. The larger remaining field usually belongs to the look, the land, or the threat.
Rule of Thirds vs Golden Ratio

Thirds splits at 33 percent. A golden-ratio or phi grid splits nearer 38 and 62 percent, a slightly tighter offset, sometimes described as a spiral. Both refuse dead center. Thirds is the faster default on a set. Phi is a quieter proportional claim.
When should I use rule of thirds?

Use it when a figure or horizon should share the frame with a larger field they do not occupy. A walk, a look off, a landscape single. Skip it when the scene is a ritual, a trap, or a poster that needs the axis.

name: Golden Ratio
definition: Golden ratio composition organizes the frame with proportional relationships near phi, about eight to five, as a phi grid or a logarithmic spiral rather than a 3x3. The main mass sits closer to center than a third, and the eye is asked to travel a curve through secondary masses instead of jumping cell to cell.
narrative: Phi is a more secret order than thirds. The diagram still asks who owns space, but the large field is not a blunt two-thirds slab.

A spiral from a corner through a face, then through a doorway, then into empty weather, can feel inevitable without announcing a grid. It is the wrong tool when the audience needs the diagram in one glance.
Action geography, comedy blocking, and most coverage live on simpler axes. If you cannot point to a curve the eye actually rides, you are decorating with math.
Painters used these proportions because canvases hold still. In a moving shot the spiral has to survive a pan, a walk, and a focus change.
Design the still first, then see if the move keeps the curve.
how_it_works:
A phi grid places lines at about 38 percent and 62 percent, inward of a thirds overlay. A golden spiral is a path, not a stamp: start at a quiet corner and coil toward the face or the object of the look.
Keep the camera level. Moderate glass (40mm to 65mm) preserves the proportions.
Ultra-wide will fake a spiral by bending the room. Prompt: Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid.

prompt_template: Name the curve and the destination. Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid.

The usual wrong cousin is thirds with a spiral graphic imagined on top. The tell is a face on a 33 percent line and a prompt that only says golden.
The fix is to move the mass inward toward 62 percent, or to build an actual path of secondary objects the eye can ride.
faq: What is golden ratio in film?

It is composition that uses proportions near 1.618, as a phi grid or as a spiral path through the masses. The subject is offset, but not as bluntly as on a thirds line. The eye is meant to travel, not to park on a cell.
Golden Ratio vs Rule of Thirds

Thirds splits the frame at 33 percent. Phi splits nearer 38 and 62 percent. Thirds is a default grid on a monitor. Golden-ratio composition is a tighter proportional claim, sometimes a curve. Both beat accidental centering. Neither is a law.
When should I use golden ratio?

Use it when a still or a slow hold has a real path of masses, and you want order that does not look like a student overlay. Skip it for fast geography, jokes, and any shot where the spiral would be a lie.

Ask for a spiral or phi placement and name the path. Example: Golden-ratio spiral composition around [Subject], the eye traveling a harmonic curve rather than a grid. State the start of the coil and the landing point. Avoid mystic math talk.

name: Central Framing
definition: Central framing, also called dead center or center punch, places the figure on the optical axis so the body sits on the crosshairs of the frame. Bilateral weight may gather around that body, but the first fact is placement: the person is the altar, not a guest in a third.
narrative: Put them on the crosshairs and the diagram changes. Off-center space no longer belongs to the look.
Both leftover fields become equal attendants. The subject owns the axis.
Everyone else owns the wings. It is the wrong tool when the character should be hunting, fleeing, or eavesdropping.
A center punch on a spy in a crowd makes them a poster. A center punch on a god, a child in costume, a dictator, or a comic stiff makes the formality legible.
You can center-punch a face in a messy room. That is still central framing.
The architecture does not have to salute. If the whole room salutes, you have walked into centered composition and maybe into symmetry.
how_it_works:
Align the lens axis with the sternum or the bridge of the nose. Keep verticals upright unless you want a joke or a threat.
A longer lens (65mm to 85mm) isolates the bullseye. A wider lens will show whether the room is also axial.
Check both ears have similar leftover, then decide if that equality is the point. Prompt: Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame.
when_to_use: Use it when a character must be presented, judged, or worshipped: an arrival through doors, a formal portrait, a comic stare into lens. Do not use it on a look-off that needs air in front of the eyes.
compared_names: Centered CompositionControl, ritual, comedy, or fate.
SymmetryThe world is designed. Or pretending to be.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Centered Composition organizes the entire field around the axis, often as a frontal tableau. Central framing can be just the body on the crosshairs.
Symmetry mirrors masses. You can punch a face dead center in an asymmetric street.
Rule of Thirds is the default you are breaking. One-Point Perspective adds a vanishing point on that same axis.

The formality is the joke and the tenderness. Grammar, not a Wes Anderson costume kit.
prompt_template: Name the axis. Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame.
prompt_example: If the room must also salute, add frontal architecture. If it must not, say messy sides, figure still dead center.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is thirds with a slightly lazy offset. The tell is more air on the look side than behind the head.
The fix is to slide the figure until both leftover fields match, or to admit you wanted Lead Room and keep the offset.
faq: What is central framing in film?

It is dead-center placement of the figure on the optical axis, a center punch. The body sits on the crosshairs. Leftover space on both sides is equal. The person is presented, not nested into a third.
Central Framing vs Centered Composition

Central framing is where the body sits: on the axis. Centered composition is the whole diagram: furniture, walls, and other bodies often join the altar. You can center-punch a face in a messy room. That is central framing without a full centered tableau.
When should I use central framing?

Use it to present, judge, or joke: a formal arrival, a portrait, a child in a uniform, a tyrant at a desk. Do not use it when the look needs air, or when the character should feel like a guest in someone else's frame.
How do I prompt central framing for AI image or video?

Say dead center and optical axis. Example: Central framing of [Subject], the figure on the optical axis, bilateral weight, a formal altar in the frame. Add square to camera. If you only write portrait, you will get thirds.

name: Centered Composition
definition: Centered composition places the dominant subject on or near the central vertical axis and organizes the rest of the picture around that axis. The frame reads as a frontal tableau: walls, furniture, and attendants arranged so the subject is an altar, not an accident of blocking.
narrative: Control, ritual, comedy, and fate all like this diagram. The person does not borrow space from a third.
The room reports to them, or pretends to. Who owns space is settled in advance by the architecture.

It is the wrong tool for eavesdropping, pursuit, and most dialogue that needs a look-off. If the sides are busy with unequal life, you have an offset picture with a centered head, which is a different sentence.
Wes Anderson made the grammar famous, which is a reason to be precise. Formality is the instrument.
Pastel luggage is not.
how_it_works:
Square the camera to the back wall. Match left and right masses, or let a planned mismatch be the only joke.
Keep the lens on the centerline of the set, not a casual handheld approximation. A 27mm to 40mm will show the room's obedience.
Longer glass will crop the salute and leave you with mere central framing. Prompt: Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar.
when_to_use: Use it for a ritual entrance, a desk of power, a dollhouse comedy, or a fate that feels designed. Do not use it on a chase or a whispered aside that should feel stolen.
compared_names: SymmetryThe world is designed. Or pretending to be.
One-Point PerspectiveDestiny has a vanishing point.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Central Framing only demands the body on the crosshairs. Centered composition demands the field.
Symmetry is the stronger claim that left mirrors right. You can center a subject in a room that is not a mirror.
One-Point Perspective adds a vanishing point on the same axis, a tunnel instead of a flat altar. Tableau holds the arrangement in time.

mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a centered head in an uncomposed room. The tell is a bullseye face with a plant on one side and a door on the other.
The fix is to square the camera, match the masses, or switch to Central Framing and let the mess be honest.
faq: What is centered composition in film?

The dominant subject sits on the central axis, and the rest of the picture is organized around that axis. The frame becomes a frontal tableau. The person is an altar. Leftover space does not belong to a look-off.
Centered Composition vs Symmetry

Centered composition puts the subject on the axis. Symmetry mirrors masses across that axis. A centered desk in a lopsided office is centered without being symmetrical. A mirrored hall with nobody in the middle is symmetrical without a centered hero.
When should I use centered composition?
Use it for control, ritual, comedy, or fate: someone presented by a room that obeys. Do not use it when the character should be hunting through space or hiding in someone else's diagram.
How do I prompt centered composition for AI image or video?

Demand the axis and the room. Example: Dead-center composition of [Subject], bilateral symmetry or frontal tableau, Wes Anderson formality, the subject as altar. Say camera square to the back wall. If you only say centered face, you will get a portrait crop.

name: Symmetry
definition: Symmetry in a symmetrical composition balances visual masses around an axis, usually the vertical centerline, so left answers right. The world looks designed, or it is pretending to be, whether or not a person occupies the middle.
narrative: When left mirrors right, nobody owns a secret side of the frame. Space is ceremonial.
A small break (a crooked tie, a missing lamp, a person one step off axis) becomes the whole event. It is the wrong tool when life should feel unarranged.
A kitchen argument, a chase, a documentary street: forcing a mirror there is a lie unless the lie is the point (a showroom, a regime, a dream). Symmetry is not the same as centering a face.
A mirrored corridor can swallow a figure who is slightly late to their mark. The architecture still owns the diagram.
how_it_works:
Place the camera on the centerline of the set. Match practicals, furniture, and verticals.
Use a level. One-point architecture helps but is not required: a flat elevation of a facade can be a mirror without a vanishing tunnel.
Stop down if both wings must stay sharp. Prompt: Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order.
when_to_use: Use it when the location is a machine of order: hotel, chapel, spaceship, courtroom, dollhouse. Do not use it as wallpaper on a location that has no axis.
compared_names: Centered CompositionControl, ritual, comedy, or fate.
One-Point PerspectiveDestiny has a vanishing point.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Centered Composition plants a subject on the axis. Symmetry mirrors the field, with or without that subject.

One-Point Perspective is a perspective construction that often produces symmetry, but two wings can match in a flat, shallow picture with no tunnel. Repetition and Pattern repeats units without requiring a mirror.
Asymmetry is the refusal.

A fingerprint on that order reads as error or omen. Grammar, not a filter.
prompt_template: Demand the mirror. Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order.

prompt_note: If a break matters, name the one unmatched object.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a centered actor in an unmatched room. The tell is a bullseye face and a window only on the left.
The fix is to move the camera onto the architectural axis, or to drop the claim and shoot Asymmetry with real counterweight.
faq: What is symmetry in film?

It is a frame whose masses balance around an axis, usually the vertical center. Left answers right. The world looks designed. A person may sit on the axis, or the architecture may be the symmetrical subject.
Symmetry vs Centered Composition

Centered composition is about the subject's seat on the axis. Symmetry is about mirrored masses. You can center a person in an asymmetric room, and you can shoot a mirrored hall with the actor late to center. They often travel together. They are not the same diagram.
When should I use symmetry?
Use it when order is the meaning: ritual, comedy of control, science-fiction design, a regime's architecture. Do not glue it onto a street that has no axis.
How do I prompt symmetry for AI image or video?

Ask for a mirror and an axis. Example: Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order. Specify matching practicals and a camera on the centerline. Name one break if the story is the unmatched thing.

name: Asymmetry
definition: Asymmetry, or asymmetrical composition, offsets the dominant mass and answers it with a different kind of weight: color, light, a small face, a dark void, or a distant doorway. The frame does not mirror, so leftover space is a counterweight rather than a matching wing.
narrative: Who owns space is unsettled. A woman in a corridor may occupy a sliver while red wallpaper and a lamp own the rest.
A driver may sit in a third of night while neon and road own the surplus. The counterweight is the point, not the empty accident of a bad mark.
It is the wrong tool when the scene is a ceremony of order. If both sides should salute, shoot the mirror.
If the character should be presented as an altar, do not hide them in a wing. Asymmetry is not automatically thirds.
Thirds is one recipe for offset. You can hang a figure in a far corner and balance them with a bright speck, which is visual weight, not a student grid.
how_it_works:
Place the main body off the centerline. Find a counterweight: a practical, a second figure, a block of color, a window.
Check the frame on a monitor without overlay first. If it tips over, add weight or crop.
A slightly wide lens (32mm to 40mm) lets the unused field stay a real place. Prompt: Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror.
when_to_use: Use it for desire, class, loneliness, and any conversation where the room is not fair. Do not use it as a default mess: unmotivated clutter is not balance.

prompt_example: Say which side holds the body and what holds the other side (lamp, doorway, red wall, dark road). Do not write unbalanced as a mood.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a failed centered shot. The tell is a person who missed their mark and nothing answering them.
The fix is to add a real counterweight, move them to a thirds intersection, or recenter and own Symmetry.
faq: What is asymmetry in film?
It is a composition that does not mirror. The main mass sits off-axis and is answered by a different mass: light, color, a small figure, empty weather. The frame holds by tension, not by reflection.
Asymmetry vs Rule of Thirds

Thirds is one offset recipe: lines at one-third. Asymmetry includes thirds and also stranger diagrams, a body in a corner balanced by a bright speck or a void. If you only know thirds, every offset will look like homework.
When should I use asymmetry?
Use it when the room is not fair: desire, class, isolation, a look that cannot have a mirror. Do not use it as leftover clutter. If nothing answers the offset, the picture just tips.
How do I prompt asymmetry for AI image or video?

State the offset and the counterweight. Example: Asymmetrical balance with [Subject] offset, counterweights of color or mass, tension instead of mirror. Name the side and the answering object. Avoid the word messy unless mess is the counterweight.

name: Leading Lines
definition: Leading lines in leading lines cinematography are edges, rails, roads, corridors, shadows, or gestures that steer the eye toward or through the image. The lines are vectors in the diagram, not decoration around a centered face.
narrative: If a corridor, a rail, or a carpet chevron aims at a person, that person owns the destination and the building owns the path. If the lines aim past them, the person is a gate and infinity owns the rest.
It is the wrong tool when the location has no honest vector. Drawing implied arrows in a bland room is a graphic lie.
A close-up that needs only a face does not need a railroad. Lines can be one-point, two-point, or even a curve.
The job is the same: decide where the eye is forced to land, and whether that landing is a face, a door, or a vanishing field.
how_it_works:
Find real edges in the set: baseboards, rails, a road, a shadow from a hard source. Place the camera so those edges converge on the intended mass.
A wider lens (24mm to 35mm) strengthens convergence. A long lens flattens lines into stacks, which is compression, not pointing.
Keep the horizon level unless the line itself is a dutch. Prompt: Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure.
when_to_use: Use it when a location can aim: station, hotel hall, highway, trench, church nave. Do not invent converging furniture in a set that is actually a box of leftovers.
compared_names: Vanishing PointThere is a long way still to go.
One-Point PerspectiveDestiny has a vanishing point.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Vanishing Point is where parallel lines appear to meet. Leading lines may never meet in frame.
One-Point Perspective is a full axial construction with one dominant vanishing point. Leading lines can be a single railing cutting a messy room.
Diagonal Composition uses bias energy even when nothing converges. Architexture fills the frame with material until pointing is secondary.

faq: What is leading lines in film?

They are real edges in the picture (rails, roads, corridors, shadows, gestures) that steer the eye toward a mass or through the frame. The architecture points. The landing is a choice: face, door, or empty distance.

One-point perspective is a camera squared to a plane with a single vanishing point, often on axis. Leading lines are any vectors that aim. A diagonal railing in a messy street can lead without being a Kubrick hall.
When should I use leading lines?
Use them when the set can honestly point: a hall, a track, a road, a nave. Skip them in a close-up that only needs a face, and skip them in a room with no true edge toward the subject.

Name the lines and the target. Example: Leading lines driving the eye to [Subject], rails, corridors, roads, or shadows converging on the figure. Specify material. If the lines should continue past the person, say so.

name: Frame within Frame
definition: A frame within a frame (doorway framing, surcadrage) puts a second rectangle inside the screen, a door, window, arch, mirror, or gap that encloses the subject. The inner aperture is a second boundary, and crossing it is a beat, not a decoration.
narrative: Someone is watched, trapped, or pictured. The inner frame decides who is allowed in the picture of the picture.
A man in a doorway is either coming home or locked out, depending on which side of the jamb we stand. It is the wrong tool when the second rectangle is only a pretty arch behind a centered face.
If nobody could enter or leave that aperture, you added a sticker. Dirty edges chew.
A frame-in-frame cuts a clean inner border. You can have both: a dirty outer view through a clean door.
Decide which border owns the subject.
how_it_works:
Compose two rectangles. Place the camera so the inner opening has readable sides, top, and (often) threshold.
Control exposure between the two spaces: interior warm, exterior cold, or the reverse. A moderate wide (32mm to 40mm) shows both borders.
If the inner frame swallows the outer, you have simply recropped. Prompt: Frame-within-frame around [Subject], doorway, window, mirror, or arch as a second rectangle, nested attention.
when_to_use: Use it for arrivals, farewells, affairs in corridors, and anyone pictured by a house. Do not drop a random arch behind a portrait and call it nested attention.

An architectural or graphic border inside the screen encloses the subject: door, window, arch, mirror, gap. There are two rectangles. The inner one decides belonging, exclusion, or being pictured.

A dirty frame chews the outer edges with shoulders, glass, foliage, or crowd, often soft. A frame within a frame is a second hard rectangle around the action. One is occupancy of the edge. The other is a nested border. They can combine.

Use it when someone is watched, trapped, welcomed, or pictured by a building. A crossing of the threshold should be able to matter. Do not use it as a pretty inner crop on a portrait.

name: Negative Space
definition: Negative space in negative space cinematography leaves a large, relatively empty area around or beside the subject so absence becomes a mass. The unoccupied field is still a world (sky, wall, snow, sea), and the subject occupies a small or unusual portion of the diagram.
narrative: Loneliness needs room. So does dread, and so does waiting.

A face low under a slab of architecture, a man tiny in a desert, a woman with a blank wall as her partner: the empty area is the other character. It is the wrong tool when the scene is crowded with story.
If the blank wall is just an unlit set, you underexposed a failure. Empty is not automatically meaningful.

Unbalanced framing and short-sided composition are cousins, not synonyms. Negative space can sit above a head (headroom as weather), beside a look (air as future), or all around a speck (the world as indifference).
how_it_works:
Decide what the unoccupied area means before you widen. Control eyeline, headroom, and background detail.
A longer lens can isolate a small figure against a simple field. A wide lens can make the field truly large.
Do not automatically rebalance. Stop down if the empty weather must stay a texture, or open up if it should melt to tone.
Prompt: Vast negative space around [Subject], the figure small, absence as weight, Antonioni emptiness.
when_to_use: Use it when isolation, waiting, or land must outweigh a person: a figure under sky, a face under ceiling, a body at the edge of a pale wall. Do not confuse a blank backdrop with a designed void, and do not auto-balance if the imbalance is the beat.

faq: What is negative space in film?
It is a large unoccupied area around or beside the subject that still reads as world: sky, wall, snow, sea. The empty field has weight. The person does not automatically own the frame.
Negative Space vs Void

Negative space is emptiness inside a place. Void erases the place: a figure against black, white, or nothing. Ida's sky is negative space. A body in an unlit nowhere is a void. Both isolate. Only one still has geography.

Use it when absence should act: isolation, waiting, land that does not care. Do not use it as an unlit wall you forgot to dress. Tie the imbalance to pressure in the scene.

name: Foreground Interest
definition: Foreground interest (a foreground anchor or occluded observation) puts a salient near object between the lens and the subject: flowers, a fence, glass, a table, or a body. The near layer creates depth, scale, a visual entry, or partial concealment, so air and obstacle sit between us and them.
narrative: The diagram now has a landlord in front of the camera. A bedpost, a shoulder, a glass of whisky can own the near third while the scene happens beyond.
We feel physically situated. Sometimes we feel we should not be there.
It is the wrong tool when the near object covers the decisive face or when it is random clutter. A plant in focus in front of an important mouth is not depth.
It is a mistake. Foreground interest can be sharp (a gun on a table, Kane's objects) or soft (flowers as a veil).
Sharp near matter stages power. Soft near matter stages eavesdropping.
how_it_works:
Place a real object close to the lens, on a plane that reads as obstacle. Coordinate its edge with eyes and hands so it conceals by design.
A wide or moderate wide (24mm to 40mm) exaggerates the near mass. Open the aperture if the layer should melt.
Stop down if the near object is information. Prompt: Strong foreground object between lens and [Subject], dirty aperture of flowers, fence, or glass, layered depth.
when_to_use: Use it to put the camera in a room that already has stuff, to spy, or to show a power object in front of a distant person. Do not let the foreground eat the expression you came for.

name: Layered Depth
definition: Layered depth, or layered composition, stages important action on at least two distances, typically foreground, midground, and background in one picture. Depth staging is that arrangement, while deep focus is a separate optical choice about how much of it is sharp.
narrative: Social geometry becomes visible at once. Adults sign a boy's future in a near room while the boy plays in a distant window.
A phone booth and a piano split a bar. Who owns space is a matter of which plane can still act.
It is the wrong tool when only one plane has story. Three pretty layers of wallpaper are not layered depth.
If you cannot imagine walking from the near object to the far door, the diagram is a collage. Do not assume every deep stage must be uniformly sharp.
You can hold two actions and still rack. The arrangement is the composition.
The iris is the optics.
how_it_works:
Place meaningful bodies or objects on separate planes with readable gaps. Keep sightlines and entrances clear.
Choose a wider lens and more distance if you want natural deep space. Stop down (and add light) if several planes must be sharp.
A split diopter is a different cheat. Prompt: Three-plane composition around [Subject], foreground, mid, and deep background all carrying information, deep staging.
when_to_use: Use it when two relationships must be true in one hold: a deal and a child, a dance and a call, a guard and a prisoner. Do not stack bric-a-brac in three zones and call it staging.

Layered depth is spatial organization: who stands where. Deep focus is optics: how much is sharp. You can stage three planes and rack between them. You can also stop down so the whole stage holds. Do not conflate the two.

name: Diagonal Composition
definition: Diagonal composition uses diagonal lines and masses (stairs, rifles, rain, a body on the bias, a street receding on a corner) to raise energy, instability, or depth. The camera can stay level, because the set supplies the tilt of the diagram.
narrative: Stillness would be a lie if the scene is a riot, a chase down stairs, or a city that will not sit square. Diagonals shove the eye and refuse a calm horizon of furniture.

It is the wrong tool for a formal treaty, a joke about order, or a face that needs to be an altar. If you roll the camera to fake a diagonal that the set does not have, you have made a dutch angle, which is a different sentence.
A single strong bias line can be enough: a banister, a shadow, a gun. Filling the frame with accidental slants is not composition.
It is a crooked set.
how_it_works:
Keep the head level unless you truly want a dutch. Find a bias vector in blocking or architecture and place the subject on it or against it.
A wider lens increases the thrust of a receding diagonal. Hard light can throw a diagonal shadow as a second line.
Prompt: Diagonal composition through [Subject], energy on the bias, unstable, rain or stairs as the line.
when_to_use: Use it for stairs, street corners, rain, battles, and any beat where a level diagram would calm the scene down. Do not roll the camera to counterfeit a line the location does not offer.

Asymmetry offsets mass without requiring a bias line.

It is a picture organized on the bias: stairs, streets, rain, bodies, shadows as diagonal vectors. Energy and instability come from those lines. The camera may remain level. The set does the tilting.

A dutch angle rolls the camera so the whole world lists. Diagonal composition uses lines already in the scene. You can have both, but a rolled horizon is not automatically a diagonal composition, and stairs on a level camera are not a dutch.

name: Triangular Composition
definition: Triangular composition arranges subjects or visual masses into a triangle so three points lock the frame. A group gets a hierarchy: the apex is usually power, witness, or the object of desire, and the base is support, threat, or the audience inside the picture.
narrative: Two people and a desk, a family and a doorway, three men and a gun: the triangle tells you who sits at the top of the diagram. Renaissance blocking taught this before cinema.
The camera inherited the altar. It is the wrong tool for a true two-hander that should be a flat axis, or for a crowd that has no hierarchy.
Forcing a triangle onto two people plus a plant is a fake court. The apex can be low (a child, a corpse, a briefcase) and still run the picture.
Height is not automatically rank. Placement in the triangle is.
how_it_works:
Block three masses with clear vertices. Check the silhouette on a wide enough lens that all three read (often 27mm to 40mm, or a longer lens at a distance).
Keep depth of field sufficient for the intended points. A Three-Shot is a size.
The triangle is the geometry inside it. Prompt: Triangular arrangement with [Subject] at an apex, three masses locking the frame, Renaissance blocking.
when_to_use: Use it when a group has a hierarchy: a don and two captains, a family portrait with a secret, a bargaining table. Do not invent a third mass to complete a shape nobody in the scene would form.
compared_names: Visual WeightThe eye should land where the story is.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Three-Shot is coverage of three bodies, which may sit in a line. Triangular composition is the pyramid, even if one mass is a doorway or a lamp.
Visual Weight decides which vertex wins the eye. Centered Composition may plant the apex on the axis.
Tableau can freeze the triangle for duration. Symmetry may split a triangle into a formal court.

The fix is to sit one figure, stand another, and give the third a doorway or a chair so the triangle actually locks.

Subjects or masses form a triangle in the frame. Three points lock the picture. The apex usually holds power, desire, or the thing being judged. The base supports or threatens.

A three-shot is a framing size: three people in the picture. They might stand in a row. Triangular composition is geometry. One vertex can even be an object or a doorway. Size is not shape.

name: Headroom
definition: Headroom in headroom cinematography is the space between the crown of the head and the top frame edge. Tight headroom applies pressure, while generous headroom hands the upper field to air, architecture, or sky.
narrative: The vertical diagram is easy to ignore until it is wrong. Too much accidental headroom makes a person sink, a student error.
Too little clips thought. Deliberate surplus (a nun under a pale wall, a man under oil derricks) makes emptiness a partner.
It is the wrong tool to 'fix' by always parking the eyes on a thirds line. Some faces need to be crushed under a ceiling.
Some need to float. The rule of thirds is a default for the eyes, not a law for the top edge.
Headroom talks to costume and architecture. A tall hat, a halo lamp, a beam: the top edge is a character.
how_it_works:
Measure from hair to the frame line, not from eyes. For a standard close-up, leave a modest band, enough that a nod will not clip.
For pressure, shave it to a hair. For weather or faith, drop the face in the lower third and let ceiling or sky own the rest.
Tilt and pedestal change headroom without changing lens. Prompt: Deliberate headroom on [Subject], either tight to the hair (pressure) or generously open (air, God, sky).
when_to_use:
Use tight headroom when the room is a trap or the thought has no ceiling. Use open headroom when land, church, or sky must outweigh the skull.

name: Lead Room
definition: Lead room in lead room cinematography (nose room, looking room) is space in the direction a subject looks or moves. More frame sits ahead of the walk or the gaze than behind the head, so the surplus is the path rather than leftover wallpaper.
narrative: The horizontal diagram assigns the future. Air in front of the nose is the path, the other person, the door.
Air behind the skull is the past or a trap. Classical coverage buys this air by default.
It is the wrong tool when the character has nowhere to go. A prisoner, a liar pinned by a question, a car about to hit a wall: giving them lead room is politeness the scene does not want.
Lead room is not automatically thirds. You can give a walker a huge field (almost a landscape) or a modest band in a close-up.
The direction of the surplus is the definition.
how_it_works:
Put the look or the motion toward the empty side. If they walk screen-left, leave more frame on the left.
Pan with a walker to keep that surplus, or let them eat it if arrival is the point. A profile needs more lead than a three-quarter.
Prompt: Lead room in front of [Subject]'s look or walk, more space in the direction of attention than behind, forward narrative.
when_to_use:
Use it for walks, looks that will be answered, and any coverage that should feel like forward grammar. Do not give lead room to a character you mean to trap.

name: Short Siding
definition: Short siding places the face near the frame edge the character looks toward, crushing look-space and leaving surplus air behind the head. The edge they face becomes a wall, so the diagram denies them a future in the picture.
narrative: Deny the character air and the scene tightens without a closer lens. An interrogator, a liar, a person who has just seen the worst thing: they look into almost nothing.
The leftover field behind them is wasted country they cannot use. It is the wrong tool for ordinary coverage.
Do it by accident and the shot feels like a student pan. Do it on every close-up and the trap stops meaning.
Short siding is not the same as a big empty wall. If they look into a vast field, you have negative space in the look.
Short siding specifically starves the look.
how_it_works:
Put the eyes close to the edge they face. Leave the larger field behind the skull.
A profile or strong three-quarter makes the crush obvious. You can still use a 50mm or 75mm.
The crop does the violence, not a wider lens. Do not correct it in the pan.

name: Visual Weight
definition: Visual weight in visual weight composition is the attention an element attracts through size, contrast, color, position, focus, faces, or motion. A small bright thing can equal a large dark mass, because scale of attention is not scale of object.
narrative: The diagram is a set of weights, not a ruler. A cigarette in a pool of light can outweigh a sofa.
A face, even tiny, will beat a mountain unless you starve the face of contrast. Who owns space is who wins the glance in the first half second, then the second glance you designed.
It is the wrong tool as a slogan. Saying visual weight without choosing a winner is a wish.
If two masses fight to a draw, the beat is confused unless the fight is the point. Motion and faces cheat.
A still landscape that was balanced becomes a different picture when a figure turns. Recheck weight when action starts.
how_it_works:
List the masses and their currencies: size, tone, chroma, sharpness, position (center and upper field weigh more), faces, movement. Dim or desaturate the losers, or throw them out of focus.
A hard key on a small object is a common way to mint weight. Prompt: Composition balancing visual weight around [Subject], a bright small thing equal to a large dark mass, scale of attention.
when_to_use: Use it whenever more than one mass could steal the shot: a deal on a table, a child in a window, a red coat in a grey street. Do not light every surface equally and hope the script will point.

name: Figure-Ground
definition: Figure-ground composition separates the subject from the field so the person or object reads in under a second. Contrast of tone, color, or focus does the split, and if figure and ground share the same value the diagram fails even if the acting is good.

The usual wrong cousin is leftover wallpaper, or a false eyeline cut. The tell is empty space on the wrong side of the face, or a next shot the look could not geometrically reach.
The fix is to put the surplus in the gaze direction and to match height and angle if you complete the look.
faq: What is look space in film?
It is the area of frame a gaze owns, usually ahead of the eyes. Often the important object is off-screen, so the air is tension. In editing, the look may be joined to a shot of what is seen.
Look Space vs Lead Room

Lead room is space in the direction of movement, and by extension a standing look. Look space is the gaze as a relationship to an object, present or withheld. A runner needs lead room. A watcher of a courtyard needs look-space. They overlap in a still profile. They are not the same job.
When should I use look space?
Use it when what matters is off-screen or about to arrive, and the face watching is the present tense. Do not confuse leftover margin on an interview with a look.
How do I prompt look space for AI image or video?

Point the eyes and empty the field they face. Example: Generous look space for [Subject], the off-screen gaze owning a field of air, tension in what we cannot see. Say the object is not in frame. For video, you can add a second shot as POV.

name: Architexture
definition: Architexture, a nickname for architectural cinematography that treats the set as subject, fills the frame with facades, grids, and materials until a person is a detail of the building. Texture, module, and mass own space, and the body is an ornament or a scale figure.
narrative: When the set is the subject, human plot becomes a visitor. Concrete, glass, carpet, and window bands do the talking.
A figure gives scale, then disappears into the pattern. It is the wrong tool when a close-up of a lie is the scene.
Architecture cannot deliver an eye twitch. If you drown a dialogue in facade, you will photograph a building and call it a conversation.
This is not automatically one-point ceremony. A flat elevation, a brutalist soffit, a repeating office ceiling can be architexture without a vanishing tunnel.
how_it_works:
Expose for the material: raking light for relief, or flat light for graphic grids. Use a longer lens to compress floors into texture, or a wide lens close to a wall so the body is tiny against a single plane.
Stop down so brick and joint stay sharp if texture is the point. Prompt: Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.
when_to_use: Use it when place outweighs person: first arrival in a city, a worker in a machine, a critic of a monument. Do not use it as the only coverage of an intimate scene.
compared_names: One-Point PerspectiveDestiny has a vanishing point.
Repetition and PatternSystems, armies, hotels, factories.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: One-Point Perspective aims space as a tunnel. Architexture may be a flat, tactile wall.
Repetition and Pattern counts units. Architexture can be irregular material, poured and stained.
Extreme Long Shot shrinks a person in land. This shrinks them in built matter.
Windows makes apertures the subject. Architexture may have almost no people in those apertures.
One-Point PerspectiveDestiny has a vanishing point.
Repetition and PatternSystems, armies, hotels, factories.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: Playtime (PlayTime) lets modern Paris eat its visitors: glass, grid, and waiting room as comedy of texture. The Brutalist language puts poured mass and material ahead of comfort.
The person remains, as scale. Grammar of buildings, not a tourist postcard.
prompt_template: Let the building win. Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.
prompt_example: Architecture as texture around [Subject], façades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building.
prompt_note: Do not crop as a portrait.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a human portrait with a famous building behind. The tell is a large face and a postcard sliver of facade.
The fix is to step back or go longer until the body is a module among modules, or to admit you wanted a portrait and drop the claim.
faq: What is architexture in film?
It is composition that treats architecture as the subject: facades, grids, and materials filling the frame. A person remains as a detail or a scale figure. The set owns space.
Architexture vs One-Point Perspective

One-point perspective is a tunnel of receding parallels, often ceremonial. Architexture is material and module, which might be a flat wall, a ceiling grid, or a poured mass with no vanishing showpiece. They can combine in a designed hall. They need not.
When should I use architexture?
Use it when the building is the story: arrival, labor, monument, a system of rooms. Do not use it as the only shot of a face that must be read.
How do I prompt architexture for AI image or video?

Make the person small in material. Example: Architecture as texture around [Subject], facades, grids, and materials filling the frame until the person is a detail of the building. Name concrete, glass, or grid. Forbid portrait crop.

name: Reflections
definition: Reflections in reflection cinematography put observer and observed in one plane by using glass, water, chrome, or a mirror. Mirror dialogue and one-way-glass staging let two spaces occupy a single composition, because optics, not a filter, do the doubling.
narrative: Show looking and the looked-at together and you skip a cut. A man and a woman speak through a booth.
A face and a street stack in a shop window. Identity splits without a dissolve.

It is the wrong tool when the reflection is an unreadable smear, or when it cheats physics (a mirror that does not answer a head turn). If you cannot map the sightline, the audience will feel the fake even if they cannot name it.
Reflections can dirty a frame or frame-in-frame a second world. Decide which space is brighter.
The brighter side writes itself onto the darker glass.
how_it_works:
Map optics before you light. Control which side is hotter: the reflection needs a brighter source to read on glass.
Hide the camera, or let it appear if that is the joke. Keep gaze and reflection geometrically honest.
Polarizers kill or manage bounce. Water needs an angle and a still or living surface.
Prompt: Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane.
when_to_use: Use it for split identity, conversations that cannot be face to face, cities on windows, a child seeing a parent in a cabinet. Do not add a random mirror because the set has one.
compared_names: Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
SilhouetteIdentity is less important than shape.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Frame within Frame uses a hard inner rectangle. A reflection may be a smear, a stack, or a perfect copy.
Silhouette can appear in glass as outline. Screen in Screen is an electronic or projected picture, not a bounce.
Dirty Frame often uses glass as an edge chew. Here the glass is the sentence.
Windows may include reflections, but windows as a technique are stacked apertures of lives.
Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
SilhouetteIdentity is less important than shape.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: The Lady from Shanghai multiplies positions in a mirror maze until aiming becomes impossible. Paris, Texas stages Travis and Jane across a one-way-glass booth so seeing is not symmetrical.
In the Mood for Love catches bodies in glass and rain. Contact uses a cabinet mirror in a child's race down a hall: reflection as geography.
Paris, Texas 1984Travis and Jane speak across the one-way-glass booth.
The Lady from Shanghai 1947The mirror-maze climax multiplies possible positions.
Contact 1997Young Ellie races for the bathroom medicine cabinet after discovering her father collapsed.
prompt_template: A man and woman speak across a one-way-glass booth. Her illuminated face is visible while his dim reflection gradually overlays the glass as the light balance changes. Keep their positions consistent and the reflection optically plausible. Slow, restrained performance; no supernatural double.
prompt_example: Name the surface and both occupants. Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane.
prompt_note: Add camera hidden if the camera must not appear.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a pasted-on double, or a mirror that ignores head movement. The tell is a reflection that does not match angle, brightness, or motion.
The fix is to build a real optic: brighter observed side, correct eyeline, and a surface that could actually see both.
faq: What is reflections in film?
Glass, water, chrome, or a mirror puts two spaces into one picture. Observer and observed can share a plane. The bounce must obey optics: angle, brightness, and motion.
Reflections vs Frame within Frame

A frame within a frame is a second rectangle, often a door or window opening. A reflection is an optical copy or overlay on a surface. A window can do both: it can be an aperture and a mirror at once if you light both sides.
When should I use reflections?
Use them to show looking and the looked-at together, to split a self, or to have a conversation that cannot be face to face. Do not insert a mirror as furniture with no optical job.
How do I prompt reflections for AI image or video?

Name the surface and both parties. Example: Reflections of [Subject] in glass, water, or chrome, observer and observed in one plane. Specify one-way glass, shop window, or water. For video, demand the reflection match head movement.

name: Screen in Screen
definition: Screen in screen (desktop film, interface as the camera) nests a monitor, phone, television, or cinema inside the cinema so someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner image has its own crop, delay, and artifacts, and nested looking is the diagram.
narrative: A picture of a picture changes ownership. The person on the inner screen is already framed by someone else: a director, a hacker, a parent, a god.
We watch the watcher, or we become them if the interface takes over the outer frame. It is the wrong tool when the inner screen is an unreadable glow.
If text, faces, or timing cannot be parsed, you have set dressing. Desktop films live or die on exact writing and cursor behavior.
This is not split screen. Split screen is a graphic of two presents.
Screen-in-screen is a nested world with a power relation.
how_it_works:
Design a real timeline and a legible inner frame. Photograph or generate the inner picture as an asset, then place it in a monitor with correct perspective, refresh, and reflections.
Do not ask a generator to invent stable UI and accurate text in one pass if the words matter. Prompt: Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking.
when_to_use: Use it when looking is already mediated: security, live TV, a search on a laptop, a projectionist, a god's control room. Do not add a TV that plays nothing relevant.
compared_names: Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Frame within Frame is usually architecture. Screen-in-screen is a display with its own image.
Split Screen tiles simultaneous presents without one being a device in the other. Windows stacks architectural panes of lives.
Voyeur may watch a screen, but voyeur is the concealment ethic. Reflections can stack a face on a dark monitor, a hybrid.
Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
Split ScreenTwo rooms, one moment.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: The Truman Show makes the world a production watched on screens. Videodrome infects the watcher through the tube.
Searching and Unfriended run investigation and terror through interfaces whose text and timing are the coverage. Sherlock Jr.
lets a projectionist enter the inner picture. Grammar of nested looking, not a wallpaper of monitors.
Searching 2018The investigation is presented through screens, calls and digital activity.
Unfriended 2014The action unfolds through a computer interface and group call.
Sherlock Jr. 1924The projectionist enters the world of the cinema screen.
The Stendhal Syndrome 1996Anna's perception carries her into a painting.
Paprika 2006Images and screens become passages between dream spaces.
prompt_template: Create a desktop-screen short: a woman starts writing an apology email, deletes it, receives an old photo and opens a video call she hesitates to answer. Generate the photo and call footage separately. Build the interface, readable text, cursor path and notification timing with code or compositing. No unreadable AI-generated UI text.
prompt_example: Specify the outer view and the inner picture. Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking.
prompt_note: Keep the inner image stable.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a blurry TV set, or a fake Split Screen. The tell is unreadable text, melting UI, or two images tiled with no device.
The fix is to treat the inner picture as a designed insert with real words and a physically plausible monitor.
faq: What is screen in screen in film?
A display inside the shot carries its own picture: monitor, phone, cinema screen. Someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner crop, delay, and artifacts are part of the grammar.
Screen in Screen vs Split Screen

Split screen tiles two or more presents as a graphic. Screen-in-screen puts one picture inside a device in the other. Power and mediation differ. A control-room wall of monitors is nested looking. A graphic half-and-half of two callers is split screen unless those halves are phones in a room.
When should I use screen in screen?
Use it when looking is already a broadcast, a search, a tape, or a show: surveillance, desktop investigation, a film within the film. Do not add a glowing panel with no content.
How do I prompt screen in screen for AI image or video?

Name device and inner content. Example: Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking. For UI stories, render text deterministically. Do not generate the whole interface as unstable video if words must be exact.

name: Tableau
definition: A tableau (tableau vivant, frontal ensemble, or frieze) is a staged composition whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Arranged bodies and objects form a living picture, so duration replaces coverage while the camera stays locked or nearly locked.
narrative: Hold the arrangement and the audience reads at their own speed: who stands where, who fails to move, who sneaks a gesture. Stillness makes a tiny action loud.
Comedy, ceremony, and dread all use that delay. It is the wrong tool when the scene needs chase geography or a close-up of a lie.
If you cut the tableau to pieces immediately, you shot a master and threw it away. If the arrangement has no readable relationships, you shot decoration.
Tableau is not automatically centered, but it likes a designed field. Dirty edges can still apply if the living picture is glimpsed from a door.
how_it_works:
Block silhouettes, spacing, and sightlines before adding motion. Rehearse separate timings inside the shared frame.
Use enough depth of field that the intended points stay readable. A locked tripod is the default.
A slow creep is a different sentence. Prompt: Tableau of [Subject], arranged bodies, a living painting, duration instead of coverage.
when_to_use: Use it for ritual, comic ensembles, processions, and any beat that should be discovered rather than prescribed by cutting. Do not hold a well-dressed but empty arrangement.
compared_names: Centered CompositionControl, ritual, comedy, or fate.
Static Locked-OffTrust blocking and duration. Movement would be noise.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Static Locked-Off is the camera lock. Tableau is the staged picture that uses that lock.
Centered Composition is a common altar for it, not a requirement. Group Shot is a size.
Tableau is duration plus arrangement. Triangular Composition may be the geometry inside the hold.
Long Take may travel. A tableau usually stays and lets time do the move.
Centered CompositionControl, ritual, comedy, or fate.
Static Locked-OffTrust blocking and duration. Movement would be noise.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: Barry Lyndon holds painterly courts until a glance is an event. Roy Andersson's films park ensembles in still rooms so a small failure is comic and awful.
PlayTime distributes gags across broad, held compositions. The Color of Pomegranates arranges people and objects as ritual friezes.
Grammar of duration, not a freeze.
PlayTime 1967Office and restaurant scenes distribute comedy across broad compositions.
The Color of Pomegranates 1969Frontal, ritualized arrangements of people and objects.
prompt_template: Locked wide frontal shot of five museum attendants preparing a display. Each performs a different small task; one repeatedly moves an object that another immediately returns. Clear spacing, readable full-body gestures, dry visual humor, no close-ups or camera motion.
prompt_example: Name positions (left standing, center seated, right in a doorway) and say camera locked off. For video, add little motion except a planned gesture, no coverage cuts.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a Master Shot you plan to chop, or a pretty still with no relationships. The tell is a posed group that exists to be pretty, then a cut to close-ups that do all the work.
The fix is to give each body a job and to let the hold be the coverage.
faq: What is tableau in film?

It is a staged picture whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Bodies and objects are arranged. Duration does the work that cutting would otherwise do. A living painting, not a freeze frame.
Tableau vs Static Locked-Off

Static is a camera that does not move. Tableau is an arranged field that uses stillness, usually with a locked camera. You can lock off a messy documentary corner and have static without tableau. You can, rarely, drift across a tableau, but the default is a hold.
When should I use tableau?
Use it for ritual, ensemble comedy, processions, and any scene the audience should read as a whole. Do not use it as a pretty pause in a chase, and do not cut it to bits immediately.
How do I prompt tableau for AI image or video?

Describe the arrangement and the hold. Example: Tableau of [Subject], arranged bodies, a living painting, duration instead of coverage. List positions. For video, specify a locked camera and a long hold with one planned gesture.

name: Void
definition: A void in void cinematography erases the set: darkness, white, or a blank field eating the world until a figure stands against nothing. Negative space still belongs to a place, while a void deletes place, leaving almost no landlord but the body or the darkness that might eat it.
narrative: Erase the set and the social world goes with it. A woman in a black room, a man in white nowhere, a beam with no walls: there is no furniture to own space, only the figure and the absence.
It is the wrong tool when geography matters. A void cannot show a door, a class, or a weather.
If you still need the kitchen, you wanted negative space or cameo light in a real room. Cameo lighting can create a void by refusing to fill.
The void is the compositional result: no readable world, not merely a moody key.
how_it_works:
Kill the surround. Black velvet, an unlit stage, fogged white, a clipped sky.
Light only the figure, or let them fall to Silhouette on nothing. Watch for stray stand legs and floor bounce.
A longer lens helps exclude leftover set. Prompt: Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing.
when_to_use: Use it for existential isolation, alien rooms, interrogation nowhere, a mind. Do not use it as a cheap way to hide a location you did not dress.
compared_names: Cameo LightingErase the world. Keep the person.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Negative Space keeps a world (sky, wall, sea) as the empty mass. Void removes the world.
Cameo Lighting is the lighting method that often produces a dark void: a pool on a figure, no environment. Clean Frame still allows a tidy place.
Silhouette is outline against a brighter field, which can be a void if that field is featureless. Low-Key Lighting may still show a room in the shadows.
Negative SpaceLoneliness needs room.
Cameo LightingErase the world. Keep the person.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: Under the Skin uses black, featureless space as a place that is not a place, bodies without social furniture. The Lighthouse isolates men in weather and dark until the world feels eaten, more void than village.
Grammar of deletion, not a crushed exposure accident.
prompt_template: Delete the place. Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing.
prompt_example: Say black void, no set, no floor detail, or white featureless field. Light only the figure.
prompt_note: Forbid furniture and windows.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is an underexposed room, or Negative Space with a visible wall. The tell is a baseboard, a plant, or grainy wallpaper in the dark.
The fix is to actually kill the surround (velvet, distance, flags), or to own the wall as designed emptiness.
faq: What is void in film?
It is a composition that erases the set. The figure stands against darkness, white, or a blank field. There is no readable place. Absence is not a sky or a wall. It is nothing.
Void vs Negative Space

Negative space is empty area inside a world: desert, ceiling, sea. Void deletes the world. A nun under a pale church wall is negative space. A body in featureless black is a void. Both isolate. Only one still has geography.
When should I use void?
Use it when place should vanish: alien interior, mind, interrogation nowhere, existential isolation. Do not use it to hide an undressed set that still needs to be a room.
How do I prompt void for AI image or video?

Forbid the set. Example: Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing. Add no environment, no furniture. Specify black or white. Models love to invent rooms. Ban them.

name: Voyeur
definition: Voyeur cinematography places the camera in concealment so the audience is trespassing: a view through foliage, glass, a grate, or a distant window, often with dirty edges. The diagram is a peephole, not coverage, and the owner of that hide does not want us there.
narrative: The audience is trespassing. That is the beat.
A couple through blinds, a conversation across a square, a tent at night: we occupy a hiding place. The subject does not present.
They are caught, or they would be if they turned. It is the wrong tool for granted intimacy.
A close-up the character knows about is not voyeur. An over-the-shoulder in a dialogue scene is coverage, even if a shoulder dirties the edge.
Offscreen sound often rides with this view (a whistle, a courtyard, a tent wall) because the hide limits what we can see. The technique itself is the concealed camera, not the soundtrack.
how_it_works:
Put a real occluder between lens and subject and stand where a watcher could stand. Keep enough aperture to melt the hide (leaves, fabric, a slit) while holding the distant face.
A longer lens is the usual cheat for distance. Do not center the peephole like a pretty wreath unless the hide is a designed iris.
Prompt: Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have.
when_to_use: Use it when watching is transgression: affairs, surveillance, a neighbor, a hunter. Do not slap dirty leaves on a scene the character is performing for us.
compared_names: Dirty FrameWe are not supposed to have this view.
Over-the-Shoulder CoverageDefault dialogue coverage with spatial glue.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Dirty Frame is the edge grammar voyeur often uses. Voyeur is the ethical position: concealment.
You can dirty a party from inside the crowd without hiding. Over-the-Shoulder Coverage is dialogue coverage with a known listener in the foreground.
Frame within Frame may be a window we are invited to look through. Windows stacks many lives.
Voyeur picks one hide. Point of View claims we are the character.
Voyeur often claims we are not supposed to be anyone.
Dirty FrameWe are not supposed to have this view.
Over-the-Shoulder CoverageDefault dialogue coverage with spatial glue.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
in_film: Rear Window makes looking across a courtyard the plot. The Conversation records and watches until privacy is a myth.

Cache (Hidden) holds distant, unauthorized views until the camera itself is an aggressor. M and The Blair Witch Project let presence arrive from beyond the visible, often as sound around a limited hide.
Grammar of trespass, not a leaf kit.

The Blair Witch Project 1999Night sounds suggest activity outside the tent and camera view.
The Usual Suspects 1995The final details destabilize the story that has been narrated.
Fight Club 1999Later information changes the meaning of earlier interactions.
The Sixth Sense 1999The ending reorganizes the viewer's understanding of earlier scenes.

Alien 1979The creature and ship's spaces are revealed selectively.

prompt_template: Locked shot inside a dim railway waiting room. An unseen suitcase rolls across the platform outside; its wheels move audibly from left to right, pause, then return. The lone passenger reacts without the camera revealing the source. Design spatially coherent audio separately, with no visible creature or arbitrary musical sting.
prompt_example: Name the hide and the forbidden view. Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have.
prompt_note: Occupy the edges with the hide.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a pretty Dirty Frame the subject could see, or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage from a scene partner. The tell is eye contact with lens, or a hide that is only a vignette.
The fix is a real occluder, a plausible hiding place, and a subject who does not present.
faq: What is voyeur in film?
The camera watches from concealment. The audience is trespassing. Dirty edges, distance, and a peephole often result. The subject does not offer the view. We take it.
Voyeur vs Dirty Frame

A dirty frame occupies the edges with matter. Voyeur is why we are standing there: we are hidden. A crowded street can be dirty without being voyeur. A clean, distant locked-off shot of an apartment can be voyeur without much edge chew, as in an unauthorized surveillance hold.
When should I use voyeur?
Use it when looking is a transgression: neighbor, spy, hunter, affair. Do not use it as default decoration on a scene performed for the camera.
How do I prompt voyeur for AI image or video?

Name the concealment and the unaware subject. Example: Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have. Specify blinds, foliage, a grate, a long lens. Forbid eye contact with camera.

name: Windows
definition: Windows cinematography treats panes as the true subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The diagram is a grid of possible pictures, not one doorway around one face.
narrative: A facade at night is a contact sheet of other people's rooms. A courtyard is a theater of windows.
Who owns space changes per rectangle: a cook, a sleeper, a fighter, an empty kitchen. The building is a montage that does not cut.
It is the wrong tool when you only need one inner frame around one encounter. That is a single frame-within-frame.
If the other panes do no work, you photographed a house. Windows can be looked through from inside (rain on glass, a face and a street) or looked at from outside (Rear Window grammar).
Decide which side of the glass we occupy, and whether reflections will stack a second world.
how_it_works:
Find a true grid: a courtyard, a block of apartments, an office elevation. Use a longer lens to flatten panes into a sheet of rectangles, or a wider lens if we are inside one room looking at many across a court.
Expose so more than one interior reads, or so most go dark except the one that matters. Prompt: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.
when_to_use: Use it when many lives share a building, or when a single life is one pane among others. Do not use it as a pretty rain window on a portrait that never acknowledges other rooms.
compared_names: Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
Screen in ScreenSomeone is watching a picture of someone.
Rule of ThirdsDefault dynamic balance. Break it later on purpose.
compared_text: Frame within Frame is usually one inner rectangle. Windows multiplies them.
Screen in Screen nests electronic pictures. These are architectural pictures.
Voyeur may watch one pane from concealment. Windows can also be a public elevation, a city showing itself.
Repetition and Pattern counts the grid. Here the content of each cell matters.
Reflections may write the street onto the same glass.
Frame within FrameSomeone is watched, trapped, or pictured.
Screen in ScreenSomeone is watching a picture of someone.

in_film: Rear Window turns a courtyard of windows into a set of simultaneous shorts. The Hours uses windows as thresholds between interior lives and the weather of a city.
A building becomes an editing machine you can hold. Grammar of panes, not a single pretty rain glass.
prompt_template: Make the panes the subject. Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.
prompt_example: Say courtyard facade at night, multiple lit interiors, or a wall of office panes. Place the subject in one rectangle among others.
prompt_note: Name at least two other lives or empty rooms.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a single rain-streaked portrait, or a Frame within Frame doorway. The tell is one face and one glass with no other cells.
The fix is to show a grid of apertures and to give at least one other pane a life, even if it is only a lamp and an empty chair.
faq: What is windows in film?
Panes become the subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The composition is a grid of possible shots. One person may occupy one cell. The other cells still work.
Windows vs Frame within Frame

Frame within a frame is typically one inner border around the action, a door or arch. Windows multiplies apertures until the building is a sheet of pictures. A single window around a couple is doorway grammar. A courtyard of ten lit rooms is windows.
When should I use windows?
Use it when many lives share glass: apartments, offices, a courtyard at night, a city block. Skip it when you only need one threshold around one encounter.
How do I prompt windows for AI image or video?

Ask for stacked panes and multiple lives. Example: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. Specify a facade or courtyard and more than one lit interior. Place the subject in one cell.

It is a color finish that keeps skin faithful and saturation restrained, so the location's real hues remain in charge. The grade refuses a stylized split or a fever.

Filmic faded is about the print curve: lifted blacks, rolled highlights. A natural grade is about hue honesty. They can combine, but a faded print can still be teal-orange, which is no longer natural.
