name: Color Shift
definition: A color shift effect is a change of color state that the audience is meant to notice: monochrome to hue, one world to another, or a slide of temperature during the shot. Color is the event, not a hidden LUT.
narrative: Dorothy opens a door and the world gains hue. A zone, a lie, a memory: the threshold can be a cut, a doorway, or a grade that travels inside the take.
The audience crosses with the character. A global saturation ramp is different from a color world revealed through a door.
It is the wrong tool when the film simply has more than one static Palette across chapters. Palettes can sit still; a shift is a change you watch.
It is also the wrong tool for Cross Process or Split Toning that never move. If the beat is one loud world from the first frame, you wanted Hyper-Saturation or a locked palette, not a shift.
how_it_works:
Choose whether the change occurs across a cut, through an opening, or gradually inside the image. Match production design and exposure so the arrival of color (or of a new temperature) feels intended.
If you go from grey to hue, expose the grey chapter so the later color has somewhere to live. Prompt: Color shift across [Subject], hues sliding mid-shot or mid-grade, a world that changes temperature in front of us.
For video: The grade around [Subject] shifts hue during the shot, warmth turning cold or the reverse.
when_to_use: Use it when color is the event: a door onto a new world, a lie that changes temperature, a zone. Do not use it as a random hue drift, and do not call two static chapter palettes a shift unless we watch the change.
compared_names: Split ToningShadows and lights belong to different gods.
Teal and OrangeYou want contemporary studio punch. Use with taste.

faq: What is a color shift in film?
It is a noticeable change of color state: grey to hue, warm to cold, or one world-color to another. The change is the event, whether across a door, a cut, or a traveling grade.

Split toning is a stable pair of highlight and shadow hues. A color shift is a transition the audience watches. If the pair never moves, it is not a shift.

name: Vintage
definition: A vintage film look treats the image as past chemistry: faded dyes, possible Halation, softened contrast, and period color that has drifted. It is a whole-file costume of time, not only old glass and not only a lifted print curve.
narrative: It already happened. Dyes have wandered.
Whites are not video-white. The past is chemistry, not a sticker of scratches.

A 1970s still, a memory sitcom, a period film that wants the stock to confess its age: the treatment says archive even when the camera is new. It is the wrong tool when the only thing you wanted was Cooke swirl on a contemporary story (Vintage Cine Glass).
It is the wrong tool when you only wanted toe and shoulder of a print (Filmic Faded) with modern dyes intact. Sepia is one brown-gold path through the past; vintage can stay in faded color.
Do not add random specks and call it time.
how_it_works:
Fade dyes (cyan often goes first in some stocks, or reds go brick), add gentle Halation on practicals, keep contrast modest, and optionally add period-accurate Film Grain. Separate dirt and weave: they are extra claims.
Prompt: Vintage treatment of [Subject], faded dyes, halation, the past as chemistry, not a sticker.
when_to_use: Use it when the image should already have happened as an artifact of time. Do not use it as a substitute for vintage glass on a present-tense scene, and do not reduce it to a scratch overlay.
compared_names: HalationHighlights should bleed like film, not clip like video.
compared_text: Vintage Cine Glass is the taking lens. Filmic Faded is print curve.
Sepia is brown-gold tone. Halation is bloom on highlights, one ingredient.
Vintage is the combined period chemistry claim.

prompt_template: Keep it color unless you also want sepia. Do not write scratch overlay as the whole look, and do not confuse it with Cooke swirl alone.

The usual wrong cousin is Vintage Cine Glass (glass only) or a dirty overlay on a modern grade. The tell is sharp modern contrast with specks, or swirl bokeh with contemporary dyes.

faq: What is vintage in film?
It is a period chemistry look: faded dyes, possible halation, and contrast that sits like an aged print or stock. The past is in the file, not only in the costumes.
Vintage vs Vintage Cine Glass

Vintage cine is the lens: coatings and aberrations. Vintage as a grade or treatment is dye fade and period color chemistry. You can shoot old glass in a modern grade, or modern glass with a vintage treatment.

name: Palette
aliases: Palette as location or story state
definition: A color palette in color palette cinematography is a restricted set of hues used as law across set, costume, light, and grade. Too many colors would be noise; a few chosen hues do all the work and can mark location, timeline, or story state.
narrative: Design as law. A yellow desert chapter, a red-cloth lie, a mint hotel: the audience learns the rule and then feels the break.
Traffic can tint strands so you know which plot you are in. A hotel can live in pinks and purples until a new room breaks the set.
It is the wrong tool when the location must keep its un-designed color science (Natural Grade). It is the wrong tool if the only restriction is no chroma (Monochrome).
A Split Toning paints the curve; a palette paints the world, including walls and clothes. Palette changes should distinguish meaningful states, not create arbitrary variety.
how_it_works:
Define a palette rule for each strand across set design, costume, lighting, and grading. Keep the rule stable enough to be learned before breaking it deliberately.

when_to_use: Use it when too many colors would be noise, or when strands of a story must be recognizable by hue. Do not use it as random look-variety, and do not confuse it with a grade-only split on a messy set.

It is a restricted set of hues used as a rule for a place, a timeline, or a story strand. Set, costume, light, and grade all obey the same few colors.

name: Overexposed
definition: Overexposed cinematography lets values clip or bloom toward white on purpose so information in the highlights is burned. It is a choice to lose the top of the scale, not the same as high-key lighting, which can stay bright while still holding detail.
narrative: Blow the whites as a choice. A window becomes heaven or fluorescent hell.
Faces can go toward erasure. The image says there is more light than the medium will hold: revelation, amnesia, a club, a death, a childhood sun that cannot be looked at.

It is the wrong tool when the scene is simply bright and even with detail in the shirts (High-Key Lighting). It is the wrong tool for a white flash as an edit event (Light Flash) if the shot itself is normally exposed.
Do not underexpose and crush, then call it the opposite. Clipping is directional: you are throwing away the top, not the bottom.
how_it_works:
Expose until the shoulder clips or the highlights bloom beyond recovery. Decide what must survive (eyes, a silhouette) and let the rest go.
A blooming lens and Halation can soften the burn; a digital clip is harder-edged unless you diffuse. Prompt: Overexposed [Subject], values clipping toward heaven or fluorescent hell, information burned on purpose.
when_to_use: Use it when blowing the whites is the sentence: a door onto blinding sun, a memory that erases, a club strobe that stays. Do not use it as a synonym for high-key beauty, and do not clip by accident and keep the take.
compared_names: High-Key LightingComedy, heaven, hospital, or candy.
Light FlashA cut that is also a wound of light.

faq: What is overexposed in film?
It is an image whose highlights are allowed to clip or bloom so information at the top of the scale is burned on purpose. Brightness plus lost detail is the fact.
Overexposed vs High-Key Lighting

High-key lighting is bright and low in contrast, but it can still hold detail in whites. Overexposure throws highlight information away. A white shirt with buttons still visible is not overexposed; it is just bright.

name: Slow Motion
definition: Slow motion cinematography plays action over more screen time than the event occupied during capture, usually by overcranking (recording 120 to 240 fps and playing at 24). The extra samples reveal fabric delay, particle hang, and impact mechanics that a 24 fps shutter would compress into a few smeared frames.
narrative: Use it when a second already contains a scene: a fall, a look that decides, a hit whose mechanics matter. Stretching the instant can turn it into dread, grief, or inspection.
Sound is half the meaning. Stretched diegetic noise makes the world heavy.
Real-time audio against slow picture can feel like a memory or a lie. It is the wrong tool when the beat needs speed, comic timing, or spatial inspection of a frozen pose.
If the camera orbits a nearly stopped body, you wanted bullet time. If frames are duplicated and smeared, you wanted step printing.
Do not slow every punch or the rate stops meaning anything.
how_it_works:
Capture at a higher frame rate than playback and keep a planned shutter (often 180 degrees, so 120 fps is about 1/240 s per frame). You need more light because each exposure is shorter.
Keep gravity, contacts, and anatomy continuous through the extra samples. For generated footage, ask for real intermediate motion, not interpolated mush.
Prompt: Slow motion of [Subject] at 120 to 240 fps playback, dust hanging, fabric delayed, continuous gravity.
when_to_use: Use it on a decisive instant a normal rate would hide, such as a glass leaving a waiter's hand. Do not use it as a default look for an entire fight.
compared_names: Speed RampMark one instant inside a fight or a look.
Step PrintingLonging that cannot move at normal speed.
Fast MotionToo much life for real time.
compared_text: Constant slow motion is not a Speed Ramp, which changes rate inside the shot and then recovers. It is not Step Printing, which duplicates low-rate, long-exposure frames into a stuttered lyric smear.
It is not Bullet Time, which decouples a traveling viewpoint from near-frozen action. Freeze Frame stops sampling altogether.
Fast Motion and Time-Lapse crush duration instead of stretching it.

in_film: Seven Samurai stretches the kidnapper's fall so the death occupies more than its wall-clock instant. The Wild Bunch fragments gunfights through varied slow-motion views so violence becomes duration.
The Matrix is often filed here, but the rooftop lean is closer to bullet time. In the Mood for Love belongs with step printing more than with clean overcranked silk.

The usual wrong cousin is Bullet Time or a freeze. The tell is a stopped body with a moving camera, or a still with no new frames of motion.

faq: What is Slow Motion in film?
Slow motion is overcranked or retimed footage that occupies more screen time than the event took to happen, so small physical details become readable.
Slow Motion vs Bullet Time
Slow motion stretches the subject's action while the camera may stay simple. Bullet time nearly freezes the action while the viewpoint travels around it.
When should I use Slow Motion?
When one second already contains the scene: a fall, a look, or an impact whose mechanics or grief need extra duration.

name: Fast Motion
definition: Fast motion cinematography compresses screen duration so action plays faster than it occurred, by undercranking the camera or by retiming a normal-rate take. Crowds smear, clouds race, and labor can look absurdly efficient because too many events occupy too little time.
narrative: Use it when real time cannot hold the life in front of the lens: a factory that never stops, a city that should feel over-efficient, a chase whose danger is relentlessness rather than one punch. Subtle acceleration can be funnier or more oppressive than a cartoon speed-up.
Keep sound on its own clock. Pitch-shifted footsteps often betray the trick.
It is the wrong tool for weather, construction, or a night becoming morning. Those need interval sampling, not sped-up continuous action.
If the camera itself steps through space while hours collapse, you wanted a hyperlapse. Do not accelerate a performance whose contacts and gravity must stay honest.
how_it_works:
Undercrank (shoot fewer frames per second than playback) or retime in the cut with a planned speed ratio. Longer exposure per frame, if the shutter stays open, increases motion blur.
Check hands, object contacts, and foot cadence after the speed change. Prompt: Undercranked fast motion of [Subject], crowds smearing, clouds racing, planned speed ratio, coherent contacts.
when_to_use: Use it when a mailroom, assembly line, or crowd must feel over-efficient, as in a comic or cosmic crush of ordinary work. Do not use it to stand in for a day-to-night sky.

name: Speed Ramp
definition: Speed ramping changes playback or capture speed inside a single shot rather than holding one retiming ratio. Approach and recovery stay energetic while one motivated instant (impact, glance, turn) stretches, then the clock returns.
narrative: Treat it as temporal close-up. The shot walks up in real time, lands on the fact that matters, and releases.
A fight, a catch, a look across a room can all take the ramp if the event is readable. The audience should feel one continuous action, not a new clip glued on.
It is the wrong tool when the whole beat should stay slow, or when you only need a smash of magnification. If rate never returns, you shot slow motion and called it a ramp.
If the picture punches in by focal length, you wanted a crash zoom. Do not ramp to hide unreadable choreography.

Capture enough temporal detail (high frame rate) that both the fast and slow portions have samples. Identify the motivated event, then shape the acceleration curve and matching motion blur.

name: Freeze Frame
definition: A freeze frame holds one image so narrative time stops while camera, subject, and world all cease to generate new samples. The hold can end a story, land a joke, or present a face as evidence.
narrative: Use it when the fact is the picture itself: a boy at the edge of the sea, a narrator labeling a life, a triumph that should not continue into the next second. Grain, dust, and expression stay.

Sound may keep running (voiceover, a song, a crowd) so the freeze feels like a caption, not a crash. It is the wrong tool when you still need motion around a stopped body, or a camera that walks around an instant.
Those are frozen-in-motion and bullet time. A posed tableau with living extras is not a freeze.
Do not freeze a line of dialogue whose meaning is in the next word.
how_it_works:
Select one frame and reprint or hold it for the required duration. An optical zoom into that still (as at the end of The 400 Blows) is a move on a photograph, not new live action.
The shutter is no longer sampling. Prompt: Freeze frame on [Subject], the world stopping on a decisive pose, grain holding, a still torn out of time.
when_to_use: Use it to end, to joke, or to offer evidence, such as a final still of a runaway on a beach. Do not use it when particles should hang while the camera still travels.

name: Time-Lapse
definition: Time-lapse cinematography captures frames at long intervals so slow change plays as continuous motion, hours becoming seconds as shadows sweep and crowds become flow. It is interval photography, not a sped-up ordinary take.
narrative: Use it to reveal a pattern no one can stand still long enough to see. Weather, construction, traffic, a plant, a city emptying and filling.
People often stop being protagonists and become a system. The camera is usually locked so the only motion is time.

It is the wrong tool for a comic undercrank of a performance, or for a still hero in a racing crowd (that is a different recipe). If the camera must walk the street while hours collapse, you wanted a hyperlapse.
Do not call a fast crowd under a stuck sun a full day-to-night lapse.
how_it_works:
Plan interval, total duration, exposure, and stability. A locked head is the default.
For day-to-night, ramp exposure so windows light as the sky dies. The sun and shadows must travel if the claim is a full day.
Prompt: Time-lapse of [Subject] or the world around them, hours in seconds, shadows sweeping, crowds as smoke.
when_to_use: Use it to show weather, construction, or a night becoming morning from a stable viewpoint. Do not use it to make an actor's performance merely faster.

name: Step Printing
definition: Step printing repeats or omits frames optically or digitally so motion advances in visible temporal steps. Combined with low-rate capture and long exposures, each frame smears internally while the sequence stutters forward, a texture of delay rather than clean high-frame-rate slow motion.
narrative: Use it for longing that cannot move at normal speed: a walk through rain, a pursuit that feels remembered, a figure isolated from a city's rush. The smear belongs inside the frame.
The step belongs between frames. Together they make memory feel unstable without a digital glitch overlay.
It is the wrong tool for a readable impact study, a fight that must stay mechanical, or anxiety that should skip like a damaged mind. Those are slow motion and stutter.
Do not interpolate the cadence away. If the walk becomes silk, you left the technique.
how_it_works:
Shoot or generate a low temporal sample (often well below 24 fps) with enough shutter time for motion blur, then duplicate frames to the delivery rate. Test the cadence.
Keep practical lights saturated and the lonely figure more readable than the crowd. Prompt: Step-printed motion of [Subject], frames duplicated, stuttering lyric delay, long-exposure smear inside each frame.
when_to_use: Use it on a rain walk or a night counter where one person should separate from the city's rush. Do not use it when you need clean 120 fps anatomy of a hit.
compared_names: Slow MotionA second contains a scene.
Fast MotionToo much life for real time.
compared_text: Step printing is not silk Slow Motion, which samples densely and interpolates smoothly. It is not Stutter / Stop-Stutter, which drops or repeats frames as anxious rhythm without requiring long-exposure smear.
Motion Blur can exist at normal cadence. Stop Motion builds poses by hand between exposures rather than reprinting live action.

Step printing repeats or skips frames, often after low-rate long-exposure capture, so motion smears inside frames and advances in steps.

name: Reverse Motion
definition: Reverse motion plays recorded action backward so causes arrive after their effects inside the shot: rain rises, smoke inhales, a shattered object reassembles. This is reversed playback, not a story told in reverse scene order.
narrative: Use it for trick photography, grief that wants an undo, or a world whose physics run the other way. The audience reads inverted inertia: water, cloth, sparks, and footsteps all lie.
A single reversed gesture can feel like a spell. A whole reversed fight can feel like entropy running downhill in the wrong direction.
It is the wrong tool when you only need a toy loop, or when the plot itself is told from consequence to cause without reversing the footage. A boomerang goes forward then back on the same path.
Memento-style chronology reorders scenes at normal playback. Do not mix those machines in one prompt.
how_it_works:
Shoot the action forward with readable contacts, then reverse the clip. Gravity, fluids, and cloth are the proof.
A person putting on a coat forward will look like an impossible undressing in reverse only if the fabric was honest on the way in. Prompt: Reverse motion of [Subject], time running backward, rain rising, a broken thing assembling.
when_to_use: Use it when a broken object should reassemble, or rain should rise, as a visible undo. Do not use it to mean reverse story order with ordinary-speed scenes.

Slow Motion only changes rate, not direction. An Infinite Loop sews last frame to first and may stay forward.

name: Bullet Time
definition: Bullet time freezes or radically slows action while the viewpoint travels around it, decoupling camera speed from subject time. The instant becomes inspectable space: a time-slice orbit around a sculpture of speed, not ordinary slow motion with a handheld camera.

It is the wrong tool for a dinner scene, a lyric walk, or a simple impact study from a locked camera. If the camera is locked, you wanted frozen in motion or a freeze.
If the fighter keeps moving at stretched rate and the camera stays put, you wanted slow motion. Do not add a zoom on top of the orbit unless you are making a different shot.

Use a synchronized or time-offset multi-camera array with interpolation, or a fully controlled 3D scene. Enforce frozen or near-frozen subject geometry while changing viewpoint.
Particles should be countable and rigid enough to survive the arc. Prompt: Bullet time around [Subject], the moment frozen while the camera orbits, a slice of time as a sculpture.

name: Long Take
definition: Long take cinematography is an unusually extended shot that preserves continuous performance, space, action, or duration without an overt cut. Blocking and camera share one sentence so the audience cannot leave the room.
narrative: Use it when incompatible facts must coexist in one geography: boredom beside danger, a joke beside a wound, a bomb in a trunk while people chat. The eye scans a functioning world instead of consuming an insert.
Duration is the tension. A dense crowd is not enough.
Each zone needs an intelligible action timed to the camera. It is the wrong tool when the scene is a virtuoso ride that may hide joins, or when coverage should isolate a face.
A oner is designed to play as one take and may be stitched. A long take's claim is continuous time.
Do not hold a static close-up for two minutes and call the endurance a panorama.
how_it_works:
Block foreground, midground, and background on a shared timeline. Give the camera a clear route (Steadicam, crane, handheld, or studio dolly) and vary its attention without losing the human anchor.
Rehearse contacts, eyelines, and extra business so the take can survive. Prompt: Long take covering [Subject] without a cut, duration as tension, blocking and camera choreographed as one sentence.

name: Motion Blur
definition: Motion blur cinematography is the streaking or softness caused by subject or camera movement during exposure. The longer the gate stays open relative to the motion, the more the image paints, so edges fail on purpose.

name: Boomerang
definition: A boomerang video effect plays a short action forward, then snaps it backward along the same samples, often looping. The gesture comes and goes on one path: reversed playback used as a round trip rather than a one-way undo.
narrative: Use it to weaponize a small motion: hair toss, splash, a jump's peak, a door that never finishes closing. Both directions must read.
If the forward pass is ugly, the reverse will not save it. Loops work when the end of the reverse meets the start of the forward without a bump.
It is the wrong tool for grief, inverted physics as story, or a seamless forward-only cycle (a pendulum designed to sew). Reverse motion one way is a spell.
An infinite loop may never reverse. Do not boomerang a line of dialogue whose words cannot run backward.

name: Infinite Loop
definition: An infinite loop video sews the last frame to the first so motion never arrives at an ending. The cycle can be a seamless visual join, or, in narrative use, a repeated day whose variables change.

name: Low Shutter
definition: Low shutter cinematography uses a short shutter angle or short exposure so moving edges stay sharp inside each frame. Normal-rate action then feels abrupt and staccato because this is reduced motion blur, not a long-exposure smear.
narrative: Use it when impact and sensory stress should feel exposed: rain as beads, limbs as chopped positions, a landing that does not silk over. You are not speeding the scene.
You are removing the blur that usually glues fragments together. Combat and panic live here.
It is the wrong tool for night-traffic ribbons, lyric smear, or silk slow motion. Photography says 'low shutter speed' for long exposure.
Film says low shutter angle for the opposite. If every lamp paints a ribbon, you shot motion blur.
Do not skip frames and call that short shutter.
how_it_works:
At 24 fps, a 180-degree shutter is about 1/48 s. A 45-degree shutter is about 1/192 s: less blur, more light required.
Compensate exposure. In generated footage, request low motion blur and crisp droplets, not missing frames.
Prompt: Low-shutter (short shutter angle) of [Subject], reduced motion blur, crisp rain and limb edges, staccato cadence.
when_to_use: Use it on a landing, a rescue run, or a fight that should feel like discrete fragments, such as Omaha-style rain and bodies. Do not use it when lamps should drag as ribbons.

name: Lens Flare
definition: Lens flare in lens flare cinematography is stray light scattered by glass, coatings, and barrel walls, producing ghosts, streaks, or veiling glare instead of a clean image. The artifacts live in the taking optic, so they track the source angle and dim when a body occludes the lamp.
narrative: When a hard source sits near or inside the frame, the camera admits it cannot contain the light. Contrast falls.
A ghost of the iris repeats across the field. The sun, a hangar opening, or a bare practical becomes a force the glass is failing to image.
Use it when the observer is overwhelmed: encounter lights, headlights, a door onto daylight. The audience should feel the camera struggling to see, not a sticker riding the grade.

name: Anamorphic Flare
definition: An anamorphic flare is a horizontal streak produced when a bright point hits the cylindrical elements of an anamorphic lens. It is a subset of lens flare, not a general haze, and it usually arrives with oval bokeh from the same squeeze.
narrative: Night lamps and headlights write a bar across the frame because the front optic stretches one axis. The streak is cyan, blue, or magenta depending on coatings, and it stays level with the squeezed world.
Oval highlights in the background confirm the same glass. Use it when the night should be written on the taking lens: wet streets, neon, a car coming toward camera.
The streak is evidence of scope optics, not of brightness alone. It is the wrong tool in spherical coverage, or when you want a circular ghost of the iris.
If the bokeh is round and the streak is a random rainbow, you have mixed two lens families.

name: Halation
definition: Halation in film is a reddish or warm glow around bright highlights caused by light passing through the emulsion, reflecting off the base, and scattering back into the image. It is a stock behavior, not a diffusion filter and not flare inside the lens.
narrative: A lamp, a window, or a candle does not clip to a hard video edge. The highlight breathes.
A thin red or amber ring forms where the bright tone meets darker density. Fine contrast softens while faces and rooms stay readable.
Use it when the picture should feel developed on film: tungsten practicals, Super 8 lamps, a window in a small apartment. Tie the bloom to a point of view, not to every specular in the grade.
It is the wrong tool when you blur the whole frame equally and call it analog. If eyes go milky and there is no extra glow at highlight edges, you applied diffusion or defocus, not halation.
how_it_works:
On film, skip or weaken the anti-halation layer, or use stocks and formats that show base scatter (some Super 8 and 16mm). In camera, keep highlights luminous but not clipped, and do not confuse this with a Promist on the lens.
Digital recreation should bloom only the brightest edges, often with a warm or red fringe, while preserving grain structure and eye texture. Prompt red-edge bloom around lamps, not a fog filter over the set.
when_to_use: A woman beside a rain window, amber practicals breathing, the neon sign outside gaining a warm halo while her eyes stay sharp. Do not frost the entire frame and destroy highlight information.
compared_names: Film GrainThe image should feel developed, not rendered.
Vintage Cine GlassMemory, period, or beauty over resolution.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Lens Flare is scatter inside the glass, ghosts and veils that track a source into the optic. Halation is scatter in the film layers around a highlight already in the image.
Film Grain is the random silver or dye texture, not the glow. Vintage Cine Glass can add both bloom and falloff, but the physical cause of halation is the emulsion, not old coatings alone.

A warm or reddish glow around highlights from light scattering in the film layers after bouncing off the base. It is emulsion physics, not a lens filter.

Flare is stray light inside the optic. Halation is a halo on the stock around a bright tone already photographed. One lives in glass, the other in the film.

When lamps and windows should bleed like film instead of clipping like video. Do not use it as a dream filter on every frame.

name: Film Grain
definition: Film grain in film grain cinematography is the random texture of silver halide crystals or color dye clouds in the emulsion, or a digital simulation of that structure. It is a developed surface, not a PNG overlay sitting on top of a clean render.
narrative: The image is made of particles that change every frame. Shadows crawl.
Midtones have a living grain. Highlights are not a separate smooth plate.
Format and stock speed set the size: 16mm reads coarser in the frame than 35mm or 65mm. Use it when the picture should feel exposed and processed, not drawn.
A rooftop at blue hour, a winter platform, a handheld interior. Grain should scale with density, not stamp the same speckle on sky and coat alike.
It is the wrong tool as a default film look on a sharp digital plate. If the grain is identical on every frame, or floats above motion blur, it is a layer, not an emulsion.
how_it_works:
On film, choose stock and format: faster stocks and smaller negatives show more grain. Push processing increases it.
Digitally, generate monochromatic grain that is denser in midtones and shadows, temporally unstable, and finer on larger implied formats. Do not sharpen after.
Prompt 16mm or 35mm texture, living grain, no overlay.
when_to_use: A charcoal coat on wet slate at blue hour, 35mm grain in the dusk, chimney smoke breaking into particles. Do not paste coarse grain on an already sharp product still and call it developed.

name: Bokeh
definition: Bokeh in bokeh cinematography is the aesthetic character of out-of-focus rendering: the disc shape, edge, and smoothness of blurred points, not the mere fact of a thin depth of field. The glass, not a blur slider, decides whether those discs are round, oval, outlined, or swirling.
narrative: A city, a string of practicals, or a wet street becomes a field of discs. Circular blades make circles.
Anamorphic squeeze makes ovals. Mechanical vignetting cats-eyes the discs at the frame edge.
Nervous, outlined, or onion-ring discs are also bokeh. They are just unkind bokeh.
Use it when the world behind or in front of a face should become light rather than information. One plane stays true.
The rest is the optic's handwriting. It is the wrong tool when you need the room.
If background signs, eyelines, or geography still have to read, creamy discs are hiding the scene. It is also the wrong word for a masked cutout with no optical discs at all.

Open the aperture, separate subject from background, and choose glass: spherical circles, anamorphic ovals, Petzval swirl, cat-eye at the edges. Point sources (practicals, speculars, rain catches) make the discs visible.
Distance and focal length set disc size. Prompt the disc shape and the source of the highlights, not blurry background alone.

faq: What is bokeh in film?
The character of out-of-focus rendering: circles, ovals, cat-eyes, swirl, onion rings. It describes how blur looks, not merely that something is soft.

name: Double Exposure
definition: Double exposure in double exposure film combines two or more image records on one frame, in camera by winding back, optically in a printer, or digitally as an additive composite. Both pictures occupy the same emulsion or file unless a matte fully holds one off.
narrative: A face in a city. A ghost in rain.
Fireplace flames laid over a locked interior. Two times share density.

The result can be lyrical (memory, a second self) or purely practical (an element you could not shoot with the first pass). Use it when two records should coexist: a thought over a room, a spirit over a landscape, fire added later.
Superimposition is the family. Actor doubling with a split matte is one application, not the whole technique.
It is the wrong tool when you need two solid bodies that occlude each other, cast contact shadows, and pass objects. That is duplication or a split-matte composite, not a ghosted overlay.
It is also the wrong tool when a dissolve would carry you from one time to the next instead of stacking them.
how_it_works:
In camera: expose, matte off part of the gate or shoot a full overlay, rewind, expose again with matched lighting. Optically: bi-pack or printer pass.
Digitally: additive mix or screened layers, or a hard split matte for twins. Lock the camera unless both passes share motion control.
Prompt two named images sharing one frame, optical overlay, not a hard cut and not a morph.
when_to_use: A face superimposed over rain-soaked rooftops so memory and place occupy one still. Do not use a translucent overlay when two twins must sit at one table and pour tea.

Two image records combined on one frame, in camera, in an optical printer, or digitally. Elements shot at different times appear together.

A dissolve is a transition that leaves shot A for shot B. A double exposure is a stack: both pictures remain visible in the same frame.

When two times, two selves, or two elements should occupy one image. Do not use it when you need two solid, occluding bodies.

name: Rack Focus
definition: A rack focus moves the sharp plane from one subject or distance to another during a continuous shot, while the composition stays largely the same. Attention changes because the helical turns, not because the camera cuts or dollies.
narrative: A brass key is sharp on a desk. The woman in the doorway is soft.
Over about two seconds the key goes, her face arrives. Nobody moved.
The audience felt a handoff inside one space. Use it to change who owns the shot without cutting: pursuer and pursued, a clue and a face, a listener and the person who just entered.
A slow rack is a sentence. A snap rack is a jab.

It is the wrong tool when both planes must stay sharp (that is deep focus or a split diopter) or when the camera should physically travel. If details morph instead of going in and out of focus, the model invented a dissolve.
how_it_works:
Mark two distances. Rehearse timing with the first AC.
Keep the head still for a clean demonstration, or coordinate the pull with a small move. Wide-open glass makes the rack readable.
Lens breathing may change field of view slightly. Decide if that is wanted.
Prompt: locked camera, named near and far subjects, a two-second pull, shallow depth of field, no zoom.
when_to_use: Focus holds on a foreground key, then pulls to the figure in the doorway over about two seconds. Do not rack when the scene needs both faces sharp at once, or when a cut would be cleaner.

name: Shallow Focus

It is the wrong tool for blocking that lives in depth, for geography, or for any beat where a background reaction still has to read. If hair is cut out like a mask and the backdrop is a smear without discs, you left photography.

name: Deep Focus
definition: Deep focus in deep focus cinematography keeps multiple near and far planes legibly sharp in one image. It is a continuous depth of field, not merely action arranged in depth while the glass stays selective.
narrative: A hand stamps a form near the lens. A visitor waits in a distant doorway.
Both are readable. The audience may look at either without a pull or a cut dictating the choice.
Cause and effect share the room. Use it when the story is the whole space: a child outside a window while adults sign papers, a street and a face, two rooms through a doorway.
Staging does the directing. The lens declines to choose.

It is the wrong tool for intimacy that should exclude the world, or when light cannot support a small aperture. Two sharp planes with a blur belt between them are a split diopter or a composite, not deep focus.
how_it_works:
Balance shorter focal length, smaller aperture, enough illumination, and subject distances that the stop can cover. Some famous deep-focus-looking shots also used in-camera composites.

name: Forced Perspective
definition: Forced perspective uses camera position, subject distance, and set geometry to alter apparent size or distance, and the lie exists only from the taking viewpoint. Bodies, furniture, and eyelines must agree or the scale collapses.

From one locked lens they share a meal. Move off the axis and the join shows.
The photograph looks ordinary. The measurements are not.
Use it to change size without a digital shrink: a hobbit beside a man, a grown actor in a giant childhood kitchen, a miniature city aligned with a live foreground. Fantasy stays inside a photograph.

It is the wrong tool for a free-moving camera unless the geometry is motion-controlled to match. It is also the wrong tool when you actually built a miniature of the whole world (that is diorama) or when you faked miniature scale with a tilted plane of focus (that is tilt-shift).
how_it_works:
Choose the viewing position first. Place the small performer farther from camera, or the large one nearer, and scale the set pieces they touch.
Match eyelines and ground contact. Light both distances as one space.
Lock the camera, or move only on a path that preserves alignment. Prompt: in-camera scale by placement, shared table or floor, coherent eyelines, not a digital resize.
when_to_use:
A tiny adult guest and a normal host at one rustic table, locked camera, feet and hands sharing scaled furniture. Do not orbit the pair.

name: Light Leak
definition: A light leak in light leak film is unfiltered light that reaches the emulsion or sensor without passing through the taking lens, usually through a gap in the body, magazine, or gate. name: Vignette
definition: A vignette in vignette cinematography darkens, desaturates, or lowers contrast toward the frame edges because of optical falloff, mechanical vignetting in the barrel, a filter, or a later grade. Optical vignette follows the lens, while a post oval is a drawing.

name: Chromatic Aberration
definition: Chromatic aberration in chromatic aberration cinematography is color fringing from different wavelengths focusing at different distances or magnifications. Lateral CA puts red-cyan (or similar) fringes on high-contrast edges, worse toward the frame edge, while longitudinal CA puts different colors in front of and behind the focus plane.
narrative: Cheap, wide, or vintage glass fails to put all colors on the same plane. A branch, a shoulder, a neon sign grows a red or cyan beard.
The optic is imperfect on purpose, or it is simply old. Use it when the glass should confess: lo-fi night, a dream that is optical rather than a grade, a wide at full aperture.
Tie fringes to contrast edges, stronger in the corners. It is the wrong tool as a full-frame RGB split, which is a channel offset, not aberration.
If the whole image is three layers of the same picture, you have a digital treatment, not CA.
how_it_works:
Wide angle, wide open, simple or vintage designs. Lateral CA scales with distance from center.
Longitudinal CA shows as color bokeh (magenta in front, green behind, or the reverse). Recreate by fringing high-contrast edges, not by sliding entire channels.

name: Infrared
definition: Infrared cinematography photographs near-infrared reflectance (roughly 700 to 900 nm), not heat, so foliage often goes pale, skies go dark, and skin can look waxy. It is a different slice of reflected light, still a photograph of the location.
narrative: The woods are white. The sky is near black.
Faces are wrong in a quiet way: veins, powder, fabric dyes all rewrite. The place is still Earth.

The spectrum is not the one the eye owns. Use it when a landscape should feel like another planet without leaving the location: a forbidden forest, a concert IR look, a surveillance still that is not green-tube night vision.
It is the wrong tool for hunting in total dark (that is image intensification) or for seeing body heat (that is thermal). If the image is green and noisy with blooming lamps, you have night vision.
If faces are ironbow masks, you have thermal.

Use an IR-pass filter and a sensor or stock sensitive to near-IR, or remove a camera's IR-cut filter. Light is still reflected sunlight or IR-rich tungsten, not emitted heat.

name: Slit-Scan
definition: Slit-scan exposes moving artwork or a moving camera through a narrow slit over time, stretching space into streaks and corridors with time laid along one axis. The result is structured geometry, not a random particle tunnel.
narrative: A slit is the only open part of the gate. Artwork or a light source moves relative to that slit.
Each frame or pass accumulates a thin slice. The stack becomes a corridor of color with a vanishing point.
Travel is not through a photographed street. It is through exposure.

Use it for passage that is not ordinary space: a stargate, a mind unspooling, a title that is time smeared into architecture. It is the wrong tool if you mean a kaleidoscope of mirrors, a time-lapse of a real street, or a nebula of sparks.
Random neon particles do not reproduce slit-scan geometry.
how_it_works:
Classic optical method: slit mask, illuminated artwork on a track, camera or art in controlled relative motion, long accumulation. Digital: procedural streaks with a stable vanishing point, ordered planes, long-exposure character along one axis.
Prompt: slit-scan streaking, time smeared along one axis, a corridor of light, ordered perspective, no random sparks.

Long parallel light streaks converge toward a stable central vanishing point, evolving through layered spatial corridors. Procedural slit-scan character, controlled acceleration, no literal starfield, random sparks or kaleidoscope cuts.

Wrong cousin: kaleidoscope, starfield, or generic long-exposure sparks. Tell: chaotic particles, no slit axis, no vanishing point, or a mirrored flower.

faq: What is slit-scan in film?
An optical process that exposes through a narrow slit while art or camera moves, accumulating streaks and corridors. Time becomes a spatial axis.
Slit-scan vs kaleidoscope
Kaleidoscope mirrors a fragment into radial symmetry. Slit-scan smears time through a slit into streaks. One is reflection. The other is temporal accumulation.
When should I use slit-scan?
When travel should not look like a photographed location. Do not use it as a stand-in for sparks, nebulas, or mirrored patterns.

Request a structured light corridor, smear along one axis, a stable vanishing point, and no random particles or kaleidoscope cuts.

name: Kaleidoscope
definition: Kaleidoscope cinematography fragments the image with mirrors or radial repetition so one subject becomes a symmetric pattern. The camera looks into angled glass, or the staging itself is a kaleidoscope: bodies arranged around an axis, often from above.
narrative: A shard repeats. A face, a limb, a lamp becomes an ornament.
Busby Berkeley built this with dancers and an overhead camera. A kaleidoscope adapter builds it with mirrors in front of the lens.
Chorus girls, jewels, a subjective break: the picture is multiplication, not smear. Use it when pattern is the point: a musical number, a jewel-box interior, a decorative fracture of a face.
It is the wrong tool for a stargate of streaks, for a simple birds-eye that does not repeat, or for a collage of torn edges. If there is no mirror logic and no radial repeat, it is just a busy frame.
how_it_works:
Physical: kaleidoscope prism or three-mirror tube on the lens, or a mirrored set. Staging: radial choreography shot from Bird's-Eye View.
Keep a clear axis of symmetry and repeating shards. Prompt: kaleidoscopic fragmentation, mirrored shards, radial repeat of [Subject], not slit-scan streaks.
when_to_use: A figure in a red dress multiplied into mirrored shards, jewel symmetry, like looking into a toy kaleidoscope. Do not stretch her along a vanishing-point tunnel and call it kaleidoscope.
compared_names: Repetition and PatternSystems, armies, hotels, factories.
Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.

Bird's-Eye View is the overhead angle Berkeley used. Without mirroring or radial design it is only a top view.

name: Light Flash
definition: A light flash transition is a brief blowout of the frame to white or near-white, then a return, as if a bulb, explosion, or memory dump hit the emulsion. It is a temporal event, often a cut hidden in the peak, not a standing lens flare.
narrative: The picture goes. For a few frames there is only density failure: a bulb, a muzzle, a Polaroid, a trauma.
Then the next image, or the same room, settles back. The flash is both a wound and a splice.
Use it when the cut should hurt: memory stings, explosions, still cameras in a crowd, a mind skipping. The white is the edit.
It is the wrong tool for a sun ghost that stays in shot, or for a smash cut that is only a hard join of two dark images. If the flare hangs and tracks a lamp, that is flare.
If you simply jump scenes with no blowout, that is a smash cut.
how_it_works:
Overexpose a practical, a strobe, or a muzzle until clipping, or animate a white frame at the cut. Recovery can carry a lingering veil.
In camera, a still photographer's flash or a door onto daylight can do it live. Prompt: frame going to white then returning, bulb or explosion or memory sting, not a persistent source-linked flare.
when_to_use: A hard flash blows out a face, then settles into the next memory, as in a sting cut. Do not leave a decorative streak parked on the lens after the white is gone.
compared_names: Smash CutThe next image should hurt.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.
compared_text: Smash Cut is an abrupt edit without a required white-out. A light flash is the white that can carry that cut.
Lens Flare is scatter that remains while a source is in the optic. Fade In / Fade Out goes slowly to black or white as a chapter mark.
A flash is fast. Iris closes a circle.
It does not blow the whole field.
Smash CutThe next image should hurt.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.
in_film: Memento uses white flashes as memory dumps between Polaroids and the present. Saving Private Ryan lets muzzle flashes and overload wipe the frame as combat sting.
Raging Bull's camera flashes in the ring are the still-photographer version of the same blowout.
prompt_template: Make it an event with a recovery. Still: Blinding light flash over [Subject], a bulb, explosion, or memory cut, the frame going to white then returning.
prompt_example: Video: A hard light flash blows out [Subject] then settles back, as a memory or explosion sting.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: persistent lens flare or a smash cut with no exposure event. Tell: a rainbow streak that never whites the frame, or a hard cut in full detail.
Fix: clip to white (or near-white) for frames, then recover. Hide the splice in the peak if it is a transition.
faq: What is a light flash in film?
A brief blowout of the image to white, then a return, used as a sting or as a cut. It is overexposure as an event, not a standing artifact.
Light flash vs lens flare
Flare is stray light in the optic that can last as long as the source is in play. A light flash is a temporal wipe of the frame, often covering an edit.
When should I use a light flash?
When a cut or a shock should be a wound of light: memory, explosion, still-camera flash. Do not use it as decoration on a quiet master.
How do I prompt a light flash for AI image or video?

For video, describe a blowout to white and a settle-back, and name the cause (bulb, muzzle, memory). For stills, show the peak or the recovery, not a parked streak.

name: Projections
definition: Projections in projection mapping film put a pictured image onto a surface that the taking camera then photographs: front projection onto a retroreflective screen, rear projection behind a window or windshield, or video mapped onto architecture. The projector is a light source, and the set is also a screen.
narrative: Actors stand on a rocky foreground. Behind them a desert plate is thrown, coaxial with the lens, onto Scotchlite.
Or a car process shot: performers in a cockpit, a plate on a screen beyond the glass. Or a city that wears moving faces.
Media is the set. Use it when a large environment must coexist with live foreground, or when architecture itself is the display.
Front projection and rear projection are in-camera composites. Mapping is the same family with a three-dimensional screen.
It is the wrong tool when you mean a double exposure (two records in the emulsion, no projector) or a digital backdrop that never hits a surface. A generated image can imitate the look.
It cannot prove a projector was used.
how_it_works:
Front projection: camera and projector aligned through a beam splitter, retroreflective screen, foreground lit so it does not wash the plate. Rear projection: a translucent screen behind the action, plate brightness matched to the foreground key.
Mapping: projectors registered to architecture, then recaptured. Prompt: projected imagery on walls or a screen behind [Subject], shared viewpoint, foreground lit to match, not a ghost overlay.
when_to_use: A rocky foreground merging into a still desert panorama, performers lit to the horizon plate, locked wide. Do not drift the mountain independently of the camera, and do not stack a translucent face over the room unless you mean double exposure.
compared_names: Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
Practical LightingLet the set light the face.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Double Exposure combines two photographic records without a projector writing on a set. Practical Lighting is lamps in the scene.

A projector can be a practical, but projection is imagery, not just illumination. Rear-projection driving in Hitchcock is the same family as 2001's Dawn of Man front projection: a plate on a surface, recaptured.

Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
in_film: 2001: A Space Odyssey uses front projection for Dawn of Man landscapes. To Catch a Thief and Vertigo use process projection for driving conversations.
Blade Runner 2049 and Ghost in the Shell treat building-scale imagery as architecture.

Vertigo 1958Driving scenes use a controlled foreground against photographed surroundings.
prompt_template: A small practical-looking rocky foreground merges into an immense still desert panorama. Locked wide camera, performers lit to match the horizon photograph, subtle boundary between physical foreground and distant projected landscape. No drifting mountain geometry or independently moving horizon.
prompt_example: Put the image on a surface. Example: Projected imagery crawling over [Subject] and architecture, a plate on a screen or faces on walls, foreground lit to match the projection, in-camera process not a double-exposure ghost.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: double exposure, or a floating hologram with no surface. Tell: a translucent overlay that ignores walls, mismatched vanishing points, or a background that parallax-slides against the foreground.
Fix: shared viewpoint, projection on a named surface, matched key, restrained plate motion.
faq: What is projection mapping in film?
Throwing a pictured image onto a screen or onto architecture, then photographing the result. Front projection, rear projection, and mapped video all belong to this family.
Projections vs double exposure
Double exposure stacks two records in the image. Projection writes one record onto a physical surface in the set. One is an overlay. The other is a lamp that is a picture.
When should I use projections?
When the environment is a plate or the building is a display, and foreground performers must share that light. Do not use it as a synonym for any composite.
How do I prompt projections for AI image or video?

Name the surface (screen, wall, windshield), keep a common viewpoint, match foreground light to the plate, and forbid a ghost overlay or drifting horizon.

name: Morph
definition: A morphing effect transforms one image, face, shape, or object into another by interpolating corresponding geometry over time. It is a continuous becoming, not a crossfade of opacities and not two exposures stacked.
narrative: A face does not cut to another face. Vertices travel.
The nose, the jaw, the silhouette pass through illegal in-between states. Identity is unstable for a measured number of seconds, then a new form is solid.
Use it when the story is transformation: a liquid metal man, a mask that is anatomy, a person becoming another person. The audience should watch the change, not infer it across a dissolve.

It is the wrong tool when two images should merely trade dominance (dissolve), coexist (double exposure), or rhyme across a cut (match cut). If you still see both complete faces as ghosts, you dissolved.
If the cut is hard and only the outline matches, you graphic-matched.
how_it_works:
Establish correspondence: eyes to eyes, contour to contour. Interpolate, often with a cross-dissolve of textures on top of the warp.
Duration is part of the grammar (a six-second become is a sentence). Prompt: [Subject] morphs into a named second form over N seconds, continuous transformation, not a dissolve, not a cut.
when_to_use: A face becomes another face over about six seconds, features traveling, one identity at the end. Do not crossfade two full portraits and call it a morph.
compared_names: DissolveMemory, passage, or a gentle death of a scene.
Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Dissolve changes opacity from shot A to shot B. Forms do not have to correspond.
Double Exposure holds both images. Match Cut joins two shots at a similar shape without interpolating the in-between.
Duplication places two solid versions of one person in a space. Morph turns one into the other.

prompt_example: Video: [Subject] morphs into another form or face over 6 seconds, a continuous transformation, not a dissolve.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: dissolve, double exposure, or match cut. Tell: two ghosts, a hard cut on similar shapes, or a texture fade with no warp.
Fix: require corresponding features to travel, show illegal in-betweens, land on one solid form.
faq: What is a morph in film?
A continuous geometric transformation from one image or body into another. Features correspond and interpolate. It is not a fade and not a stack.
Morph vs dissolve
A dissolve is opacity. A morph is shape. In a dissolve you can see two complete pictures. In a morph you see one picture whose anatomy is traveling.
When should I use a morph?
When identity or matter is unstable and the change must be watched. Do not use it as a fancy dissolve between unrelated scenes.
How do I prompt a morph for AI image or video?

Name the start form, the end form, and the duration. Demand continuous transformation with traveling features. Ban dissolve and double exposure.

name: Altered State
definition: Altered state cinematography makes the mind the location: smear, afterimage, wrong color, unstable time, optics and cutting that no sober observer would report. It is a bundle of techniques motivated by consciousness, not a single filter name.
narrative: Edges trail. Hue unhooks from the room.
A face leaves a stain. Focus and speed refuse to sit still.
The set may be an apartment. The picture is a nervous system.
Use it when perception is the plot: drugs, vertigo, dying, revelation. Pick a few physical tells and repeat them so the state has rules.
A smear plus a color unhook is a language. Everything at once is noise.
It is the wrong tool for a single clean optic (one fisheye, one flare) that the character would still recognize as the room. If the codec collapses, that is datamosh.
If two times overlay as density, that is double exposure. Altered state may borrow those, but it has to be motivated as seeing.
how_it_works:
Combine a short list: long shutter smear, step-printed time, wrong white balance, afterimages, a diopter or a distorting optic, occasional overlay. Keep the body of the subject readable enough to stay in the scene.
Prompt: perception bent, edges trailing, color unhooked from the room, as if consciousness is slipping, not a random glitch pack.
when_to_use: A close interior where the frame warps as a character slips, trailing edges, hue wrong, time sticky. Do not apply it to a wide establishing shot that still has to map the street.
compared_names: Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
compared_text: Dreamcore is a genre look of liminal rooms and childhood lighting gone wrong. Altered state is the perceptual event, often in an ordinary set.
Datamosh is codec collapse. Double Exposure is a stacked record.
Distortions are geometric lies in the glass. Altered state may include distortion, plus time and color that will not sit.
DreamcoreNostalgia with the safety removed.
DatamoshBreak the file on purpose.
Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
in_film: Enter the Void binds camera, smear, and color to a consciousness that will not stay in a body. Requiem for a Dream uses speed, close optics, and cutting as intoxication and crash.
Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas is the wide-angle, wrong-color cousin.
prompt_template: List the perceptual tells. Still: Altered-state image of [Subject], smear, afterimage, wrong color, time that will not sit still.
prompt_example: Video: The frame around [Subject] warps as if consciousness is slipping, edges trailing, color unhooked from the room.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: a single fisheye, a datamosh, or a dreamcore bedroom with no perceptual event. Tell: a clean room with one sticker effect, or total illegibility.
Fix: motivate two or three repeating tells, keep the subject locatable, let the room remain a room that is failing.
faq: What is altered state in film?
Subjective photography in which smear, afterimage, color, and time report a mind rather than a sober room. It is a motivated bundle, not one optic.
Altered state vs distortions
Distortions are geometric warps from glass or air. Altered state may use those, plus color and time errors, as consciousness. Distortion can be sober (a peephole). Altered state is not.
When should I use altered state?
When the mind is the location. Do not use it as decoration on coverage that still has to be geographically clear.
How do I prompt altered state for AI image or video?

Name two or three tells (trail, afterimage, wrong hue, sticky time) and say consciousness is slipping. Forbid a generic glitch overlay and keep the subject readable.

name: Anthropo
definition: Anthropomorphic cinematography stages an object or animal as a performer: human scale in the frame, a gesture, an eyeline, reaction shots, as if the inanimate had a will. The camera does not need a face so much as an actor's grammar.
narrative: A red balloon waits, follows, sulks. A robot tilts its head at a trash cube.
The object is not a prop in a still life. It is covered like a person: singles, looks, pauses.
Will is implied by blocking and eyeline, not by a drawn smile unless the story needs one. Use it to give a thing agency: a balloon, a machine, a relic, an animal shot as a colleague.

The rest of the scene should treat it as a presence. It is the wrong tool when you simply shoot an object from its own optical position (that is object POV) or when a tableau arranges bodies as a picture.
Anthropo is performance coverage of a nonhuman. Object POV is a camera mount.
how_it_works:
Assign an eyeline height. Cover the object with the same sizes you would give an actor: wide for entrance, medium for dialogue, close for reaction.
Let humans look at it as a partner. Puppet, wire, or animation can supply gesture.
Prompt: an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, the inanimate performing, not a POV from inside the object.
when_to_use:
A balloon at head height, held in a single, a child looking to it as if it might answer. Do not bolt the camera to the balloon and call that anthropo.
That is object POV.
compared_names: Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Object POV puts the camera in the object's position. Anthropo looks at the object as an actor.
Tableau freezes people into a composed picture. Anthropo keeps a will in motion.
Macro can isolate an object as texture without giving it an eyeline.
Object POVThe prop has eyes.
TableauHold the arrangement.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
in_film: The Red Balloon covers a balloon as a companion, with waits and follows that belong to a performer. WALL-E plays a machine with human gesture and eyeline without needing a human face.
Those are coverage choices, not mascots to copy.
prompt_template: Cover the thing like a person. Example: Anthropomorphic frame of [Subject], an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, singles and looks as if it had a will, not a camera inside the object.
prompt_example: Anthropomorphic frame of [Subject], an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, the inanimate performing.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: object POV, a cute sticker face, or a still-life insert. Tell: the camera is mounted in the object, or the object sits as a prop with no eyeline.
Fix: assign a look, a height, and reaction coverage. Let others treat it as a partner.
faq: What is anthropo in film?
Staging and covering an object or animal as if it were a performer: scale, gesture, eyeline, reactions. Agency is in the blocking, not necessarily in a painted face.
Anthropo vs object POV
Object POV is the camera from the thing's position. Anthropo is the camera looking at the thing as an actor. One is a mount. The other is a performance.
When should I use anthropo?
When a nonhuman should have a will in the scene. Do not use it for a mere product insert or for a true POV from inside the object.
How do I prompt anthropo for AI image or video?

Specify human scale, a clear eyeline, gesture, and coverage as if the object were a player. Forbid interior POV unless you want that cousin.

name: Cinemagraph
definition: A cinemagraph is a still photograph in which one isolated element continues to move on a loop (steam, rain on glass, hair, a blink) while the rest of the frame is frozen. It is not a freeze-frame of a whole shot, and it is not a full clip that happens to loop.
narrative: The picture looks dead, then a kettle breathes. A coat is still.
Only the rain tracks the window. Time is allowed in one masked region.
The rest is a still. Use it when a photograph should refuse to fully stop: fashion, a poster that lives, a memory with one leak of motion.
The moving part must be plausible as a cycle. It is the wrong tool when the whole scene moves, or when all motion stops (freeze-frame).
If every element loops, that is an infinite loop of a shot, not a cinemagraph. If the loop is a boomerang of the entire take, that is a different toy.
how_it_works:
Shoot a locked camera. Choose one motion that can cycle (steam, rain, flicker).
Mask that region in post, freeze the rest from a single frame, loop the live patch so the join is invisible. Prompt: almost a still, only one named element loops, locked camera, no other motion.
when_to_use: A woman at a rain window, body frozen, only the rain and a thread of steam looping. Do not let her blink, the curtains blow, and the neon flicker all at once.
compared_names: Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Freeze Frame stops everything. Infinite Loop repeats the entire shot.
Boomerang plays a whole action forward and back. A cinemagraph freezes the majority and loops a patch.
Time-Lapse advances the whole world in steps.
Infinite LoopDuration without progress.
Freeze FrameEnd, joke, or evidence.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
in_film: The form comes from fashion stills (Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg) and advertising, not from a single feature grammar. Fashion films and window displays are the well-known uses: one living detail in a still.
La Jetee is a cousin of stills and motion, not a cinemagraph loop.
prompt_template: Freeze the frame, license one cycle. Still: Cinemagraph of [Subject], almost a still, one isolated motion looping: steam, hair, a blink, rain in a window.
prompt_example: Video: Almost still on [Subject], only one named element loops, locked camera, seamless cycle.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: freeze-frame, full-shot loop, or a normal live take. Tell: several motions alive, a visible loop bump, or a frozen frame with no live patch.
Fix: one masked element, invisible join, everything else from a single still.
faq: What is a cinemagraph in film?
A still image with one isolated looping motion. The rest is frozen. It sits between a photograph and a clip.
Cinemagraph vs freeze-frame
A freeze-frame stops all motion. A cinemagraph stops almost all motion and keeps one element alive on a loop.
When should I use a cinemagraph?
When a still should have one living detail: steam, rain, a flicker. Do not use it if the whole scene needs to play, or if nothing should move.
How do I prompt a cinemagraph for AI image or video?

Say almost still, locked camera, and name the single looping element. Forbid additional motion and a visible loop cut.

name: Collage
definition: Collage cinematography builds a frame from torn, cut, or mixed pieces: different stocks, paper, print, and live action sharing one plane with visible joins. Edges are graphic, and the stack is a construction, not an optical blend.
narrative: A head from one still, a building from another, newsprint, a painted sky. You can see the scissors.
Mixed grain, mixed contrast, maybe a bit of tape. One image was not enough, so the frame was assembled.

Use it when sources should remain sources: titles, satire, memory as scrapbook, a graphic sequence that refuses photographic unity. It is the wrong tool when two photographs should fuse as density (double exposure) or when live action and animation share a photographed space without torn edges.
Mixed media can do either. Collage insists on the cut.
how_it_works:
Shoot or collect plates. Cut them.
Leave borders, torn fiber, misregistered printing, different grain structures. Composite with hard or torn masks, not a screen blend.
Prompt: torn layers, mixed stocks, cut paper and live action sharing one plane, visible joins, not a smooth double exposure.
when_to_use: A portrait built from a live face, a city fragment, and newsprint, joins visible. Do not dissolve the same elements into a ghosted overlay and call it collage.
compared_names: Mixed MediaNo single medium owns the truth.
Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Double Exposure is an optical or additive stack without scissors. Mixed Media is the broader family (animation plus live, print plus plate).
Collage is the cut-and-paste grammar inside that family. Split Screen divides the frame into simultaneous pictures with a designed border, usually live.
Collage can ignore a shared timebase.

Bruce Conner's A Movie is found-footage collage as a film, which is grammar for the cut, not a look to clone.

Wrong cousin: double exposure or a clean split-screen. Tell: translucent blend, matching grain across pieces, or a hard live divider without paper or tear.
Fix: mismatched stocks, torn or cut borders, graphic stacking.
faq: What is collage in film?
A frame assembled from cut or torn pieces of different images and materials, with joins meant to be seen. It is construction, not a seamless composite.

Double exposure blends records as density. Collage keeps edges: scissors, paper, mixed stocks. One is optical stack. The other is cut and paste.

When one photograph is not enough and the sources should stay visible. Do not use it for a ghosted memory overlay or a seamless twin shot.

name: Datamosh
definition: Datamosh is intentional codec failure: inter-frame prediction continues after keyframes are removed or broken, so motion vectors smear the previous picture into the next GOP and faces bleed into the following shot. The image is file wreckage, not a lens error.
narrative: The I-frame never arrives. P-frames keep describing motion that no longer has a valid picture.
A mouth stretches into a wall. A cut happens in time but not in pixels.
Digital ruin is the style. Use it when the file should break on purpose: a music video, a corrupted memory, a broadcast that fails.

The smear should follow motion vectors, not a random RGB offset. It is the wrong tool for a stutter of whole frames (that is stop-stutter), for chromatic fringing, or for an altered-state smear from a long shutter.
If the image trails because the shutter was open, that is photography. If it trails because the codec predicted the wrong future, that is datamosh.
how_it_works:
Encode with inter-frame compression, drop or repeat I-frames, let P-frames or B-frames run. The artifact is temporal and blocky, often with residual macroblocks.
Prompt: inter-frame collapse, faces smearing into the next GOP, codec wreckage, not RGB split, not film smear.
when_to_use: A cut from a face to a city in which the face's pixels are dragged across the skyline by leftover motion vectors. Do not step-print the same clip or add red-cyan edge fringe and call it datamosh.
compared_names: Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.
compared_text: Stutter / Stop-Stutter repeats or steps whole frames as a temporal rhythm. Datamosh destroys the picture between frames.
Altered State is perceptual and photographic. Chromatic Aberration is optical color fringing.
Datamosh is codec wreckage, not a general noise overlay.

Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.

prompt_template: Break prediction, not the lens. Still: Datamosh of [Subject], inter-frame collapse, faces smearing into the next GOP, digital ruin as style.
prompt_example: Video: Datamosh corruption around [Subject], frames bleeding into the next, codec wreckage as image, not a shutter smear.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: stutter, long-shutter smear, or RGB split. Tell: clean frame repeats, photochemical motion blur, or three colored copies of the subject.
Fix: blocky temporal bleed across a cut, leftover pixels from the previous picture, no new I-frame.
faq: What is datamosh in film?
Deliberate video-codec collapse. Without a fresh keyframe, motion vectors smear the last valid picture into the next, producing inter-frame wreckage.
Datamosh vs stutter
Stutter repeats or steps complete frames. Datamosh lets predicted frames destroy the image. One is a rhythm of whole pictures. The other is a melt between them.
When should I use datamosh?
When the file should fail as the point: music video, corrupted feed, a digital breakdown. Do not use it as a substitute for optical smear or a simple jump cut.
How do I prompt datamosh for AI image or video?

Ask for inter-frame collapse, GOP smear, codec wreckage across a cut. Forbid shutter blur, RGB channel split, and freeze-frame stutter unless those are extra.

name: Diorama
definition: Diorama cinematography photographs a physical scale model so that it stands in for a much larger object or environment, with real light hitting real miniature surfaces. Scale is sold by texture, camera speed, depth of field, and movement, not by a toy-like tilt of focus.
narrative: A city, a ship, a hotel wing sits on a table or a stage, built at an inch to the foot or another ratio. The camera treats it as full size: enough stop for deep focus, a slow pass, fine windows, hard distant key.
Water, fire, and smoke are the hard parts, because fluids do not scale. Use it when a world should be tactile and built: a spacecraft, an industrial skyline, a storybook hotel.

The pleasure is that light is true on small surfaces. It is the wrong tool when you point a tilt-shift lens at a real city to make it look like a model, or when you align two live actors at different distances to lie about size.
Those are cousins. If depth of field is a thin band, the miniature will look like a miniature.
how_it_works:
Build surface scale (panel lines, dirt, tiny lights). Light with a hard, distant key as if the sun were far.
Stop down. Move slowly.
For water and fire, high-speed capture can help scale. Prompt: miniature world photographed as full size, deep enough focus, tactile model surfaces, not tilt-shift toy blur.
when_to_use: An orbital freighter as a detailed model, slow camera pass, tiny windows, deep focus against a black field. Do not add a thin horizontal band of focus that announces tabletop scale.
compared_names: Tilt-ShiftMake a city a model, or slice focus through a crowd.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Tilt-Shift tilts the plane of focus to make a real landscape look like a toy. Diorama is an actual model, usually shot deep to hide scale.
Forced Perspective uses live people and scaled set pieces from one viewpoint. Macro is close focus on small things as small things.
Diorama wants the small thing to read as large.

Photography of scale models standing in for large objects or places. Real light on real miniature surfaces, sold as full size by focus, speed, and texture.

Diorama is a real model, usually shot with enough depth of field to look large. Tilt-shift is a focus trick that makes a real full-size scene look small.

When a world should be a built, tactile miniature. Do not use it if you only want a toy look on a real city, or a live-action size lie between two actors.

name: Distortions
definition: Lens distortion cinematography warps space so straight lines bow, stretch, or melt: barrel, pincushion, mustache, extreme wide stretch, or a physical distorting optic such as a diopter, a bottle, or rain on glass. The lens is lying about geometry, not adding flare.
narrative: Walls lean. Faces balloon as they near the glass.
A hallway breathes. Space is not trustworthy.

The cause can be a very wide spherical, a fisheye, anamorphic mumps, heat shimmer, or a shot through a glass of water. Use it when the location should feel unsafe or subjective: a droogs' wide, a binge, a peephole, a fever.
Pick a distortion family and keep it consistent with the glass. It is the wrong tool for a clean normal-lens master, for flare without warp, or for a kaleidoscope of mirrors.
If color fringes without bent lines, that is chromatic aberration. If the whole mind is unhooked, consider altered state, of which distortion may be one part.
how_it_works:
Choose the glass: 14 mm or fisheye for barrel, long glass for pincushion, anamorphic for mumps and wave, a close diopter for melt at the edge. Get too close to faces on a wide and perspective distortion adds to optical distortion.
Prompt: optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, melted geometry, named wide or fisheye, not a flare overlay.
when_to_use: A close wide on a face in a tense interior, edges stretching, the room bowing, space untrustworthy. Do not keep a 50 mm rectilinear room and paste melted corners as a sticker.
compared_names: FisheyeThe mind is warped, or the space is a dome.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.
compared_text: Fisheye is the extreme barrel member of this family, with a circular or strongly bowed field. Lens Flare is scatter, not geometry.
Chromatic Aberration fringes color on edges. 14mm Ultra-Wide distorts through field of view and proximity even when the designer corrects barrel.
Altered State may include distortion plus time and color.

Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.
in_film: A Clockwork Orange uses extreme wides so rooms and faces are geometrically hostile. Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas melts space as intoxication.
Those are glass and proximity, not a warp filter parked on a normal lens.
prompt_template: Bend the space with glass. Example: Optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, barrel or melted geometry from ultra-wide or fisheye glass close to the face, the lens lying about space, not a flare pack.
prompt_example: Optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, melted geometry, the lens lying about space.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: lens flare, fisheye circular crop without the scene, or altered-state color smear with straight walls. Tell: rainbow streaks, a round porthole sticker, or a clean rectilinear room with a melted overlay.
Fix: choose a lens family, bow lines, let near faces balloon, keep the warp attached to the optic.
faq: What is lens distortion in film?
Geometric warping of space by the optic or by shooting through a distorting surface. Straight lines bow or stretch. The map of the room is no longer true.
Distortions vs fisheye
Fisheye is a specific extreme barrel lens. Distortions is the larger family: barrel, pincushion, anamorphic wave, heat, glass of water. Fisheye is one tool in that kit.
When should I use distortions?
When space should not be trustworthy. Do not use them on coverage that still has to be architecturally honest.

Name the glass (ultra-wide, fisheye) or the surface, describe bowed lines and stretched edges, and forbid flare-only artifacts or a sticker warp.
