name: Duplication
definition: A duplicate subject effect puts the same performer in a frame more than once as solid bodies: twins, a self across a table, copies in one room. It is usually a split matte, motion control, or a locked-camera composite, not a translucent double exposure.
narrative: One person is not a single self. Two performances share a kitchen.
They argue, pass a look, fail to occupy the same chair. Contact shadows, eyelines, and any exchanged object are the hard problems.
Two similar-looking people are not automatically this effect. Use it when identity splits in space: twins, a writer and his brother, a man meeting himself.

The encounter should feel physically ordinary. It is the wrong tool when the second self is a ghost (double exposure), when the frame is simply divided (split-screen as the visible device), or when one body melts into another (morph).
If they cannot sit in depth and occlude, you have the wrong cousin.
how_it_works:
Lock the camera or repeat the move with motion control. Record a clean plate.
Shoot each performance with matched light. Use a split matte where bodies stay apart, or tracked masks where they overlap.
Plan contact and handed objects as separate shots or as later help. Prompt: the same figure twice in one frame, solid bodies, matched lighting, not a ghost overlay, not a visible split line unless you want split-screen.
when_to_use: Two versions of one woman across a kitchen table, distinct posture and clothing, shared shadows, locked camera. Do not stack them as translucent densities, and do not leave a vertical join down the table.
compared_names: Double ExposureTwo times or two selves occupy one frame.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Double Exposure is additive overlay. Ghosts, not two sitters.
Split Screen shows two pictures with a designed border, which can be how duplication is done if the join is visible. Seamless duplication hides the join.
Morph turns one form into another over time. Duplication keeps both.

prompt_example: Duplication of [Subject], the same figure twice or more in one frame, twins of time or identity.
mistakes:
Wrong cousin: double exposure, split-screen with a hard line, or two lookalikes who are not the same face. Tell: translucent stack, a seam down the set, mismatched grain or key, hovering hands.
Fix: locked or motion-controlled plates, identical identity, shared shadows, planned occlusion.
faq: What is duplication in film?
The same performer appearing more than once in a shot as solid bodies, usually via split mattes or motion control. It is a spatial double, not a ghost overlay.
Duplication vs double exposure
Double exposure stacks densities so both images show through. Duplication composites two performances so each body can occlude, sit, and cast shadow.
When should I use duplication?
When one person must meet themselves as a physical other. Do not use it for a memory ghost or for a morph from one face into another.

name: Echo Print
definition: An echo print is an echo print effect that leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, so the last pose is still printed on this frame. The ghost is a stain of a previous exposure, not a second complete picture sharing the same plane.
narrative: Use it when a gesture has already happened and the present cannot shake it. A head turns and the old profile hangs a few pixels away.
A step leaves a faint body where the foot was. Time reads as a registration error.
It is the wrong tool for a clean double of two living people in conversation. If both images are fully exposed and equally sharp, you shot a superimposition, not a stain.
how_it_works:
Keep the camera locked or on a short path. Copy the previous frame, offset it along the motion vector by a few pixels or a few milliseconds, and print it at lower opacity.
Optical printers did this with a slight mis-register. Video echo does it with delay.
One key still lights the live body. The ghost has no second key.
Prompt an afterimage offset in time or register, and say that the last frame is still printed on this one.
when_to_use: Use it for the beat after a look, a blow, or a departure, when the last pose should remain as a stain. Do not use it to introduce a twin who must occupy the room as a solid person.

Step PrintingLonging that cannot move at normal speed.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Double Exposure combines two complete pictures. An echo print is a faded offset of the same action.
Step Printing repeats discrete frames to slow or stutter a take. The echo is a smear of register, not a held frame.

prompt_example: For video: Afterimages of [Subject] trail the present, an echo print of the previous moment. Name the offset direction.
prompt_note: Ban a second full scene.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Double Exposure. The tell is two equally solid bodies, both keyed, both sharp.
The fix is one live subject and a fainter, offset copy of the same pose, no second lamp.
faq: What is echo print in film?
Echo print leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, as if the last frame were still printed on this one. The past of the gesture remains visible as a stain.
Echo print vs double exposure
Double exposure combines two complete images. Echo print reprints a delayed or mis-registered copy of the same action at lower strength. One is two pictures. The other is a trail.
When should I use echo print?
Use it when a movement should leave a mark: a turn, a blow, a person already gone. Skip it when you need two solid people sharing a scene.

name: Feedback
definition: Video feedback is made by pointing a camera at its own live output so the picture nests into a recursive corridor of the same face. Each generation is a rephotograph of the monitor, with bloom, lag, and a tunnel of shrinking frames.
narrative: The medium stares at itself. A face on a tube is recaptured, recaptured again, and the room becomes a hallway of the same look.
Use it when the story is about watching, broadcast, or a mind that cannot get out of the signal. It is the wrong tool for a simple loop of action.
If the last frame merely sews to the first, you have a cycle in time, not a camera eating its monitor.
how_it_works:
Aim the taking lens at a playback screen that shows the live feed. A slight off-axis angle builds a corridor.
Dead-on nesting builds rectangles inside rectangles. Gain, lag, and the phosphor or pixel bloom set how fast the tunnel eats itself.
The subject is usually close to the screen so the first generation is readable. Prompt video feedback around the subject: camera looking into its own output, infinite corridor of the same face.
when_to_use: Use it when a person is trapped in a transmission, a title, or a night of monitors. Do not use it as wallpaper behind a dialogue scene that still needs geography.
compared_names: Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
compared_text: Kaleidoscope mirrors facets of one image into symmetry. Feedback nests generations of the same capture.
Infinite Loop sews the last frame to the first in time. Feedback is optical recursion, not a cycle of action.
KaleidoscopeOrnament, drugs, or chorus girls.
Infinite LoopDuration without progress.
Lens FlareLight is too strong to be polite.
in_film: 1960s tape experiments pointed cameras at monitors until the image tunnelled. The Doctor Who howlaround titles are the famous broadcast version.
Music videos still use the same recursive corridor. Grammar, not frames to copy.
prompt_template: Video feedback around [Subject], camera looking into its own output, infinite corridor of the same face. For video: Recursive video feedback of [Subject], the image eating itself into a tunnel.
prompt_example: Recursive video feedback of [Subject], the image eating itself into a tunnel.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Kaleidoscope or a simple video loop. The tell is mirrored wedges or a repeating walk with no nested screen.
The fix is a camera aimed at its own output, generations shrinking down a tunnel.
faq: What is feedback in film?
Video feedback is a camera looking into its own output so the image rephotographs itself into a nested corridor. Bloom, lag, and a tunnel of the same face are the picture.
Feedback vs kaleidoscope
A kaleidoscope mirrors one image into symmetric facets. Feedback recaptures the live picture from a monitor, stacking generations rather than folding the frame.
When should I use feedback?
Use it when the story is the signal watching itself: broadcast, hypnosis, a face trapped in a tube. Skip it for ordinary looping action.

definition: Floating UI, or HUD overlay cinematography, places readable interface, callouts, and data planes in the air of the scene so information lives in space, not only on a physical screen. The cockpit is the room.

Photograph the subject with a real key in the room. Composite interface planes with their own vanishing points, a few centimeters to a few meters in front of the face.

A faint self-illumination on the planes is allowed. It should not replace the key on the skin.
Prompt floating UI over the subject: HUD, callouts, and interface planes in 3D space, the screen as a cockpit.

name: Focal Shift
definition: A focal shift moves the plane of sharpness from one subject or distance to another during the shot, so attention travels as a pull. The camera body can stay put, and only the focus mechanism walks the depth.
narrative: Someone in the foreground owns the frame, then the helix turns and a face in the room takes over. No cut.
The blur itself is the sentence. Use it when who matters changes while geography stays.
It is the wrong tool if both planes must stay readable at once, or if you only need a static shallow portrait. If nothing is sharp at either end, you did not shift focus.

how_it_works:
Mark two distances. Keep depth of field shallow enough that only one plane is crisp, often a 50mm to 85mm near T2.
A follow-focus or remote motor walks the helical from A to B. The camera is usually locked or slow so the pull is the only event.
Lens breathing may thicken the image slightly as glass moves. Prompt a focal shift: the plane of sharpness traveling from one fact to another.
For video, pull from a foreground object onto the subject, or the reverse.
when_to_use: Use it for the beat when a glass, a gun, or a listener in the foreground yields to the person who must answer. Do not use it as decoration on a single face with no second plane.

name: Wigglegram
definition: A wigglegram is a short stereo shiver: two or three frames rocking so depth reads as a fidget. The viewpoints are a few centimeters apart, so depth is a twitch, not a dolly.

Foreground shifts more than the back, which is the disparity. No motion blur from a pan.

name: Match Cut
definition: A match cut joins two shots through a visual, spatial, sonic, or conceptual correspondence the viewer can read at the splice. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a shape, motion, object class, or idea, so the cut argues a relationship instead of only changing the view.
narrative: One side of the join is complete. The other side is complete.
What they share is the point: a bone leaving a hand, then a craft in the same screen path; a match blown out, then a sun the same size in the frame. The splice is the sentence.

Use it when two images are the same idea and you want that idea to land in one frame of time. It is the wrong tool when you only need a new camera position on the same gesture: that job belongs to match on action, and forcing a rhyme will feel like decoration.
If the second image does not change what the first one meant, skip the trick. A contour rhyme with no conceptual load is a graphic match wearing a bigger name.
how_it_works:
Design both frames as a pair before either is shot. Match the dominant contour, screen position, motion vector, or sonic envelope, then cut hard.
There is no optical mix: A is 100 percent, then B is 100 percent, and the correspondence is what the viewer supplies in the gap. Keep the shared property honest.
A door that sticks in the first shot must stick for the same mechanical reason later. Prompt both sides: name the outgoing object, the incoming object, the shared geometry or motion, and a hard cut, not a morph.
when_to_use:

definition: Match on action cuts during one continuous action so the movement itself bridges two camera positions. The outgoing shot starts the gesture; the incoming shot finishes it, which is why the edit can change size or angle without feeling interrupted.

name: Smash Cut
definition: A smash cut makes an abrupt, high-contrast transition in image, sound, tone, scale, or time. The outgoing side has earned a state (quiet, prayer, resolution); the incoming side contradicts it without a polite blend.
narrative: A night walk tightens. A bus door hisses into the frame.
The scare was a vehicle, not a monster, and the cut is the joke and the slap at once. Or: a grave visit settles, then a hand breaks the earth.
The next image should hurt. Use it when contrast is the meaning.
It is the wrong tool when the two sides are similar, or when you still need the audience inside one continuous action. Similar frames with missing time are a Jump Cut.

Hold A long enough to establish tone, scale, or apparent closure. Cut to B with a large change in brightness, loudness, shot size, or subject class: silence to noise, interior to blast, hymn to murder.
No dissolve, no fade, no matched contour unless the match is itself the insult. Coordinate picture and sound so they smash together, or delay the sound for a second smash (the blast seen, then heard).

when_to_use:

name: Dissolve
definition: A dissolve gradually overlaps the outgoing shot with the incoming shot so both images occupy the frame for a measurable duration. Opacity of A falls as opacity of B rises; at the midpoint you are looking at two ghosts.
narrative: A face thins. A landscape thickens through it.
Time has passed, or memory has, and the cut did not want to be a door slam. Dissolves are for passage, recollection, or the gentle death of a scene.
It is the wrong tool when the next image should hurt, or when the correspondence should snap. Hurt is a Smash Cut.
Snap-rhyme is a Match Cut or Graphic Match. If you hold the overlap as a meaning in itself, you are in Double Exposure territory, not a transition.
A dissolve does not automatically mean years have passed. Duration, sound, and context do that work.
A two-frame dissolve is just a soft cut.
how_it_works:
Mix A and B over time: typically a dozen frames to a few seconds. Keep a shared compositional hook if you want the overlap to read (a fan through a rotor, a face through a ceiling).
Decide whether sound dissolves with picture or bridges first. This is an optical or digital mix, not a camera move.
Prompt: dissolve from [Subject] into another time or place, overlapping ghosts, longer than a cut admits.
when_to_use:
Use it for memory, montage-like passage, or a scene that should die instead of stop. Do not use it to hide a bad match on action.
If the two sides should collide, cut hard.

name: Fade In / Fade Out
definition: A fade in or fade out takes the picture to or from a uniform field of black or color, rather than handing the frame straight to another visible scene. One side of the join is a world; the other side is absence, sleep, death, or a chapter break.
narrative: The room goes. Red remains, or black does, long enough to feel like a closed book.
Then another room is born from the same field. A fade is punctuation, not a mix of two stories.

Use it when a scene is a chapter, when consciousness drops, or when you want a pause the audience can rest in. It is the wrong tool for a gentle bleed between two images that should both stay present: that is a Dissolve.
It is also the wrong tool if you only want to point at a face inside a shrinking circle: that is an Iris. A fade does not automatically mean a long period has passed.
Sound that continues over black can mean a second of unconsciousness. Sound that dies with the picture can mean an ending.
how_it_works:
Reduce the picture to a field (or raise a picture out of one). Choose black for neutral chaptering, or a color (deep red, white) when the field itself should feel like a mood.
Coordinate whether sound survives the empty picture. Do not fill the room with fog or smoke to fake a fade; the image must leave, not get weather.
Prompt: fade to or from black around [Subject], chapter punctuation, sleep, death, or the start of a world.
when_to_use:
Use it to open a film, close an act, or mark a blackout of awareness. Do not use it between every scene in a contemporary dialogue piece unless you want a period cadence.
If two pictures should overlap, dissolve.

name: Wipe
definition: A wipe replaces one image with another through a moving boundary that travels across the frame. One side of the join is still A; the other side is already B; the edge between them is the edit, and it is meant to be seen.

name: Iris
definition: An iris transition reveals or conceals the picture with a moving circular or shaped mask. The mask's center is a pointer: one side of the join is the full world, the other is a hole closing on a face, a detail, or black.

It is also not a zoom into a dark tunnel. The camera can sit still while the mask moves.

name: Cross-Cutting
definition: Cross-cutting alternates two or more locations or action lines, often implying they are happening at the same time. Each side of the join is a complete strand; the engine is meanwhile, two clocks racing.

The film does not wait for one to finish. It braids them so ritual and murder share a tense.

Or: a team at a door, a listener at another door, and the cut teaches you they are about to meet until a reverse proves they are not. Use it when simultaneity, comparison, or false geography is the engine.
It is the wrong tool when you need one compressed idea from unlike images: that is Montage. It is also the wrong tool when two rooms must be visible at once: that is Split Screen.

Shoot each line so it can be interrupted: clear geography, readable time of day or clock, compatible but not identical details if you plan a wrong-door surprise. Alternate with tightening duration if you want the clocks to race.

name: Split Screen
definition: Split screen shows two or more image fields at once, so separate spaces share a single moment on the same frame. Both sides of the join are visible together; there is no waiting for the next cut.
narrative: A phone call places two apartments in one picture. A party splits into the night you wanted and the night you got.
Dual identity, dual time, or dual witness: the pane is the grammar. Use it when two rooms must be one moment, or when comparison is the joke.
It is the wrong tool when the audience should assume contact and then be wrong: that surprise is often better as Cross-Cutting. It is also not a window, doorway, or mirror inside the set.
That is Frame within Frame, a diegetic frame, not a panel. Replaying an event from another angle does not automatically make the accounts unreliable.

Shoot or generate each pane with matched eye-lines, horizon, or motion if you want the split to feel like one organism (a Match Split). Or keep the panes frankly separate for a phone call.

prompt_template: Show one lost-wallet incident three times: from the owner's view, a cleaner's view and a distant passenger's view. prompt_example: Split screen with [Subject] in one pane and another life in the other, simultaneous spaces, phone-call cinema or dual identity. Name the boundary, whether eyelines match, and what each pane contains.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Frame within Frame (a real window) or Cross-Cutting (sequential). The tell: a doorway in the set, or the model giving you one wide with a scratch down the middle.
The fix: two fully directed spaces, a graphic divide, simultaneous time.
faq: What is Split Screen in film?
Split screen shows multiple image fields at once. Both sides of the join occupy the frame together, so two rooms or two versions share one moment.
Split Screen vs Cross-Cutting
Cross-cutting alternates lines so you see one, then the other. Split screen presents them simultaneously. Alternation creates meanwhile; panels create co-presence.
When should I use Split Screen?
Use it when two spaces must be one moment: a call, twins, expectation versus reality. Do not use it as a substitute for a window in the set or for ordinary coverage.

name: Montage
definition: Film montage creates meaning or compression through the ordered juxtaposition of shots. Each side of a join is a complete image; the claim lives in the order, the collision, or the months squeezed into a minute.
narrative: Workers, then a slaughterhouse. The cut is an argument.
Or: sweat, rope, steps, a breath, the same stairs later, a body that can now climb. Time has collapsed, and the sequence did the climbing.
Use it when you need months in a minute, or an idea neither image holds alone. It is the wrong tool when two ongoing actions must remain simultaneously alive: that is Cross-Cutting.
It is the wrong tool when you only want to skip a few seconds in one setup: that is a Jump Cut. An evocative analogy is not factual proof.
Do not let the sequence imply unsupported real-world causation.
how_it_works:
State the intended inference or the time curve first. Choose images whose relation is legible: matching geometry for analogy, progressive sizes or sweat for training, repeated rituals for addiction.
Control duration as a metric (shortening toward a peak, or a held pause as payoff). Prompt: montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots.
when_to_use:
Use it for training, a marriage dying over breakfasts, a city arriving, an essay of images. Do not use it to cover a scene you could have played in continuity.
If the audience must follow one fight blow by blow, shoot the fight.
compared_names: Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: Cross-Cutting braids parallel actions that continue. Montage often finishes each shot as a unit in an argument or a time-lapse of life.
Jump Cut holes out one setup. Fragments withhold a complete view of one event; montage may show complete views whose collision is the event.
Quick Cuts are a duration pattern; they become montage when the order makes a claim.
Cross-CuttingMeanwhile is the engine.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: Rocky and The Karate Kid compress training into progressive labor. Strike and October collide images into political argument.
Citizen Kane breakfasts a marriage down to silence. Up condenses a life into selected moments.
Steal the function (compress, argue), not the needle-drops.

prompt_template: Create an essay montage alternating an automated sorting line with commuters moving through identical ticket gates. Match recurring barriers and mechanical rhythms to suggest institutional organization, while keeping humans visibly individual. No captions asserting the analogy as an objective fact.
prompt_example: Montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots. List the ordered images, what the collision claims, and whether time or idea is the engine.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Quick Cuts with no claim, or a single moving camera. The tell: twenty angles of the same five seconds, or a morphing collage.
The fix: pick an inference or a time span, choose distinct images, cut on order, let the join do the work.
faq: What is Montage in film?
Montage is meaning or compression made by the order of shots. Each side of a join is a picture; the idea appears in the juxtaposition, not in either image alone.
Montage vs Cross-Cutting
Cross-cutting keeps two action lines running in implied simultaneity. Montage compresses duration or collides images to make a claim. One races clocks; the other builds an argument or a month.
When should I use Montage?
Use it when you need months in a minute, or an idea that only exists between images. Do not use it as a pile of unused coverage from one scene.
How do I prompt Montage for AI image or video?

List the shots and the claim. Example: Montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots. Specify order, not a single moving take.

name: Axial Cut
definition: An axial cut jumps closer or farther along approximately the same camera axis, changing shot size without changing angle. The outgoing frame and the incoming frame share a viewpoint; only distance snaps.
narrative: A farmhouse kitchen, then the same kitchen larger, then an eye socket you were not ready to occupy. Recognition arrives as a series of shocks, not as a walk.
Change shot size without changing angle. Use it for stepwise emphasis: a date in a book, a wound, a face that must suddenly fill the world.
It is the wrong tool when you want a continuous approach. A Crash Zoom In is an optical move in time.
A dolly-in is a walk. An axial cut is an edit.
If the angle changes more than a few degrees, you have ordinary coverage, not an axial cut. If time is what you skipped inside one size, you have a Jump Cut.
how_it_works:
Capture or generate matched wide, medium, and close compositions on the same axis. Preserve pose, eyeline, and background alignment enough that the jump is only scale.
Choose deliberate steps (for example 50mm at 3 meters, then 50mm at 1 meter, or a punch-in crop that matches a true closer camera). Do not animate a zoom between the frames if the point is the snap.
Prompt: axial cut jumping toward or away from [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom.
when_to_use:
Use it when a detail must land as a blow: the date stamp, the empty eye, the gun on the table. Do not use it as a substitute for a motivated push-in during a long take.
If the camera should walk, walk.
compared_names: Crash Zoom InPunctuate a hit, a realization, or a comic sting.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Crash Zoom In is a continuous, fast focal-length change. An axial cut is a splice.
A Jump Cut skips time in a similar size; axial cut skips distance on one axis. Match on Action needs a bridging gesture; axial cut can hit a still figure.
A push-in has parallax; a punch-in crop of one take has none, and is a cheaper cousin of a true closer camera on the same axis.
Crash Zoom InPunctuate a hit, a realization, or a comic sting.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: The Birds sends Lydia through successive closer views of the dead farmer, the axis held, the scale jumping. The Shining uses hard axial emphasis on rooms and faces so space feels like a trap.
Goodfellas punches in for recognition rather than a polite zoom. Use the snap, not a copied kitchen.
The Birds 1963Lydia's discovery of the dead farmer is emphasized through successive closer views.
prompt_template: A librarian notices an impossible new date stamped inside an old book. Make three hard cuts on the same axis: desk-wide, book close-up, extreme close-up of the date. Keep the page and hands fixed, with no zoom animation, morph or lateral angle change. Add exact date text in compositing.
prompt_example: Axial cut jumping toward or away from [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom, a snap of scale. Name two or three matched framings, same angle, same pose, hard cuts.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a Crash Zoom In or a digital crop sold as a camera move. The tell: the lens breathes, or the angle walks off axis, or the subject morphs larger.
The fix: two (or three) still-matched compositions, same axis, hard cuts, pose locked.
faq: What is Axial Cut in film?
An axial cut jumps closer or farther along the same camera axis. Both sides of the join share an angle; only shot size changes, as a snap rather than a move.
Axial Cut vs Crash Zoom In
A crash zoom is a continuous optical move. An axial cut is an edit between matched distances on one axis. One is a whoosh; the other is a punch.
When should I use Axial Cut?
Use it to change shot size without changing angle, when recognition should shock. Do not use it when you want the camera to walk or the lens to zoom in time.
How do I prompt Axial Cut for AI image or video?

Ask for matched wide and close frames on the same axis, then a hard cut. Example: Axial cut jumping toward [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom. No zoom animation.

name: Invisible Cut
definition: An invisible cut hides an edit through motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or digital stitching. One side of the join and the other are meant to feel like a single take; the splice is a seam the audience should not find.
narrative: A coat fills the lens. When it leaves, the room is later, or the body is gone, or the street has changed.
You needed a cut the audience must not feel. Stop-trick cinema did this with a locked camera and a substitution.
Contemporary oners do it with whips, walls, and stitches. Use it to simulate a long take, to vanish a person, or to change time inside an apparently continuous walk.
It is the wrong tool when the cut should be a sentence: a Match Cut, a Smash Cut, a Wipe. If you want the join seen, do not hide it.
The trick depends on spatial continuity around the substitution. A wandering unmatched camera exposes an unintended jump.
how_it_works:
Plan a hiding place: a passing body, a dark wall, a whip-pan blur, a matched doorway, a digital stitch on a texture. Lock exposure and lighting across plates if you are substituting.
For a stop trick, lock the camera, hold actors, change the object, splice on the occlusion. For an oner illusion, match motion blur and grain at the whip.
Prompt: invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body, the oner illusion.
when_to_use:
Use it to extend a take through a theatre, a trench, a street, or to make a woman vanish from a chair. Do not use it to avoid writing a scene change.
If the geography actually transforms as you watch, that may be a Set Transition instead of a hidden splice.
compared_names: Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Oner is the long take you are faking or actually shooting. A Whip Pan can be the bandage over the splice.
Match on Action hides a cut in a readable gesture but still changes the view on purpose. Set Transition lets the location rewrite itself.
Morph is a visible interpolation, the opposite of invisible.
OnerThe scene is a ride.
Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.

Rope hides joins in dark foregrounds. 1917 and Birdman stitch walks so trenches and theatres feel continuous.
Spectre's opening presents multiple spaces as one shot. Grammar of concealment, not a take to clone.

prompt_template: A stage magician drops a cloth over an empty chair. At the instant the cloth fills the chair silhouette, cut to an identically framed plate with a bouquet beneath it. The magician lifts the cloth. Locked camera, matching hands and shadows, no liquid morph or camera move. Generate two plates and join them at the occlusion.
prompt_example: Invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body, the oner illusion. Name the hiding action, the before plate, the after plate, and that the camera path should appear continuous.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a visible Whip Pan that never hides a join, or a morph. The tell: a pop in grain, a jump in crowd, a morphing wall.
The fix: a true occluder or blur that fills the frame, matched lighting, a hard splice inside that fill, continuous motion on both sides.
faq: What is Invisible Cut in film?
An invisible cut hides the edit in motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or stitching. Both sides of the join are meant to play as one continuous shot.
Invisible Cut vs Oner
A oner is a long take. An invisible cut is how you fake or extend one: the splice sits inside a whip, a wall, or a passing body. One is the apparent shot; the other is the seam.
When should I use Invisible Cut?
Use it when the audience must not feel the edit: a vanishing act, a stitched walk, a time jump inside a continuous-looking path. Do not use it when the join should speak.
How do I prompt Invisible Cut for AI image or video?

Name the hiding place and both plates. Example: Invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body. Demand matched lighting and no morph.

name: J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)
definition: A J-cut or L-cut visual setup is a picture designed so sound can lead or lag across the splice. One side of the join is a face, a room, or a listener that can hold; the other side is a space already speaking, or still speaking after we have left it.
narrative: We hear the next room before we see it (J-cut): the picture stays on the walker, the voice has already arrived. Or we see the listener while the speaker's words continue (L-cut): the face is the bridge.
Sound will lead or lag. The face is the bridge.

Use it when picture and track should not cut on the same frame, so thought can cross a doorway. It is the wrong tool when you need both rooms visible at once (Split Screen) or when you only need a mute reaction insert with no overlapping track.
Randomly mismatched music is not automatically meaningful counterpoint. Define what the lag reveals: dread, irony, a voice that will not let the face go.
how_it_works:
On the timeline, a J-cut lets incoming audio start under the outgoing picture. An L-cut lets outgoing audio continue under the incoming picture.
The visual setup is a shot that can bear that overlap: a Reaction Shot, a walk toward a door, an empty office. Keep the sound's source clear enough that the overlap is information, not muddle.
Prompt: a frame of [Subject] designed as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking.
when_to_use:
Use it to enter a conversation before the room, to stay on a listener after a confession, to let a song continue over a packing scene it does not belong to. Do not use it as default dialogue cutting if both faces should share the same on-camera words.
If you need meanwhile geography, Cross-Cutting.
compared_names: Reaction ShotThe important action is watching.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Reaction Shot is the picture; J-cut and L-cut are how that picture meets sound. Cross-Cutting alternates whole lines.
A smash in sound on a picture cut is closer to Smash Cut. Counterpoint (cheerful music on a cruel image) can ride an L-cut, but the technique here is the staggered splice, not the playlist.
Reaction ShotThe important action is watching.
Cross-CuttingMeanwhile is the engine.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: The Social Network and Heat keep speech living over listeners' faces so thought continues across the join. The Conversation makes incoming sound a threat before the picture explains it.
Yi Yi lets piano arrive before its source is located. A Clockwork Orange and Reservoir Dogs place cheerful tracks against behavior the picture will not bless.
Use the stagger, not the needle-drop.

Reservoir Dogs 1992The radio song contrasts with the warehouse torture scene.
Yi Yi 2000Piano music is heard before its source is fully located visually.

prompt_template: A cheerful original corporate jingle plays over a spotless office being emptied after a sudden closure. Workers quietly pack plants and family photographs while the tune maintains its bright tempo. Generate restrained visual coverage and compose an original cue; do not imitate an existing recording or melody.
prompt_example: A frame of [Subject] designed as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking. For stills, describe a listening face or a doorway that can hold offscreen voice.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a mute Reaction Shot with picture and sound cutting together, or a Cross-Cutting that never overlaps track. The tell: lips in the new room are already talking in sync at the picture cut, with no pre-lap.
The fix: hold the first picture while the second track starts, or hold the first track after the picture has moved.
faq: What is J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup) in film?
A J-cut starts the next shot's sound before its picture; an L-cut keeps the last shot's sound after the picture has changed. The visual setup is a frame that can hold while the other space speaks.
J-Cut / L-Cut vs Reaction Shot
A reaction shot is a picture of listening. J-cut and L-cut are how that picture is joined to another space's sound. You can have a reaction with a straight cut; the J/L is the stagger.
When should I use J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)?
Use it when sound should lead a scene in, or linger after we have left. Do not use it if picture and track must hit together as a smash.
How do I prompt J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup) for AI image or video?

Describe a face or room that can hold offscreen voice. Example: A frame of [Subject] as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking. For video, say which track pre-laps.

name: Crash Cut
definition: A crash cut slams two images together with no blend, so the join itself stings. One side of the splice and the other collide; unlike a smash that breaks an earned quiet, a crash cut often starts inside the event or hits like a drum from the first frame.
narrative: A trunk, a man, a knife already in play, then the story will explain how we got here. Or a cymbal, a face, a rehearsal that never had a polite establishing wide.
The next image must hurt, and it must hurt immediately. Use it as percussion, as in medias res, as a refusal of the soft open.
It is the wrong tool when you have just built a hush that should be betrayed: that betrayal is a Smash Cut. It is the wrong tool when you only skip time in one seat: that is a Jump Cut.
A few frames of interrupt are a Flash Cut, not a committed new scene. Do not open on a sensation the rest of the story cannot causally earn.
how_it_works:
Cut A to B with maximum difference in scale, brightness, or violence of content, and with no mix. Often B is already mid-action (a trunk, a gun, a kit).
Mark any later temporal reset clearly (a title, a younger haircut) so the crash is a structure, not an accident. Prompt: crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting.
when_to_use:
Use it to open on the consequence, to hit a downbeat, to refuse an establishing courtesy. Do not use it between two similar wides.
If A was a long prayer, consider smash. If B lasts three frames, consider flash.
compared_names: Smash CutThe next image should hurt.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Smash Cut breaks an earned state (quiet, closure, prayer). A crash cut is the collision as a blow, often before a state was offered.
A Jump Cut stays similar. A Flash Cut is too short to become the new scene.
Quick Cuts are a run of short shots; a crash is one brutal splice.
Smash CutThe next image should hurt.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: Goodfellas opens in the trunk, then later supplies the life that led there. Fight Club starts inside a crisis and then rewinds the path.
Whiplash and Requiem for a Dream use hard joins as rhythmic blows. Use the sting and the delayed explanation, not a copied trunk.

Fight Club 1999The opening crisis is followed by the path that led there.
prompt_template: Design three sequences: begin with a violinist standing alone on a flooded stage holding an unopened letter; cut to a calm morning before the concert; later return to the stage with the meaning of the letter now clear. Generate each sequence separately and edit the order deliberately. No unrelated mystery props.
prompt_example: Crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting. Name A and B, the scale or sound collision, and that B may already be mid-event.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Smash Cut (after a hush) or Flash Cut (a few frames). The tell: a long quiet setup before the hit (that is smash), or B vanishing before it can be a scene (that is flash).
The fix: collide two committed images, start inside the event if that is the structure, cut hard.
faq: What is Crash Cut in film?
A crash cut is a hard join where two images collide with no blend. Both sides are committed shots; the splice stings, often by starting inside an event or hitting like a drum.
Crash Cut vs Smash Cut
A smash cut betrays an earned quiet or closure. A crash cut is the collision itself, frequently from the first frame of a scene or as in medias res. Smash breaks a state; crash refuses to offer one.
When should I use Crash Cut?
Use it when the next image must hurt immediately, or when the story should start inside the consequence. Do not use it as a skip inside one similar frame.
How do I prompt Crash Cut for AI image or video?

Name two colliding images and forbid a blend. Example: Crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting. Let B be mid-action if the structure needs it.

name: Flash Cut
definition: A flash cut interrupts the present image with a few frames of another picture, then returns or races on before the insert can be studied. One side of the join is the ongoing scene; the other is lightning: a thought, a future, a wound, lasting a blink.
narrative: A face in a room. Three frames of a well, a tape, a child.
The room again. You cannot inventory what you saw, but it has already happened to you.
A thought that lasts three frames. Use it for intrusion: prophecy wearing the clothes of memory, a trauma tic, a subliminal threat.
It is the wrong tool when the other image should become the scene. That committed landing is a Crash Cut or Smash Cut.
A white frame that is only exposure is a Light Flash, not another picture. Keep the insert temporally honest enough that a later anchor can fix it.
Mystery is not the same as no clue.
how_it_works:
Hold the present shot. Insert 1 to 8 frames of a different image (often high contrast, closer, or from another time).
Return to the present, or chain flashes. Do not dissolve; the brevity is the grammar.
Picture may be silent or carry a tick of sound. Prompt: flash cut through [Subject], a few frames of another image interrupting, lightning in the edit.
when_to_use:
Use it when a mind is leaking another time, or when a threat should be unreadable but present. Do not use it as decoration on a trailer.
If the audience must read the insert, give it a shot, not a flash.
compared_names: Crash CutThe next image must hurt.
Light FlashA cut that is also a wound of light.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Crash Cut stays with the new image. A Light Flash is a burst of light, not a second diegesis.
A Jump Cut skips time in a similar frame without inserting a foreign picture. Smash Cut commits to contrast as the new present.
Flash cut is an interrupt.
Crash CutThe next image must hurt.
Light FlashA cut that is also a wound of light.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.

prompt_template: Show brief intimate images of a woman teaching a child to repair a radio, initially without dates or age labels. In the present, she has never met the child. prompt_example: Flash cut through [Subject], a few frames of another image interrupting, lightning in the edit. Name the present scene, the insert (and its duration in frames), and the return.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Light Flash (no second image) or Crash Cut (the insert stays). The tell: a white blink, or a new scene that never returns to the present.
The fix: a countable handful of frames of a different picture, then the original scene, hard cuts.
faq: What is Flash Cut in film?
A flash cut inserts a few frames of another image into an ongoing shot. One side is the present; the other is a blink of a different picture, too short to become the scene.
Flash Cut vs Crash Cut
A crash cut lands in a new committed image. A flash cut interrupts and (usually) returns. Duration is the difference: a scene versus a handful of frames.
When should I use Flash Cut?
Use it for a thought, a leak of another time, or a threat too brief to inventory. Do not use it when the other image needs to be read as the new present.
How do I prompt Flash Cut for AI image or video?

name: Match Motion
definition: A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the splice so the cut rides a vector even when location, time, or reality changes. One side of the join starts a movement; the other side keeps that movement, and the world around the body may be new.
narrative: A fall toward a mattress becomes a fall toward grass. A dive into a pool completes as a lunge onto a bed.
Hide the cut inside a vector. The body is the continuity; the room is allowed to lie.

Use it to carry someone through an impossible transition: dream to street, train to meadow, one chase into another. It is the wrong tool when you are still in the same room and only changing cameras on one gesture: that is Match on Action.

Matching only the actor's face, with no shared phase of motion, will not hide the leap. A whip can supply the blur that sells the vector (Whip Pan), but the match is the body's direction and speed, not the smear alone.
how_it_works:
Match pose, screen position, camera angle, motion direction, and speed at the cut. Plan the two shots as a pair (or a shared rig).
Cut at a readable phase: mid-fall, mid-turn, mid-stride. The outgoing world and the incoming world can disagree; the vector must not.
Prompt: match-motion cut on [Subject], direction and speed continuing across the join so the cut rides the movement.
when_to_use:
Use it to leave a dream, to stitch a chase across towns, to let a dance continue in another decade. Do not use it as ordinary coverage inside one hallway.
If the action is the same event, match on action. If only the contour matches and the body is still, use a Graphic Match or Match Cut.
compared_names: Match on ActionHide the cut in a movement.
Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: Match on Action is one continuous event, two views, same world. Match-motion can change the world if the vector holds.
A Whip Pan hides a cut in camera blur; match-motion hides it in subject motion (they can combine). A Match Cut may be still.
Invisible Cut conceals a splice in occlusion; the motion match is a visible, readable continuation.
Match on ActionHide the cut in a movement.
Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.

Baby Driver rides motion from music and cars across joins. Lawrence of Arabia's match-to-sun is more a still match cut; use it only if you are matching a rising gesture, not just a circle.
Borrow the vector, not the wardrobe.

mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Match on Action (same room) or a Match Cut of two stills. The tell: the walk resets, speed changes, or the subject is static on both sides.
The fix: match phase, direction, and speed; let geography jump; cut during the move.
faq: What is Match Motion in film?
A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the edit so the splice rides a vector. One side starts the movement; the other keeps it, even if place or reality changes.
Match Motion vs Match on Action
Match on action hides a camera change inside one continuous event in one world. Match motion can carry that event's vector into another location, time, or dream.
When should I use Match Motion?
Use it when a body should tow the viewer through an impossible change of world. Do not use it for ordinary coverage of one gesture in one room.

name: Match Split
definition: A match split continues a graphic line or motion across a divide, so one contour belongs to two worlds at once. One side of the join is a pane or half-frame; the other is its partner; the shared edge, horizon, or gesture is the match.
narrative: A table edge runs from a 1960s kitchen into a present-day diner. A face is halved: left is the party you imagined, right is the party you got.
One line, two worlds. Use it when a split should feel like one organism rather than two televisions.

It is the wrong tool when the panes have no shared contour and are only simultaneous: that is ordinary Split Screen. It is also the wrong tool when you cut from one full frame to another rhyming full frame: that is a Match Cut or Graphic Match.
The divide is not a scratch. It is a designed seam that the eye can follow.
how_it_works:
Compose both halves so a line, eyeline, horizon, or motion vector continues across the boundary. Match scale of heads if two versions of one person share a couch.
Keep lighting motivated per world unless the gag is that light also matches. Prompt: match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space.
when_to_use:
Use it for twins, double lives, expectation versus reality, a road that is two times of day. Do not use it if the two spaces should not touch graphically.
If you need a phone call with frankly separate rooms, a clean split is enough.
compared_names: Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
Graphic MatchForm carries you across time.
compared_text: Split Screen co-presents; match split is a split whose form rhymes or continues. A Match Cut replaces one full image with another.
Frame within Frame is a window in the set. Graphic Match happens across a hard cut in time, not across a simultaneous seam.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
Split ScreenTwo rooms, one moment.
Graphic MatchForm carries you across time.
in_film: The Parent Trap seats two versions of one girl in a shared graphic so the split is a relationship. (500) Days of Summer divides a party into expectation and reality along a readable seam.
Use the continued line, not the plot.
prompt_template: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space. Name the shared contour (horizon, table, eyeline), what each half contains, and that both are simultaneous.
prompt_example: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is a generic Split Screen with unmatched eyelines, or a Match Cut in sequence. The tell: two stacked clips with no shared line, or a cut instead of a co-present seam.
The fix: design the divide, continue one contour, hold both worlds at once.
faq: What is Match Split in film?
A match split is a divided frame where a line, motion, or contour continues from one world into the other. Both sides of the join are visible together and graphically related.
Match Split vs Split Screen
Split screen shows two fields at once. Match split is a split that rhymes or continues a line across the seam. All match splits are splits; not all splits match.
When should I use Match Split?
Use it when one contour should belong to two worlds at the same time. Do not use it for a simple phone-call panel with no shared geometry.
How do I prompt Match Split for AI image or video?

Name the continued line and both halves. Example: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space. Simultaneous panes, no morph.

name: Quick Cuts
definition: Quick cuts editing strings shots shorter than a breath, so duration itself becomes rhythm, pressure, or music. Each side of a join is a full view from a changing setup; the meaning is the rate, not a skip inside one frame.
narrative: Eyes, hands, a kit, a face, the room, the stick, faster. You feel a release coming before the last hit lands.
Pace is the meaning. A sudden hold in that pattern can be the climax.

Use it when acceleration or a metric pulse should do narrative work: a showdown tightening from bodies to eyes, a raid, a practice that becomes punishment. It is the wrong tool when the similar frame is losing time: that is a Jump Cut.
It is the wrong tool when you are withholding the complete event in shards: that is Fragments. Faster is not always more tense.
Contrast between acceleration and a held pause often carries the payoff.
how_it_works:
Design a duration curve and a progression of shot sizes. Alternate angles enough that each cut is a new view, not a hole in one view.
Use musical or physical accents selectively; not every splice must land on a beat. Prompt: quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music.
when_to_use:
Use it to tighten a duel, a performance, a chase through hands and gauges. Do not use it on a conversation that needs air.
If the pattern never rests, the last hit has nowhere to land.
compared_names: Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Crash CutThe next image must hurt.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: A Jump Cut is a skip inside a similar setup. A Crash Cut is one brutal join.

Montage may use short shots, but montage's job is collision of meaning or collapsed months; quick cuts' job is rate. Fragments hide the whole action; quick cuts often show the action in many complete, brief views.
Jump CutDo not soothe. Show the skip.
Crash CutThe next image must hurt.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly tightens the three-way showdown from bodies and positions toward faces and eyes. Whiplash binds image duration to pressure and rhythm.
Mad Max: Fury Road and Requiem for a Dream use short shots as pulse. Steal the curve, not the coverage plan.

Whiplash 2014Performance passages bind image duration to pressure and rhythm.
prompt_template: Create a tense three-person card-game ending. Begin with wide spatial views, then progressively shorter shots of faces, hands and one face-down card. Accelerate the cutting while preserving who sits where, then hold a long silent close-up before the card turns. Assemble rhythm in the edit.
prompt_example: Quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music. List a progression of sizes (wide to eyes, or hands to kit) and a duration curve.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Jump Cut (same frame, missing time) or chaos with no curve. The tell: every shot is the same length and size, or the camera never changes axis.
The fix: new views, shortening (or a designed break), a last image that can resolve the pulse.
faq: What is Quick Cuts in film?
Quick cuts are a run of very short shots from changing setups, so duration becomes rhythm. Each side of a join is a new view; the rate is the meaning.
Quick Cuts vs Jump Cut
A jump cut skips time inside a similar framing. Quick cuts change angle, size, or subject every breath. One is a hole in a setup; the other is a metric pattern.
When should I use Quick Cuts?
Use it when pace should tighten a duel, a performance, or a chase. Do not use it as default coverage, and do not confuse it with a jump inside one frame.
How do I prompt Quick Cuts for AI image or video?

Ask for many short, distinct shots and a duration curve. Example: Quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music. Name the progression of sizes.

name: Set Transition
definition: A set transition lets the location change in camera: walls walk, architecture rewrites, one space becomes another without a hard cut. Both sides of the join are geographies that share a continuous camera path; the set itself is the editor.
narrative: A dressing room wall slides and you are in a nightclub. A theatre door is a street.
Geography itself edits. The subject may not have cut; the world did.

Use it when the story's spaces are porous: backstage as mind, city as stage, a lobby that rewrites under fire. It is the wrong tool when you only need to hide a splice in a whip: that is an Invisible Cut.
It is the wrong tool when A melts into B as a picture: that is Morphing. If the camera passes through a wall into another place as a portal gag, you are next to Pass Through.
Set transition is the room changing around the body.
how_it_works:
Build two (or more) complete spaces that can physically or digitally replace each other on a continuous move: sliding flats, revolving walls, a stitch on a doorway, a digital set extension that rewrites. Keep lighting motivated as the space changes, or let the lights change as part of the trick.
Prompt: set transition around [Subject], the location transforming in camera, walls walking, one space becoming another. Motion brief: the set around [Subject] transforms into a new location without a hard cut.
when_to_use:
Use it to walk from rehearsal into performance, from memory into a street, from one building into another without admitting an edit. Do not use it if a hard cut or a wipe would tell the truth faster.
Virtuosity with nothing new in the second space is empty.
compared_names: Pass ThroughCut the building, not the film.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: An Invisible Cut conceals a splice; the set may stay the same. A Pass Through drives the camera through a surface into another space.
Morphing interpolates the image. A set transition rewrites architecture along a continuous path, theatrical or digital.
Match Motion can change worlds on a body vector without the walls walking.
Pass ThroughCut the building, not the film.
MorphingBecoming is visible.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: Birdman lets theatre and city feel like one porous set. 1917 hides joins so trenches, ruins, and fields play as continuous geography.
The Matrix lobby rewrites a space through action and spatial continuity. Use the porous building, not a copied tracking path.
prompt_template: Set transition around [Subject], the location transforming in camera, walls walking, one space becoming another. Name the starting architecture, the ending architecture, and that the camera does not hard-cut.
prompt_example: For video: the set around [Subject] transforms into a new location without a hard cut. No morphing faces; the room is what changes.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Morphing the actor, or a visible cut in a doorway. The tell: the person melts, or there is a pop at the threshold.
The fix: keep the body continuous, let walls or set extension rewrite, hide or omit the splice, match lighting across the change.
faq: What is Set Transition in film?
A set transition changes location in camera as architecture rewrites around the subject. Both sides of the join are places on one continuous path, not two shots with a hard cut.
Set Transition vs Invisible Cut
An invisible cut hides an edit; the set might not change. A set transition makes geography the edit: walls walk, rooms become other rooms. One conceals a splice; the other rewrites space.
When should I use Set Transition?
Use it when spaces should feel porous and the camera should not admit a cut. Do not use it as a flex when a straight scene change would be clearer.
How do I prompt Set Transition for AI image or video?

Name both locations and a continuous camera. Example: Set transition around [Subject], walls walking, one space becoming another. Video: the set transforms without a hard cut. Keep the body stable.

name: Transitions
definition: Film transitions are designed joins: the splice treated as a visible gesture rather than as continuity glue. One side of the join and the other are planned as a pair, and the audience is meant to notice how we left A and entered B.
narrative: A wipe turns a page. A match claims an idea.
A dissolve remembers. A whip throws you.
The cut should be seen. This is the parent of those gestures, not a substitute for choosing one.
Use it when invisible continuity would lie, or when the join is the joke, the thesis, or the chapter mark. It is the wrong tool when the scene should feel found and unedited.
Then hide the cut, or do not cut. Pick a species.
'A cool transition' is not a shot list. Name wipe, match, mix, light, or whip.
how_it_works:
Decide what the join must do: rhyme (Match Cut), mix (Dissolve), empty (Fade In / Fade Out), travel an edge (Wipe), point (Iris), blur (Whip Pan), or rewrite space (Set Transition). Design A and B together so the chosen gesture has material to work with.
Prompt: a designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light.
when_to_use:
Use it at act breaks, world leaps, jokes about cinema, or any time the how of leaving matters. Do not use a designed transition on every reverse in a talk scene.
If nothing in the story changes at the splice except the camera, a straight cut is the design.
compared_names: Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.
DissolveMemory, passage, or a gentle death of a scene.
compared_text: A Match Cut is a correspondence across a hard cut. A Dissolve is a mix.
A Whip Pan can hide or announce a join through blur. A Wipe shows a traveling edge.
This page is the choice to make the join a gesture; those pages are the species. Invisible Cut is the opposing doctrine.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
Whip PanTransition, punchline, or sudden attention shift.
DissolveMemory, passage, or a gentle death of a scene.
in_film: Star Wars makes scene changes into directional wipes, a serial grammar. 2001: A Space Odyssey makes a hard match the largest leap in the film.
Use them as proof that a visible join can carry story, not as a kit to paste on every cut.
prompt_template: For video, generate A and B as complete shots, then specify the gesture (hard match, mix, traveling edge, whip). Do not write 'cool transition' or 'seamless' if you want the join seen.
prompt_example: A designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light. Name both sides and the species of join.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is an Invisible Cut you accidentally made visible, or a morph used because no join was chosen. The tell: A and B have no designed relationship, and a filter slurries them.
The fix: pick a species, give both sides a job, execute that physics only.
faq: What is Transitions in film?
Transitions in this sense are designed joins, splices the audience is meant to notice. Both sides of the join are planned as a pair, and the gesture (wipe, match, mix, light) is part of the sentence.
Transitions vs Match Cut
A match cut is one species of designed join: correspondence across a hard cut. Transitions as a heading means choosing a visible gesture at all, which might be a match, a wipe, a dissolve, or a whip.
When should I use Transitions?
Use a designed transition when the how of leaving A is story. Do not decorate every reverse. If the join should vanish, do not design it as a gesture.
How do I prompt Transitions for AI image or video?

Name A, B, and the species of join. Example: a designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light. Forbid vague words like seamless or cool.

name: Fragments
definition: Fragments, or fragmented editing, build an event from partial views, so the audience infers an action more complete than anything shown in one shot. Each side of a join is a shard: a blade, a mouth, a drain, a hand too late; the whole lives in the gaps.
narrative: You never get the master. You get a sleeve, a missed catch, a face, ceramic already on the floor, and one offscreen crash.
Do not give the whole. The viewer assembles the blow.
Use it to make an impact intense while withholding explicit depiction, or to show a night that will not assemble. It is the wrong tool when the audience must see a legal, continuous action.
It is also not just speed: Quick Cuts can show complete blows rapidly. Fragments hide the complete blow.
Fast shards alone do not guarantee clarity. Direction, causal order, and sound have to let the viewer reconstruct the event.
how_it_works:
Break the event into distinct visual elements that can be shot safely: the approaching object, a body part, a reaction, the aftermath. Preserve screen direction and order.
Bind with timing and sound; do not require the dangerous contact on camera. Prompt: fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment, the scene as shards.
Name what is missing.
when_to_use:
Use it for a shower, a staircase massacre built from details, a panic, a memory. Do not use it for a demonstration that must be readable as one take.
If the pieces cannot be ordered into a cause, you have a Collage, not an event.
compared_names: CollageOne image is not enough; stack them.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
compared_text: Quick Cuts are a rate pattern and may show complete actions. Montage collides complete images for an idea or a month.
Collage is a paper or composite of pieces as a surface. Jump Cut holes one setup.
Fragments are incomplete views of one action whose whole is inferred.
Quick CutsPace is the meaning.
CollageOne image is not enough; stack them.
Match CutTwo images are the same idea.
in_film: Psycho constructs the shower from brief fragments, reactions, and sound rather than one continuous explicit view. Battleship Potemkin builds the Odessa Steps from details and reactions.
Requiem for a Dream and Memento use shards as a nervous or backward structure. Use inference, not a copied stab.
Psycho 1960The shower murder is constructed from brief fragments, reactions and sound rather than one continuous explicit view.
Battleship Potemkin 1925The Odessa Steps sequence builds violence through details and reactions.
prompt_template: Imply a valuable vase being accidentally knocked over without showing the full break. Generate separate shots of a sleeve brushing its base, a hand reaching too late, a startled face and ceramic pieces already on the floor. Join with one offscreen crash. No real hazardous stunt or incoherent object duplication.
prompt_example: Fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment, the scene as shards. List the shards in causal order and name the missing master.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Quick Cuts of the same complete wide, or a Collage texture. The tell: a master already shows the whole, or the pieces have no direction.
The fix: withhold the complete contact, keep a causal line, let sound and order finish the blow in the viewer's head.
faq: What is Fragments in film?
Fragmented editing constructs an event from partial views. Each side of a join is a shard; the audience infers an action more complete than any single shot.
Fragments vs Quick Cuts
Quick cuts are short complete views in a rhythm. Fragments are incomplete views of one event. Speed is not the definition; withholding the whole is.
When should I use Fragments?
Use it when the blow should be inferred: violence, panic, a night that will not assemble. Do not use it when a continuous demonstration is required.
How do I prompt Fragments for AI image or video?

List the shards and what is missing. Example: Fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment. Keep causal order and a binding sound; forbid a complete master of the contact.

name: Rain
definition: Rain in film is falling water that makes air visible as streaks and turns the ground into a mirror. Drops are matter in the optical path; without backlight they vanish, and without a wet-down the street stays dry under a fake storm.
narrative: Silver needles between a lamp and the lens. Shoulders darken.
Puddles double the neon. Weather is percussion you can see.
Make the air visible and the ground reflective. Use it when the scene must be wet in depth, not only on a window pane.
It is the wrong tool when you only need specular streets at night with no falling drops: that is a Wet-Down. It is also the wrong tool when you want a still veil that hides geography: that is Fog.
Rain against a bright overcast sky reads as nothing. Put a light behind the drops, toward camera, or lose the storm.
how_it_works:
Put water in the air (rain bars, towers, or a real front) and light it from behind or the side so droplets scatter toward the lens. Keep a darkish background so streaks separate.
Wet the ground even if the rain is light. Shutter angle controls streak length versus beads.
Prompt: heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion.
when_to_use:
Use it for a night street, a rooftop, a prison yard, any beat that needs falling water as a layer. Do not use it as a grade or as window tracks only.
If the air is empty and the asphalt is merely shiny, you shot a wet-down.
compared_names: Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
compared_text: A Wet-Down soaks surfaces so lights double; it need not rain. Atmospheric Haze is a distant scatter, not falling drops.
Snow is ice that settles and accumulates. Fog is a local veil that hides figures.
Rain falls, streaks when backlit, and leaves the ground wet.
Wet-DownNight exteriors that must sparkle.
Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
FogHide geography. Delay the reveal.
in_film: Blade Runner builds night as backlit rain and reflective streets. Seven uses rain as a constant layer over investigation.
The Shawshank Redemption lets a yard storm become a body-length release. Use drop, backlight, and wet ground, not a copied coat.
prompt_template: Heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion. Name the backlight (a streetlamp, a sign, a HMI behind the rain), the wet ground, and drop size.
prompt_example: Heavy cinematic rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, umbrellas, silver streaks, weather as percussion.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Wet-Down (shiny street, empty air) or a blue LUT called rain. The tell: no streaks against lamps, dry shoulders, no puddles.
The fix: put drops in the air, backlight them, wet the ground.
faq: What is Rain in film?
Rain is falling water used as visible matter: backlit streaks in the air and reflective ground. Both the optical path and the pavement have to be wet.
Rain vs Wet-Down
A wet-down sprays surfaces so night lights specularize, often with no weather in the air. Rain adds falling drops. You usually wet-down under rain; you can wet-down without rain.
When should I use Rain?
Use it when air must streak and ground must mirror. Do not use it if you only need a shiny street, and do not expect rain to read against a bright empty sky without backlight.
How do I prompt Rain for AI image or video?

Name backlit drops and wet ground. Example: heavy rain around [Subject], backlit drops, wet-down pavement, silver streaks. Specify the lamp behind the rain and forbid dry asphalt.

name: Fog
definition: Fog is a dense local suspension of water droplets that collapses depth, turns lamps into globes, and delays the reveal of figures. The air is matter close to camera; geography hides until someone walks into the last few meters.
narrative: A sodium lamp becomes a ball. A platform ends in nothing.
A coat arrives late, as if the world were only as large as a flashlight. Hide geography.
Delay the reveal. Use it for horror, docks, London streets, any beat that should withhold the next plane.
It is the wrong tool when you still want kilometers of readable landscape: that is Atmospheric Haze. It is the wrong tool when the veil is thin and lyrical: that is Mist.
Combustion with a source is Smoke. If faces at three meters are crisp and only the grade is grey, you do not have fog.
You have a LUT.
how_it_works:
Fill a volume with dense droplets (machines or weather) so contrast falls with distance on a short scale. Backlight or sidelight the fog to make globes around practicals; front light flattens it to milk.
Keep practicals inside the soup, not only a filter on the lens. Prompt: dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late, horror or London grammar.
when_to_use:
Use it when a figure should appear late, a road should end in white, a house should have no yard. Do not use it on a vista you still need to read.
If the far ridge must stay a ridge, use haze or mist.
compared_names: MistSofter mystery than fog. Lyric, not monster.
Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
RainMake the air visible and the ground reflective.
compared_text: Mist is thinner: layered, see-through, lyric. Atmospheric Haze stacks paler planes over kilometers, not a wall at ten meters.
Smoke has a source and a direction and is not weather. Steam rises from heat and thins as it cools.
Fog is a local, dense water veil.
MistSofter mystery than fog. Lyric, not monster.
Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
RainMake the air visible and the ground reflective.
in_film: The Exorcist and The Others use fog to withhold houses, lamps, and bodies. Sicario lets dust and fog-like veils erase desert edges (a cousin in opacity).
Use delayed reveal and globes around lamps, not a copied graveyard.
prompt_template: Dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late. Name density (visibility in meters), the practicals blooming, and what is hidden.
prompt_example: Dense fog around [Subject], depth collapsing, lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late, horror or London grammar.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Atmospheric Haze (distance) or a desaturated grade. The tell: sharp buildings a block away, lamps with no globes, faces fully lit at thirty meters.
The fix: short visibility, backlit bloom on lights, late arrivals.
faq: What is Fog in film?
Fog is a dense local cloud of water droplets that hides depth. Lamps bloom into globes and figures appear only when they enter the near ground.
Fog vs Mist
Fog is opaque enough to collapse geography at short range. Mist is thinner, layered, and still lets you read the next plane. Fog withholds; mist veils.
When should I use Fog?
Use it to hide geography and delay a reveal. Do not use it when you need a long, readable landscape, and do not fake it with a grey LUT.

Name the soup and the bloom. Example: dense fog around [Subject], lamps becoming globes, figures appearing late. Give a short visibility distance and forbid crisp far detail.

name: Mist
definition: Mist is a thinner water suspension than fog: pale layered air that still lets you read the next plane. Droplets are matter, but the veil is lyric, a morning or mountain breath rather than a wall.
narrative: Ridges stack as paler copies of themselves. A horse is readable, then a second ridge, then a paler third.
Softer mystery than fog. Lyric, not monster.
Use it for dawn, river valleys, high cold air, a courtyard that should glow rather than vanish. It is the wrong tool when a killer should appear at two meters with no yard behind them: that is Fog.
It is the wrong tool when the paleness is only far, far away over desert: that is Atmospheric Haze. If you cannot see the subject at all, you overshot into fog.
If every plane is equally sharp, you have no mist.
how_it_works:
Use a light density of droplets or a real inversion layer. Backlight the layers so each plane separates (aerial perspective at short-to-medium range).
Keep contrast on the near subject; let receding planes lift in value and lose saturation. Prompt: light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air.
when_to_use:
Use it for a hunt at dawn, a mountain pass, a wet garden. Do not use it as horror soup, and do not fill an interior with it unless the windows are open on a cold morning.
Interiors with volume are often Smoke or haze juice, not mist.
compared_names: Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
RainMake the air visible and the ground reflective.
compared_text: Fog hides. Atmospheric Haze is scattering over long distance, often without local wetness on skin.
Smoke has a source. Rain falls.
Mist hangs, layers, and remains see-through at working distance.
FogHide geography. Delay the reveal.
Atmospheric HazeShow kilometers, not just meters.
RainMake the air visible and the ground reflective.
in_film: The Revenant uses morning and mountain moisture as stacked pale planes around bodies. Raise the Red Lantern lets courtyard air go milky without erasing architecture.
Use layered breath, not a white-out.
prompt_template: Light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air. Name near-subject readability, paler far planes, and a backlight or low sun.
prompt_example: Light mist around [Subject], softer than fog, morning or mountain breath, layers of pale air.
mistakes:
The usual wrong cousin is Fog (too dense) or Atmospheric Haze (only the horizon pales). The tell: the hero vanishes, or only the skyline is pale while mid-ground is hard.
The fix: keep the subject readable, stack two or three paler planes, backlight the moisture.
faq: What is Mist in film?
Mist is a light suspension of water droplets that layers the air without erasing the subject. It is thicker than clear air and thinner than fog.
Mist vs Fog
Fog collapses depth at short range and delays figures. Mist leaves the near ground readable and stacks pale planes. One is a wall; the other is breath.
When should I use Mist?
Use it for morning, mountains, and lyric distance at human scale. Do not use it when geography must disappear for a scare.

name: Ocean
definition: Ocean cinematography treats the sea as the other actor: swell, a horizon, salt light, a person against water that does not care. The atmosphere is spray, haze over distance, and a moving floor; the camera is in air, on a hull, or on rocks, not yet in the lung of the sea.
narrative: A mole, a boat, a body: small. The horizon is a line that can kill you.
Swell has a period. Salt in backlight is weather.
The sea is the other actor. Use it for exile, work, awe, war at the rail.
It is the wrong tool when you have left the surface (Underwater). It is the wrong tool when the water is a still lake used as silk behind a posed figure.
If there is no swell and no scale, it is not ocean. A bathtub, a pool, a harbor with no fetch: different jobs.
Name the swell.
how_it_works:
Shoot wide enough for scale. Put real swell in the frame (period, whitecaps or long rollers).
Backlight spray. Let far water go paler with Atmospheric Haze.
Keep the human or boat small unless the story is a face against a rail. Practical water on lens is allowed; fake silk water is not.

If the camera goes under, switch techniques.
